title: GitHub Copilot Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Is GitHub Copilot worth it in 2026? A hands-on look at pricing tiers, agent mode, code review, and who each plan actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is GitHub Copilot worth it in 2026?

GitHub Copilot is a solid AI pair-programmer for most developers, especially anyone already living inside VS Code or a JetBrains IDE. The free tier is genuinely usable for light work, but the $10/month Pro plan is where it earns its keep — unlimited completions plus agent-mode tasks that go beyond autocomplete. Teams needing governance controls should look at Business or Enterprise instead.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free (limited); $10/month for Pro |
| **Free tier** | 2,000 code completions/month, limited chat |
| **Best for** | Individual developers and small teams already on GitHub |
| **Standout feature** | Agent mode — autonomous multi-file coding tasks, not just autocomplete |

GitHub Copilot is built by GitHub in partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft. It's the AI coding assistant most developers meet first, mainly because it's baked directly into GitHub.com, VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Xcode, Neovim, and the command line via Copilot CLI. It started as a glorified autocomplete in 2021 and has since grown into something closer to a junior engineer you can assign tasks to.

## What GitHub Copilot actually is

At its core, Copilot suggests code as you type, based on the surrounding file, open tabs, and (on paid plans) broader repository context. GitHub says it was trained on natural language and public source code, and today it routes requests across multiple large language models rather than relying on one. Depending on your plan, you can pick between models like GPT-5 mini, Claude, and Anthropic's Opus family, or let Copilot auto-select the model for a given task.

The bigger shift over the past couple of years is **agent mode**. Instead of only completing the line you're on, you can hand Copilot a task — "add pagination to this API," "fix the failing test in this file" — and it will explore the codebase, make edits across multiple files, run commands, and open a pull request for review. GitHub also added a **Copilot code review** feature that comments on pull requests the way a human reviewer would, and a **Copilot CLI** for running agent tasks from the terminal instead of an IDE.

## GitHub Copilot pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date (see below) and can change — check GitHub's official [Copilot plans page](https://github.com/features/copilot/plans) before buying, since AI coding tool pricing and usage limits move quickly.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/month | 2,000 completions/month, limited chat, access to a smaller model set, Copilot CLI, community support |
| Pro | $10/month | Unlimited code completions, chat, agent mode access, code review, third-party agent integration, $15 of monthly AI credits |
| Pro+ | $39/month | Everything in Pro, plus premium model access (including Opus-tier models), audit logs, and roughly 4x the usage allowance of Pro |
| Business | $19/user/month | Org-wide policy management, IP indemnification, and centralized billing on top of Pro-level features |
| Enterprise | $39/user/month | Custom knowledge-base indexing over private repos, fine-tuned models, and enterprise governance controls |

GitHub also sells a **Max** individual tier at roughly $100/month aimed at developers running sustained, high-volume agent workflows, with a larger monthly AI-credit allowance than Pro+. Most solo developers and small teams will land on Pro or Pro+ rather than Max or the org-level tiers.

There's no matching store entry for GitHub Copilot on this site yet, so there's no coupon-page link to include here — GitHub doesn't run discount codes for Copilot subscriptions anyway; student and open-source maintainer accounts get free Pro access instead, which is worth checking if you qualify.

## Features that actually differentiate it

**Inline completions in real IDEs.** This isn't unique to Copilot anymore, but it remains the most polished version of it. Suggestions show up as you type, and "next edit suggestions" try to predict the next change you'll make elsewhere in the file, not just at the cursor.

**Agent mode for multi-file tasks.** Rather than babysitting every line, you can describe a task and let Copilot plan, search the repo, and make coordinated edits. GitHub's own framing is that you can "assign tasks to agents like Copilot, Claude by Anthropic, and OpenAI Codex" and let them work semi-autonomously — a meaningfully different workflow than pure autocomplete tools.

**Copilot code review.** It reviews pull requests inline on GitHub, flagging potential bugs or style issues before a human reviewer even opens the diff. Useful on small teams without a dedicated senior reviewer for every PR.

**Model choice.** Paid plans let you switch between multiple underlying models depending on whether you want speed, lower cost, or higher-effort reasoning for a given task, instead of being locked to one vendor's model.

**Deep GitHub integration.** Copilot Chat can reference issues, pull requests, and GitHub Actions workflows directly, which tools bolted onto an editor from outside the GitHub ecosystem can't match as cleanly.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo developers and hobbyists**: the Free tier's 2,000 completions/month is enough for casual side-project work, but anyone coding daily will hit the ceiling fast and want Pro.
- **Professional individual developers**: Pro at $10/month is the sweet spot — unlimited completions, agent mode, and code review cover most day-to-day needs without paying for premium-model overage.
- **Power users on agentic workflows**: developers running long agent sessions (large refactors, generating and iterating on whole features) will burn through Pro's credit allowance and should budget for Pro+ or Max.
- **Small teams**: Business adds policy controls (blocking public-code suggestions, managing seats centrally) without full enterprise overhead — a reasonable middle ground.
- **Regulated or large organizations**: Enterprise is built for private-repo indexing, IP indemnification at scale, and audit requirements that Business doesn't fully cover.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Deep, native integration with GitHub and major IDEs | Premium/agent usage can burn through credits fast on Pro |
| Agent mode handles real multi-file tasks, not just line completions | Free tier's 2,000 completions/month is limiting for daily use |
| Multiple model choices instead of a single vendor lock-in | Suggestions can be confidently wrong on unfamiliar frameworks or niche languages |
| Code review feature catches issues before a human reviewer does | Enterprise-grade governance requires the priciest tier |
| Student and open-source maintainer programs offer free Pro access | No official discount codes/coupons outside those programs |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Copilot works inside VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, etc.), Xcode, Neovim, Eclipse, and directly on github.com's pull request and issue views. Copilot CLI brings agent tasks to the terminal for developers who don't want to leave a shell session. There's no public general-purpose API for third-party apps to call Copilot directly the way you'd call an LLM API — it's designed to be used through GitHub's own surfaces rather than embedded into arbitrary external products. Enterprise plans support connecting private knowledge bases and internal documentation so suggestions can reference internal APIs, not just public code patterns.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Teams and individuals already working primarily in GitHub repos, where Copilot's context (issues, PRs, Actions) adds real value beyond a generic autocomplete.
- Developers who want to delegate well-scoped, mechanical tasks (adding tests, fixing a known bug, updating a dependency's usage across files) to an agent instead of doing it by hand.
- Anyone who wants model flexibility instead of being tied to a single AI vendor's coding assistant.

## Where to think twice

- If you need a **fully free** tool for serious daily use, the Free tier's completion cap will frustrate you quickly — budget for Pro.
- If your organization needs **strict compliance/audit tooling** (SOC 2-style governance, fine-tuned private models), you'll need Enterprise, not Pro or Business, and that's a real budget jump.
- If you work heavily in a **niche language or framework** with little public training data, expect more hallucinated or subtly wrong suggestions — always review agent-generated diffs before merging.
- If you want **offline or fully on-prem** inference for air-gapped environments, Copilot isn't built for that; it's a cloud service even on Enterprise.
- If you're deep in the OpenAI Codex CLI or Anthropic Claude Code ecosystem already, switching may mean relearning workflow habits rather than gaining new capability — the underlying models overlap more than the branding suggests.

## The bottom line

GitHub Copilot has grown from a clever autocomplete into a genuinely capable coding agent, and for developers who already live in GitHub's ecosystem, it's hard to beat on convenience alone. Pro at $10/month covers most individual needs comfortably; Pro+ and Max exist for people running heavier agent workloads who'll actually use the extra credits. The main thing to budget for isn't the sticker price — it's how fast agent-mode usage can eat through the included AI credits once you move past simple autocomplete into multi-file task delegation. Review what it generates before merging, especially outside mainstream languages, and it's a reasonable default choice for most teams.

[Try GitHub Copilot](/go/offer/github-copilot)

## Frequently asked questions

**Is GitHub Copilot free?**
There's a genuinely free tier with 2,000 completions per month and limited chat access, but most developers coding daily will outgrow it and move to the $10/month Pro plan.

**Do students get GitHub Copilot for free?**
Yes — verified students and maintainers of popular open-source projects can get free access to Copilot Pro through GitHub's Education and open-source programs; check eligibility on GitHub's site since terms can change.

**What AI models does GitHub Copilot use?**
GitHub says Copilot routes across multiple models depending on plan and task, including options like GPT-5 mini and Claude-family models, with premium tiers unlocking access to higher-effort models such as Opus-tier options.

**Does GitHub Copilot store or train on my private code?**
GitHub states that Copilot Business and Enterprise do not use customer code snippets to train the underlying models; specifics on data retention and training policy differ by plan, so review GitHub's current trust center documentation before using it on sensitive proprietary code.

**Is GitHub Copilot good for beginners?**
It can help beginners see working code patterns quickly, but relying on it too early can short-circuit learning fundamentals — it's more valuable once you already understand what "correct" code should look like so you can catch its mistakes.

**How is Copilot different from ChatGPT or Claude for coding?**
Copilot is purpose-built into your IDE and GitHub workflow (PRs, issues, Actions), while general chat tools like ChatGPT or Claude's own coding tools are more general-purpose and need to be copy-pasted into your workflow unless you're using their dedicated coding products.

**Can I cancel GitHub Copilot anytime?**
Yes — paid plans are monthly (or annual, at a discount) subscriptions managed through your GitHub billing settings, and you can downgrade to Free at any time.

**What's the difference between Copilot Business and Enterprise?**
Business focuses on org-wide policy and billing controls at $19/user/month; Enterprise, at $39/user/month, adds private-repo knowledge indexing and deeper governance/compliance features aimed at larger organizations.

Looking at other AI tools for your workflow? Browse more [AI & software deals](/category/software) for additional reviews and coupons.

title: ChatGPT Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Is ChatGPT worth paying for in 2026? A hands-on look at pricing tiers, GPT-6 Astra, features, limitations and who should upgrade.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is ChatGPT still worth it in 2026?

Yes, for most people — the free tier alone handles everyday research, writing and coding help, and the $20/month Plus plan adds OpenAI's current flagship model, image generation and much higher usage limits. It's the most broadly useful AI assistant on the market, though power users doing heavy daily work will bump into limits fast.

**At a glance**

| | ChatGPT |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (Plus from $20/month) |
| Free tier | Yes — limited daily messages, older/lighter model access |
| Best for | General research, writing, coding help, brainstorming |
| Standout feature | GPT-6 Astra reasoning + built-in web search, image generation and code execution in one interface |

ChatGPT is OpenAI's consumer-facing chatbot, and it's the product that put "AI assistant" into daily vocabulary for millions of people back in late 2022. It's built on OpenAI's GPT family of large language models — currently headlined by **GPT-6 Astra**, the flagship model OpenAI rolled out starting in September 2026, following GPT-4o and the o-series reasoning models. Free-tier users still get routed to lighter, older models with tighter usage caps; paid tiers get priority access to the current flagship as it becomes available.

## Pricing: what you actually get at each tier

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | Limited daily messages, access to a lighter model, basic web search and image generation with caps |
| Go | ~$4–8/month (region-priced, e.g. ₹399/month in India) | Higher message limits than Free, still capped, available in select markets |
| Plus | $20/month | Extended access to the current flagship model, higher limits, image generation, voice mode, custom GPTs, Advanced Voice |
| Pro | $200/month | Near-unlimited flagship model access, higher-compute reasoning modes, priority access to new features first |
| Team | ~$25–30/user/month (billed annually, 2-seat minimum) | Everything in Plus, shared workspace, admin controls, no training on workspace data by default |
| Business / Enterprise | Custom pricing | SSO, SCIM, higher context windows, dedicated support, enterprise data controls, custom retention policies |

A quick note on the numbers above: OpenAI has changed ChatGPT's plan lineup more than once since 2023 (Go, Pro and Team were all added after the original Free/Plus split), and per-seat Team/Business pricing is the kind of detail that shifts. Treat the Team and Business figures as directional, and confirm live numbers on OpenAI's [pricing page](https://openai.com/chatgpt/pricing) before buying — accurate as of this post's publish date, but AI tool pricing moves fast.

## Core features that actually matter

**Model quality and reasoning.** The headline reason people pay for Plus or Pro is model access — free users get routed to older or lighter models with tighter caps, while paid tiers get the current flagship (GPT-6 Astra as of late 2026) with materially better reasoning, coding and multi-step task handling. For anything beyond casual Q&A — debugging real code, working through a multi-step analysis, drafting something that needs to hold together across a long conversation — the model tier you're on matters more than almost any other setting.

**Built-in web search.** ChatGPT Search pulls live results into a conversation instead of relying purely on training data, with citations to source pages. It's not a replacement for a dedicated search engine, but it closes a lot of the "this info might be stale" gap that plagued earlier versions.

**Image generation and editing.** OpenAI folded its image model directly into the chat interface, so you can ask for an image, iterate on it conversationally ("make the background darker," "add text here"), and generate variations without switching tools. It's convenient rather than best-in-class — dedicated image generators still edge it out on fine control.

**Custom GPTs and Projects.** Paid users can build reusable custom assistants (a fixed prompt, specific instructions, sometimes custom actions) and organize related conversations, files and instructions into Projects. This is the feature that turns ChatGPT from "a chat box" into something closer to a lightweight workflow tool, especially for recurring tasks like reviewing the same type of document repeatedly.

**Voice and multimodal input.** Advanced Voice Mode lets you have a live spoken conversation with natural interruption handling, and the app accepts photos, screenshots and documents as input. It's genuinely useful for anything hands-busy (cooking, driving, walking through a problem out loud) rather than typing.

**Code execution and data analysis.** The advanced data analysis tool runs actual Python in a sandbox — upload a spreadsheet and ask it to clean, chart or summarize the data, and it writes and executes the code rather than just describing what code would do.

## Who ChatGPT is actually for

- **Casual users and students** — the free tier covers homework help, résumé edits, and everyday research without paying anything, though you'll hit message caps during heavy use periods.
- **Solo professionals and freelancers** — Plus at $20/month is the sweet spot: enough usage headroom for daily writing, coding assistance and research, plus custom GPTs for repeatable tasks.
- **Power users and developers** — Pro's $200/month is steep for casual use but makes sense if you're running long reasoning sessions or heavy coding workloads daily and keep hitting Plus limits.
- **Small teams** — Team gives you a shared workspace with admin controls and a default no-training-on-your-data policy, useful once more than one or two people at a company are using it for work.
- **Companies with compliance needs** — Business/Enterprise adds SSO, SCIM provisioning and enterprise-grade data controls, which is the tier IT and security teams will actually sign off on.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free tier is genuinely usable, not just a trial gimmick | Free and Go tiers get capped and routed to lighter models during busy periods |
| Broadest general-purpose feature set of any AI assistant (search, images, voice, code) | Pro at $200/month is a big jump for anyone who isn't a heavy daily user |
| Custom GPTs and Projects add real workflow structure | Still hallucinates confidently-wrong answers, especially on niche or fast-changing topics |
| Frequent model and feature updates, often first-to-market | Team/Business pricing and seat minimums make it awkward for very small teams |
| Mobile, desktop and web apps all stay in sync | Heavy users report the interface getting cluttered as more features (GPTs, Projects, search, voice) pile in |

## Integrations and ecosystem

ChatGPT ships with an official API separate from the consumer subscription, priced per token and billed independently — useful for building ChatGPT-style features into your own product. Beyond the API, OpenAI supports:

- **Custom GPTs and Actions** — connect a custom GPT to external APIs so it can fetch live data or trigger actions mid-conversation
- **Plugins/connectors** for services like Google Drive on higher tiers, letting ChatGPT reference your own files
- **Zapier and third-party integrations** — not built by OpenAI directly, but widely available through automation platforms that treat the API as a connectable app
- **Desktop and mobile apps** for macOS, Windows, iOS and Android, syncing history across devices

If you're evaluating ChatGPT specifically because of interest in OpenAI's newest model, see our breakdown of [how to use GPT-6 Astra for free](/blog/how-to-use-gpt-6-astra-for-free) — it covers which plans include Astra automatically and the legitimate ways to try it without a full subscription.

## Where it's a strong fit

ChatGPT earns its reputation as the default AI assistant for a reason: it's the most feature-complete single tool for general knowledge work, and the free tier means there's essentially no cost to trying it seriously before deciding whether to pay. If your work mixes writing, research, light coding and the occasional data question, one subscription covers all of it instead of stitching together separate tools. It's also a strong fit if you value being first to new capabilities — OpenAI tends to ship new features (voice modes, search, image tools, agentic browsing) to ChatGPT before or alongside its API.

## Where to think twice

Skip Plus or Pro if you need a fully free tool and your usage fits comfortably inside the free tier's caps — there's no reason to pay if you're not hitting limits. Skip ChatGPT generally if your organization needs strict on-prem or fully offline deployment, since there's no self-hosted version; everything runs through OpenAI's cloud, even on Enterprise. Think twice if your team needs SOC 2 or similar compliance documentation locked in before rollout — Business/Enterprise offers enterprise data controls, but get your own compliance/legal review of the current terms rather than taking a marketing page at face value. And if accuracy on narrow, fast-changing, or technical subject matter is critical, don't treat any ChatGPT answer as verified fact — it still generates confident-sounding errors, and web search reduces but doesn't eliminate that risk.

## The bottom line

ChatGPT remains the easiest on-ramp into AI assistance because the free tier is actually usable and the paid tiers scale sensibly from casual power user ($20) up to genuine enterprise deployment (custom pricing). It's not the cheapest option in every category — dedicated writing tools can out-format it, dedicated image generators can out-render it, and dedicated coding assistants can out-code it in their narrow lanes — but as a single generalist tool that most people will actually open every day, it's hard to beat. Start free, upgrade to Plus the moment you're hitting daily limits, and only look at Pro if $200/month buys back more time than it costs.

[Try ChatGPT](/go/offer/chatgpt)

## FAQ

**Is ChatGPT free to use?**
Yes, there's a genuine free tier with no time limit, though it caps daily messages and routes you to a lighter model rather than OpenAI's current flagship.

**What's the difference between ChatGPT Plus and Pro?**
Plus ($20/month) gives extended access to the current flagship model with day-to-day usage limits; Pro ($200/month) removes most of those limits and adds priority access to higher-compute reasoning modes and new features first.

**Does OpenAI train its models on my conversations?**
Free and Plus users can opt out of having conversations used for training in settings; Team, Business and Enterprise plans exclude your data from training by default. Always check OpenAI's current privacy settings and data controls before assuming a specific policy, since these have changed over time.

**Can I use ChatGPT for coding?**
Yes — it can write, explain and debug code across most common languages, and the data analysis tool actually executes Python. It's genuinely useful for boilerplate, debugging and learning, but treat generated code the way you'd treat a junior developer's first draft: review it before shipping.

**What is GPT-6 Astra?**
It's OpenAI's current flagship model as of late 2026, included on Plus, Pro, Team and Business/Enterprise plans within their usage allowances. See our guide on [using GPT-6 Astra for free](/blog/how-to-use-gpt-6-astra-for-free) for the legitimate ways to access it without a full subscription.

**What are the main alternatives to ChatGPT?**
Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude, and Microsoft Copilot are the closest general-purpose competitors, each with different strengths in reasoning style, context window size and platform integration. Which one wins depends heavily on which ecosystem (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or standalone) you're already using.

**Is ChatGPT beginner-friendly?**
Yes — the chat interface requires no setup or technical knowledge to start. The learning curve shows up later, once you want to use custom GPTs, Projects, or the API, which take more effort to configure well.

**Does ChatGPT have a mobile app?**
Yes, official apps exist for iOS and Android with conversation history synced to the web and desktop versions.

For more AI and software coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Claude AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Claude AI review 2026: pricing (Free, Pro, Max), Claude Code, Artifacts, 200K context, pros/cons, and who Anthropic's assistant is really for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Claude a good AI assistant in 2026?

Claude, made by Anthropic, is one of the strongest general-purpose AI assistants for writing, coding, and long-document analysis, with a free tier that's genuinely usable and a Pro plan ($17–20/month) that unlocks Claude Code and higher usage caps. It's not the cheapest or the most feature-loaded chatbot, but its reasoning quality and 200K-token context window are hard to beat.

| At a glance | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free; Pro from $17/month (billed annually) |
| Free tier limits | Chat, web search, Artifacts, up to 5 Projects, capped daily messages |
| Best for | Writing, coding, research, and long-document work |
| Standout feature | Claude Code + Artifacts for building and previewing real output inline |

## What Claude actually is

Claude is Anthropic's family of large language models and the chat app, browser extensions, desktop/mobile apps, and developer API built around them. Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI researchers and has positioned Claude around what it calls "Constitutional AI" — training the model against a written set of principles rather than relying only on human feedback, with the stated goal of making outputs more predictable and less prone to harmful or evasive answers.

The current lineup spans a range of model sizes under the Claude naming scheme, from fast, lower-cost models built for high-volume tasks up to flagship models tuned for deep reasoning, coding, and "extended thinking" — a mode where the model spends more computation reasoning through a problem before answering. Anthropic doesn't publish full architecture details (parameter counts, training data composition), which is standard across major labs but worth naming plainly rather than treating vendor capability claims as verified fact.

Where Claude tends to distinguish itself is at longer context lengths (a 200,000-token window on paid tiers, per Anthropic's documentation) and in code generation and editing — Claude Code, Anthropic's terminal/IDE-integrated coding agent, has become a significant part of the product's identity, not just an add-on chat feature.

## Claude pricing

Claude uses a tiered subscription model similar to other major chat assistants, plus a separate usage-based API for developers who want to build Claude into their own products.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/month | Web, desktop, and mobile chat; web search; file creation and code execution; Artifacts and memory; up to 5 Projects; capped message limits |
| Pro | $17/month billed annually, or $20/month billed monthly | Everything in Free, plus higher usage limits, Claude Code, unlimited Projects, access to more models, and Chrome/Microsoft 365 extensions |
| Max | From $100/month | Everything in Pro, plus a choice of 5x or 20x Pro's usage allowance, higher output limits, and priority access during peak load |
| Team | $20–25/seat/month (standard), $100–125/seat/month (premium) | Central billing, admin controls, SSO, and enterprise search on top of individual-plan features |
| Enterprise | $20/seat/month plus API-rate usage charges | SCIM, audit logs, custom data retention, role-based access, and a HIPAA-ready configuration |

There's no store coupon page for Claude on this site yet, so treat the figures above as sourced directly from Anthropic's own pricing page rather than a discounted or affiliate rate.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability above were accurate as of this post's publish date and can shift — Anthropic has changed plan structure and usage caps more than once, so it's worth checking the [official pricing page](https://claude.com/pricing) before you commit to an annual plan.

One practical wrinkle: usage limits on every tier, including Max, reset on rolling five-hour windows with a weekly cap layered on top for paid plans. That's meaningfully different from a flat monthly message count, and it means heavy users can still hit a wall mid-session on a paid plan.

## Core features that actually differentiate Claude

**Extended thinking.** On its higher-tier models, Claude can be told to reason step by step before producing a final answer, effectively trading response latency for better performance on math, logic, and multi-step coding problems. This isn't unique to Claude, but Anthropic has built it in as a first-class toggle rather than a separate product tier.

**Artifacts.** When Claude generates something substantial — a code snippet, a webpage, a document, a diagram — it renders that output in a separate panel you can view, edit, and iterate on live, instead of scrolling through a wall of chat text. For anyone prototyping a small app, drafting a structured document, or building a quick data visualization, this is a genuinely different interaction model from a plain chat thread.

**Claude Code.** This is Anthropic's agentic coding tool that runs in a terminal or IDE, capable of reading a codebase, planning multi-file changes, running commands, and iterating based on the results — rather than just answering isolated code questions in a chat window. It's included with Pro and up, and has become one of the more talked-about products in the current wave of AI coding agents, largely because it operates directly on a real project rather than a sandboxed snippet.

**Long context and document handling.** A 200,000-token context window (roughly 500 pages of text) means Claude can hold an entire codebase or a long contract in a single conversation without re-pasting sections. This matters for research, contract review, and technical documentation, where losing earlier context mid-conversation is a real cost.

**Projects.** Projects let you group a set of files, custom instructions, and chat threads around a specific piece of work — a client, a codebase, a research topic — so Claude has persistent context without you re-explaining the setup every time. Free accounts get up to 5 Projects; Pro and above get unlimited.

## Who Claude is actually for

- **Solo writers and researchers** get a capable free tier with Artifacts and a handful of Projects — enough to draft, revise, and organize ongoing work without paying, as long as message volume stays modest.
- **Developers and technical teams** are the clearest case for Pro or Max: Claude Code plus higher usage caps and more model access turns Claude into a working coding assistant rather than an occasional chatbot, and the jump to Max mainly buys headroom for teams that hit rate limits on Pro.
- **Small businesses and agencies** fit the Team plan, which adds seat management and central billing without the compliance overhead of Enterprise — useful once more than a couple of people need shared access and admin visibility.
- **Regulated industries and larger organizations** are the target for Enterprise, where SCIM, audit logs, custom data retention, and a HIPAA-ready configuration matter more than any single feature in the chat interface itself.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Strong reasoning and coding performance, especially in Claude Code | No flat unlimited tier — even Max has rolling usage windows |
| Large 200K-token context window on paid plans | Fewer built-in multimedia features (image/video generation) than some competitors |
| Artifacts make iterative building and editing genuinely easier than plain chat | Free tier message caps can feel tight for daily heavy use |
| Free tier is functional, not just a demo | Anthropic doesn't publish full model architecture or training data details |
| Enterprise-grade compliance options (SOC 2, HIPAA-ready, audit logs) | Team/Enterprise pricing requires annual billing, less flexible for small orgs testing the waters |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Claude ships browser extensions for Chrome and connectors for Microsoft 365, letting it read and act on content inside those apps for Pro subscribers and up. Anthropic's developer API is the broader integration path — it powers Claude inside a growing number of third-party coding tools, writing apps, and support platforms, and it supports function calling and tool use for developers who want Claude to call external APIs or run code as part of a response. There's no native Zapier-style no-code hub built by Anthropic itself, but Claude is reachable through Zapier's own AI-app connectors and through the API directly.

## Where Claude is a strong fit

Claude tends to earn its subscription price in a few recurring situations: reviewing or drafting long documents where context length matters, coding work where Claude Code's ability to operate across a real project saves time, and workflows where a wrong answer is costly enough that careful, hedged reasoning is worth a slower response. Teams already inside Microsoft 365 or needing HIPAA-ready compliance also get more out of Claude's plan structure than a generic chatbot subscription.

## Where to think twice

Claude isn't the right pick if you need a fully free, unmetered tool — the free tier's daily caps will frustrate primary-tool use, and even Max's higher allowance is still capped on a rolling window rather than unlimited. If your priority is image or video generation, Claude's multimedia capabilities lag behind assistants built around those use cases. And if you're comparing on raw plugin/app-store breadth, Claude's ecosystem is smaller and leans more on its own API than on a marketplace of add-ons. Teams needing offline or on-premises deployment should also look elsewhere — Claude is cloud-hosted only.

## The bottom line

Claude earns its reputation on reasoning quality, context length, and Claude Code rather than on being the flashiest or cheapest option in the category. The free tier is enough to seriously evaluate it before paying anything, and Pro at $17–20/month is a reasonable jump for regular coding or long-document work. It falls short on multimedia generation and the rolling usage-window model that still caps paying users — worth testing your workload against the free tier's limits before assuming a paid plan removes friction entirely.

[Try Claude](/go/offer/claude)

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Claude free to use?**
Yes. Anthropic offers a free tier with web, desktop, and mobile chat, Artifacts, up to 5 Projects, and capped daily/session message limits. It's usable for regular light-to-moderate use, but heavy users will likely hit rate limits.

**How much does Claude Pro cost?**
Claude Pro costs $17/month billed annually or $20/month billed monthly, based on Anthropic's published pricing as of this post's date. It adds Claude Code, unlimited Projects, higher usage limits, and access to more models.

**What is Claude Code?**
Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool that runs in a terminal or IDE. It can read a codebase, plan and make multi-file changes, run commands, and iterate on the results, rather than just answering standalone code questions in chat. It's included with Pro and higher plans.

**Does Claude have a usage limit even on paid plans?**
Yes. All plans, including Max, use rolling five-hour usage windows with an additional weekly cap on paid tiers, rather than a flat unlimited allowance. Max buys a 5x or 20x larger allowance than Pro, not unlimited use.

**How does Claude handle data privacy?**
Policies vary by tier — Enterprise adds custom data retention, audit logs, and a HIPAA-ready configuration, while consumer plans follow Anthropic's standard privacy policy. Confirm current terms on Anthropic's official privacy pages before handling sensitive or regulated data.

**What's the context window size on Claude?**
Paid Claude plans support a 200,000-token context window per Anthropic's documentation, letting it hold long documents or codebases in a single conversation without losing earlier context.

**Is Claude beginner-friendly?**
The core chat interface is straightforward and comparable to any other AI chatbot. Claude Code and the API have more of a learning curve, since they assume familiarity with a terminal, IDE, or basic development workflow.

**What are the main alternatives to Claude?**
The most commonly compared alternatives are OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini. ChatGPT leans on a larger plugin/app ecosystem, Gemini integrates tightly with Google Workspace, and Claude leans on reasoning quality and coding depth through Claude Code. For a related look at flagship-model access elsewhere, see this site's guide to [using GPT-6 Astra for free](/blog/how-to-use-gpt-6-astra-for-free).

title: Notion AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Notion AI review 2026: real pricing across Free, Plus, Business and Enterprise, AI Meeting Notes, Enterprise Search, and who it's actually worth it for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Notion AI Worth It in 2026?

Notion AI is worth it if you already live inside Notion for docs, wikis, or project tracking — the writing, search, and meeting-notes features save real time without leaving the app. It's a weaker pick if you want a standalone AI writer or chatbot, since most of its useful features now require the $20/seat Business plan rather than a cheap add-on.

**At a glance**

| | Details |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (limited AI trial); Plus at $10/seat/mo |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — Free plan includes a limited AI trial; no dedicated free AI tier beyond that |
| Best for | Teams and individuals already using Notion for docs, wikis, and project management |
| Standout feature | AI Meeting Notes + Enterprise Search bundled into the Business plan, working across Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub |

## What Notion AI Actually Is

Notion AI isn't a separate product you sign up for — it's a layer of AI features bolted onto the Notion workspace you already have (or would build from scratch). Notion, the company, builds it directly into the editor, the database views, and now a dedicated "Notion Agent" that can act across your workspace and connected apps.

Notion describes its own architecture as "model agnostic," meaning it routes requests across different underlying language models rather than committing to a single provider, and says this lets it switch models without losing workspace context. Notion doesn't publish which specific models power which feature, so treat that framing as the vendor's own description rather than a verified technical spec.

This matters for how you should think about it: you're not evaluating Notion AI as you would ChatGPT or Claude as a standalone assistant. You're evaluating whether the AI layered on top of Notion's docs, wikis, and databases is good enough to replace copy-pasting your notes into a separate chatbot tab.

## Notion Pricing (Including AI Access)

Notion restructured its plans in 2026 so AI features are tiered by plan rather than sold as a flat $8–10/user add-on, as in earlier years. As of this post's publish date, per-seat monthly pricing looks like this:

| Plan | Price (per seat/month) | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | Trial AI capabilities, basic forms/sites, Notion Calendar, databases with subtasks, up to 10 guests |
| Plus | $10 | Everything in Free, plus custom forms/sites, unlimited file uploads, basic app connections (Slack, Google Drive) |
| Business | $20 | Everything in Plus, plus Notion Agent, AI Meeting Notes, Enterprise Search (beta), SAML SSO, premium app connections (GitHub, Asana) |
| Enterprise | Custom | Everything in Business, plus zero data retention with LLM providers, SCIM provisioning, audit logs, dedicated customer success manager |

Notion also sells credit-based AI add-ons for power users: **Custom Agents** (automations you build yourself) run roughly $10 per 1,000 monthly Notion credits after a free trial, and a beta **Workers** feature follows a similar credit model. These sit apart from the writing/search AI bundled into Business and Enterprise.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability above were accurate as of this post's date (2026-09-18) and can change — Notion has adjusted its AI pricing structure more than once in the past two years, so confirm current numbers on [Notion's official pricing page](https://www.notion.com/pricing) before buying.

## Core Features Walkthrough

**In-line AI writing and editing.** Highlight any block of text and Notion AI can rewrite it, shorten it, fix grammar, change tone, or translate it, without leaving the page. This is the oldest and most reliable part of the product — it's essentially a well-integrated text-editing assistant sitting inside your existing docs.

**AI Meeting Notes.** Available from the Business plan up, this transcribes and summarizes meetings directly inside a Notion page — Notion says it works "right where you work" without requiring a separate meeting bot to join the call. For teams that already run standups and syncs logged in Notion, this removes a manual note-taking step entirely.

**Enterprise Search.** Still in beta at the time of writing, this lets you query across Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, and other connected tools from inside Notion's search bar, rather than tabbing between apps to find where a decision was made. It's the feature that most directly competes with dedicated AI search tools like Glean.

**Notion Agent and Custom Agents.** The Agent can create and edit pages or databases on your behalf using workspace context; Custom Agents extend that into scheduled or triggered automations (for example, auto-answering recurring Slack questions or routing incoming tasks). This is the newest and least proven part of the product — it's positioned closer to an autonomous assistant than a writing tool, and Notion's own credit-based pricing for it signals the company still expects usage to be metered carefully.

**Database autofill and AI formulas.** Inside Notion databases, AI can populate properties automatically (summarizing a linked doc into a status field, for instance) and help write formulas in plain language. It's a smaller feature but genuinely useful if you run project trackers or CRMs inside Notion.

## Who It's Actually For

- **Solo notetakers and freelancers** get some AI writing help on the Free plan, but the meaningful features (Meeting Notes, Enterprise Search) sit behind Business, which may be overkill if Notion is just a personal wiki.
- **Small teams already standardized on Notion** for docs and project tracking are the clearest fit — the $20/seat Business plan replaces a separate meeting-transcription tool and reduces app-switching for search.
- **Larger orgs with compliance requirements** need Enterprise for zero data retention with LLM providers, SCIM, and audit logs — a real requirement if legal or security teams need to sign off on any AI tool touching company documents.
- **Teams that want an AI-first writing tool** rather than a workspace with AI bolted on may find a dedicated tool like Jasper or a general assistant like ChatGPT a better direct fit, since Notion AI's writing features are secondary to Notion's core job as a docs/database app.

## Pros and Cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| AI is embedded directly in docs and databases — no copy-pasting between apps | Meaningful AI features (Meeting Notes, Enterprise Search) require the $20/seat Business plan |
| AI Meeting Notes removes manual note-taking for teams already meeting inside Notion | Enterprise Search is still in beta, so reliability and coverage can vary |
| Autofill and AI formulas add real automation to databases, not just chat | Custom Agents use metered, credit-based pricing that can get harder to predict at scale |
| "Model agnostic" design avoids lock-in to a single AI provider, per Notion | Notion doesn't publish which specific models power which feature |
| Enterprise plan offers zero data retention with LLM providers for compliance-sensitive teams | Free and Plus tiers only offer a "limited trial" of AI, not full access |

## Integrations and Ecosystem

Notion AI's biggest integration story is Enterprise Search and premium app connections: Slack and Google Drive on Plus, and GitHub and Asana on Business. This is different from a typical AI writing tool's Zapier/API integration story — Notion is folding other tools' content into its own search layer rather than pushing Notion content out. Notion does also offer a public API for building custom integrations against your workspace, though AI-specific API access for third-party developers is more limited than the workspace-level automation features sold directly through Custom Agents and Workers.

## Where It's a Strong Fit

- Teams that already store their documentation, specs, and meeting notes in Notion and want AI to work on that existing content rather than a separate silo.
- Organizations that run recurring meetings and want automatic summaries logged next to the agenda, without adding a third-party bot to every call.
- Teams using Notion databases as lightweight CRMs or trackers who want AI to fill in and summarize fields automatically.

## Where to Think Twice

- **If you need a fully free AI tool**, Notion AI isn't it — real usage requires at least the $10 Plus plan, and the features most people actually want sit behind the $20 Business plan.
- **If your team needs enterprise compliance sign-off today**, note that Enterprise Search is still in beta; confirm current beta status and any SLA commitments directly with Notion's sales team before committing budget.
- **If you want a standalone AI writing tool** you can use outside a workspace app — for pure long-form drafting, a dedicated tool built around that single job may fit better.
- **If you need predictable AI costs at scale**, the credit-based pricing for Custom Agents and Workers means costs can vary with usage rather than being a flat per-seat number.

## Bottom Line

Notion AI earns its keep for teams that have already committed to Notion as their docs-and-database hub — it turns AI Meeting Notes and cross-app search into something that lives where the work already happens, instead of one more tab. It's a much harder sell as a first AI tool if you don't already use Notion, since you'd be paying a $20/seat plan largely to unlock features that exist as cheaper standalone products elsewhere. For existing Notion users weighing whether to upgrade to Business, the meeting-notes and search features are the two to actually test before paying for the seat bump.

[Try Notion AI](/go/offer/notion-ai)

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Notion AI free?**
Notion's Free plan includes a limited trial of AI features, but full ongoing access requires at least the Plus plan ($10/seat/month), and the most useful features (AI Meeting Notes, Enterprise Search) require Business ($20/seat/month).

**Does Notion AI still cost $10 per month as an add-on?**
Not as of this post's publish date. Notion moved away from selling AI as a flat per-seat add-on and instead bundles different AI features into its Plus, Business, and Enterprise plans, with separate credit-based pricing for Custom Agents and Workers.

**What models power Notion AI?**
Notion says its AI is "model agnostic" and can route across different underlying providers, but it doesn't publish a full breakdown of which model handles which feature. Confirm current details on Notion's own product pages if this matters for your evaluation.

**Does Notion AI work with tools outside Notion?**
Yes, to a degree — Enterprise Search (beta) can pull results from Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub, and Business-tier premium app connections extend to tools like Asana. Full workspace automation across apps is handled through Notion Agent and Custom Agents.

**Is my data safe with Notion AI?**
Notion offers zero data retention with LLM providers as an Enterprise-tier feature, which is the strongest privacy commitment it publishes. Teams with strict compliance needs should confirm current data-handling terms directly with Notion before rolling AI out company-wide.

**How does Notion AI compare to using ChatGPT alongside Notion?**
ChatGPT (or a similar standalone assistant) works better as a general-purpose writing and research tool you can use anywhere. Notion AI's advantage is that it operates directly on your existing docs and databases without you having to copy content back and forth.

**Is Notion AI good for beginners?**
The in-line writing and autofill features are simple to pick up if you already know basic Notion. Notion Agent and Custom Agents have a steeper learning curve since they involve setting up triggers and automations rather than just editing text.

**What's the best alternative to Notion AI?**
It depends on the job: for pure AI writing, a dedicated writing assistant may suit better; for AI-powered search across company tools, dedicated enterprise search products compete directly with Notion's Enterprise Search beta.

For more AI and software coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Cursor AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Cursor's AI-native code editor tested: pricing tiers, Agent mode, Tab autocomplete, integrations and who should actually pay for Pro.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Cursor Review 2026: Is the AI Code Editor Worth It?

Cursor is a fork of VS Code built around AI-assisted coding, and for most developers who write code daily it's worth trying, at least on the free Hobby plan. The Pro tier ($20/month) is the meaningful upgrade for anyone who hits the free plan's agent-request ceiling within the first week, which most active users do.

## At a glance

| | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Free (Hobby plan) |
| Paid plans from | $20/month (Pro) |
| Free tier limit | Limited monthly Agent requests, no credit card needed |
| Best for | Developers who want AI-assisted autocomplete and agentic coding inside an editor they already know |
| Standout feature | Agent mode that can plan, edit across files, run commands and iterate without constant hand-holding |

## What Cursor actually is

Cursor is made by Anysphere, a startup that built the editor as a fork of Microsoft's VS Code. Because it's a fork rather than an extension, Cursor can go deeper than a typical Copilot-style plugin — it controls the editor's own indexing, diffing and command execution, not just a chat sidebar bolted onto someone else's app.

Cursor isn't tied to one model provider. It routes requests across multiple frontier models, and the vendor states its lineup includes options from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI alongside Cursor's own in-house model tuned for fast completions. Which specific models are available changes fairly often as providers ship new versions, so treat any specific model name as a snapshot rather than a fixed spec — check the in-app model picker for what's actually live when you sign up.

Because it's a full editor rather than a bolt-on, migrating from VS Code is close to frictionless: Cursor can import your extensions, keybindings and themes in one step during onboarding.

## Pricing

Pricing, free-tier limits and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — AI coding tools iterate on both pricing and usage caps frequently, so confirm current numbers on Cursor's official pricing page before subscribing.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hobby | Free | Limited Agent requests per month, Tab autocomplete, no credit card required |
| Pro | $20/month | Extended Agent limits, access to frontier models, MCP/skills/hooks support, cloud agents, usage-based billing once included usage runs out |
| Pro+ | $60/month | Roughly 3x the Agent limits of Pro, same feature set at higher ceilings |
| Ultra | $200/month | Roughly 20x the Agent limits of Pro, priority access to new features |
| Teams / Enterprise | Custom / invoice-based | Pooled team usage, centralized billing, admin controls, advanced security options |

All paid individual plans get roughly 20% off with annual billing. A detail worth flagging: once you burn through a plan's included usage, Cursor bills usage-based overage automatically rather than just throttling you — so a heavy month can cost more than the sticker price if you're not watching consumption. Budget-conscious users should check the usage dashboard regularly rather than assuming the flat monthly fee is a hard cap.

## Features walkthrough

**Tab autocomplete.** This is Cursor's bread-and-butter feature and the one most people notice first. It predicts multi-line edits, not just the next few tokens, and it's aware of recently edited files elsewhere in your project, so it can suggest a change in one file based on an edit you just made in another.

**Agent mode.** This is the feature that separates Cursor from a plain autocomplete tool. Point Agent at a task — "add pagination to this API route and update the tests" — and it plans the change, edits multiple files, runs the project's build or test command, reads the output, and iterates until things pass or it needs your input. An "autonomy slider" lets you dial how much independence the agent gets, from a targeted inline edit (Cmd+K) up to a fully autonomous multi-file task.

**Cloud/background agents.** Beyond agents that run in your local editor session, Cursor can launch agents that keep working in the background — including on longer tasks — and check back in when they're done or stuck, which matters if you want to kick off a refactor and go do something else.

**Codebase-aware chat and semantic search.** Cursor indexes your codebase so chat and agent requests can pull in relevant files by meaning, not just filename or open tabs. For anything beyond a small script, this context-awareness is what keeps suggestions relevant instead of generic.

**MCP, skills and hooks.** Cursor supports the Model Context Protocol, letting you connect it to external tools and data sources (databases, ticketing systems, internal docs) so the agent can act on more than just the files in front of it, plus hooks for running custom logic at points in the agent's workflow.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo developers and freelancers**: the free Hobby plan is a reasonable way to try Tab autocomplete and light agent use before committing to $20/month; most will outgrow the free agent-request cap within days of using it seriously.
- **Individual power users**: Pro ($20/month) is the sensible default for anyone using Cursor as their primary editor for real client or product work — the extended agent limits and frontier model access are where the tool actually pays for itself.
- **Heavy agentic users**: if you're running Agent on large multi-file tasks daily, or dispatching multiple background agents at once, Pro+ or Ultra remove the friction of hitting usage-based overage constantly, at a real cost premium.
- **Teams and companies**: the Teams/Enterprise tier adds pooled usage, centralized billing and admin/security controls that matter once more than a couple of engineers are expensing it — solo pricing doesn't scale cleanly to a team without this.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Full VS Code fork, not a limited extension — deep editor integration | Usage-based overage billing can surprise you if you don't watch consumption |
| Agent mode genuinely automates multi-file, multi-step changes | Free Hobby plan's agent limits are tight for daily real work |
| Multi-model routing means you're not locked to one provider's quality swings | Agent output still needs review — it can misread intent on ambiguous or under-specified tasks |
| Familiar VS Code keybindings/extensions import easily | Indexing large monorepos can be slow, and very large codebases stress context limits |
| MCP support extends the agent to real external tools, not just your file tree | No fully-featured offline/air-gapped mode for teams that need on-prem-only tooling |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Cursor extends past the editor window itself. It ships a CLI so you can invoke agents from the terminal, a Slack integration so agents can be triggered or reported to from a channel, and GitHub integration for agent-driven pull requests and reviews. MCP support is the broader extensibility layer here — it's how Cursor connects to arbitrary external tools (issue trackers, internal APIs, databases) rather than being limited to whatever Anysphere builds in natively. Because Cursor is a VS Code fork, most existing VS Code extensions also carry over, which matters if your workflow depends on language-specific tooling that isn't AI-related at all.

## Where it's a strong fit

Cursor is a strong fit if you already work primarily in VS Code and want to add AI assistance without switching your whole toolchain — the migration is close to zero-friction. It's also a strong fit for teams doing a lot of repetitive, well-specified refactoring or feature work, where Agent mode's ability to plan and execute across files saves real time versus writing every diff by hand. If you want flexibility on which underlying model powers your suggestions rather than being locked into one vendor, the multi-model routing is a genuine advantage over single-model competitors.

## Where to think twice

Skip Cursor, or at least stay on the free plan longer, if you need a fully free tool with no ceiling — the Hobby plan's agent limits are real, and serious daily use pushes most people toward Pro fairly quickly. Think twice if your organization requires strict on-prem or air-gapped tooling, since Cursor's core agent features depend on calling out to hosted models rather than running fully offline. Teams with hard compliance requirements (specific SOC 2 scope, data-residency rules, or a "no code leaves our network" policy) should verify Cursor's current security documentation directly rather than assume it matches a generic AI tool. And if you're skeptical of AI-generated code quality, remember Agent's output still needs a human reviewing diffs before merge — it speeds up the first draft, not the review step.

## The bottom line

Cursor earns its reputation as one of the more capable AI-native code editors available right now, mainly because Agent mode goes beyond autocomplete into actually planning and executing multi-file changes, and because it isn't locked into a single model provider. The free plan is a low-risk way to test it, but the real value shows up on Pro once you're using Agent regularly enough to need the extended limits. The overage billing model is the one thing to watch closely — it's usage-based, so a busy month can cost more than the flat $20, and that's easy to miss if you're not checking the usage dashboard.

[Try Cursor](/go/offer/cursor)

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Cursor free to use?**
Yes — the Hobby plan is free with no credit card required, but it caps how many Agent requests you get per month. Tab autocomplete is available on the free tier too.

**How much does Cursor Pro cost?**
Pro is $20/month (or discounted roughly 20% with annual billing), and adds extended Agent limits, frontier model access, MCP/skills/hooks support and cloud agents.

**What happens if I use more than my plan's included usage?**
Cursor bills usage-based overage automatically once you exceed a plan's included allowance, rather than simply cutting you off — worth monitoring in the usage dashboard so a heavy month doesn't cost more than expected.

**Does Cursor work with my existing VS Code setup?**
Yes. Cursor is a VS Code fork, so it can import your existing extensions, keybindings and themes during onboarding, and most VS Code extensions continue to work.

**Which AI models does Cursor support?**
Cursor routes across multiple model providers rather than locking you into one, and the specific lineup changes as providers release new versions — check the in-app model picker for the current options rather than relying on any specific model name staying fixed.

**Is Cursor good for beginners, or only experienced developers?**
Both, but in different ways. Beginners get real value from Tab autocomplete and simple chat-based help; experienced developers get more out of Agent mode's ability to handle larger, multi-step tasks independently. Either way, some comfort with reading code diffs is expected — Cursor accelerates writing code, it doesn't remove the need to understand what got written.

**What are the main alternatives to Cursor?**
[GitHub Copilot](/blog/github-copilot-review) (as a VS Code/JetBrains extension rather than a standalone editor), Windsurf, and various AI features now built directly into JetBrains IDEs are the closest comparisons. The core trade-off is usually the same: a full AI-native editor like Cursor versus an AI layer added to an editor you already use.

**Does Cursor offer team or enterprise plans?**
Yes — Teams and Enterprise tiers add pooled usage across seats, centralized/invoice-based billing, and admin and security controls, priced separately from the individual Pro/Pro+/Ultra tiers. Contact Cursor directly for current per-seat Teams pricing, since self-serve individual pricing doesn't map directly onto team billing.

For more coding and productivity tool coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Runway AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: An honest look at Runway's AI video tools, Gen-4.5 model, Act-One, Aleph, pricing tiers and who it's actually worth paying for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Runway worth it for AI video generation?

Runway is worth it if you need genuinely production-capable AI video — its Gen-4.5 model, Act-One performance tool and Aleph editing model outperform most consumer text-to-video apps on motion consistency and control. It's less worth it if you only want occasional, casual clips, since the credit system gets expensive fast for heavy daily use.

## At a glance

| | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Free (125 one-time credits); paid plans from $15/month ($12/month billed annually) |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — 125 one-time credits, no ongoing free monthly allowance |
| Best for | Filmmakers, agencies, VFX/production teams, marketing creatives |
| Standout feature | Gen-4.5 video model plus Act-One performance capture and the Aleph video-editing model |

## What Runway actually is

Runway (runway.com, formerly Runway ML) is an AI research and applications company building generative video, image and audio models, shipped through a browser-based creative suite. It's one of the earlier players in AI video — Runway's tools were used in Hollywood editing workflows, including on the Oscar-winning film *Everything Everywhere All at Once*, years before general-purpose text-to-video generation went mainstream. That production pedigree still shapes the product: Runway leans toward giving editors granular control rather than a single-prompt "generate and hope" box.

The current flagship model is Gen-4.5, which Runway describes as its most capable video model yet for motion quality, prompt adherence and visual fidelity. Runway also ships specialized models for narrower jobs — Act-One for translating a real performance (facial expression, motion) onto a generated character, and Aleph, built specifically for editing and transforming existing video rather than generating from scratch. Beyond the consumer-facing Creative Suite, Runway Dev offers API access to these models plus others from third-party labs, aimed at developers building video features into their own products.

## Pricing

Runway prices access through a monthly (or discounted annual) subscription plus a credit system — credits get consumed per generation based on model, resolution and length, so your effective cost per finished clip depends heavily on how much you re-roll or upscale.

| Plan | Monthly price | Annual price | Credits | Notable inclusions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | $0 | 125 one-time | Limited model selection, 5GB storage, watermarked output |
| Standard | $15/month | $12/month | 625/month | All video/image models, no watermarks, up to 3 projects, 4K upscaling, 20GB storage |
| Pro | $35/month | $28/month | 2,250/month | 15 parallel generations, 1 brand kit, 1 custom voice clone, Runway MCP, unlimited 4K upscaling, 100GB storage |
| Max | $95/month | $76/month | 9,500/month (1-month rollover) | Early access to new models, 20 parallel generations, 3 brand kits, HDR/ProRes export, 500GB storage |
| Enterprise | Custom | Custom | Custom | SSO, custom access controls, model-weight licensing, SOC 2 Type 2, dedicated support |

Credits on Standard and Pro don't roll over month to month; Max is the only self-serve tier that carries one month of unused credits forward. Purchased top-up credits (minimum 1,000 at a time) never expire, which matters if your workload is project-based rather than steady month to month. Pricing, free-tier limits and included features above were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change, so confirm current numbers on Runway's own pricing page before subscribing.

## Features that actually differentiate it

- **Gen-4.5 video generation.** Runway says Gen-4.5 improves motion consistency and prompt adherence over its earlier Gen-3 models — meaningful if you've tried older AI video tools and found characters warping mid-clip. That "world's best video model" framing is Runway's own marketing claim, not an independently verified benchmark.
- **Act-One.** Drives a generated character's facial performance and motion from a reference video of a real person acting it out — a genuinely different workflow from typing a text prompt and hoping for the right expression, and one of the clearer differentiators against prompt-only competitors.
- **Aleph — editing, not just generating.** Most competing tools generate new video from scratch; Aleph transforms footage you already have (changing an environment, object or camera angle within an existing shot). If your workflow starts with real footage, this is the feature worth testing first.
- **Camera controls and motion tools.** The Creative Suite includes directable camera movement and motion-brush-style control over what parts of a frame move, giving more of a director's toolkit than a single "generate" button.
- **Runway Dev / API access.** Available on Pro and above (custom on Enterprise), letting developers route requests across Runway's models and select third-party models through one API key — useful for building video generation into a separate product.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo creators and hobbyists** get real value from Standard — enough credits for regular short-form content, no watermark, 4K upscaling — but should watch credit usage closely if they regenerate clips often.
- **Freelance video editors and small production teams** are the natural fit for Pro: parallel generations mean less waiting on renders, and brand kit plus voice clone support consistent, on-brand output across a client project.
- **Agencies and studios with heavier throughput** should look at Max for rollover credits and HDR/ProRes export, which matter once output needs to slot into a real post-production pipeline.
- **Larger organizations with compliance requirements** — agencies, media companies, anyone needing SSO and a SOC 2 Type 2 attestation before AI tools touch client work — are the target for Enterprise, which also opens custom model-weight licensing conversations.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Gen-4.5 and Aleph give real editing control, not just prompt-and-generate | Credit system makes real per-clip cost hard to predict up front |
| Act-One is a genuinely distinct performance-capture workflow | No monthly free allowance beyond the one-time 125 free credits |
| API access (Runway Dev) for building video features into other products | Credits don't roll over below the Max plan |
| SOC 2 Type 2 and SSO on Enterprise for regulated/larger teams | Heavy iterative use (lots of re-rolls) burns through credits fast |
| Free plan lets you test the actual tools before paying | Higher tiers get expensive relative to casual/hobbyist budgets |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Runway Dev exposes a unified API for developers, with support for routing requests across Runway's own models and select models from other labs, plus pre-built "recipes" for common use cases and node-based custom workflows. Pro and above include Runway MCP (Model Context Protocol) support, letting Runway's models plug into MCP-compatible AI agent tooling. Runway has also referenced a ChatGPT plugin integration on its site. It doesn't advertise native Zapier or Slack integrations the way many mainstream SaaS tools do — confirm current integration support directly on Runway's site if a no-code automation connection matters to your workflow.

## Where it's a strong fit

Runway earns its price for anyone whose output needs to look intentional rather than merely "AI-generated" — filmmakers previsualizing shots, agencies producing client video ads, and teams that need to edit existing footage (via Aleph) rather than generate everything from a blank prompt. The camera controls, brand kit and export formats on the higher tiers point squarely at people who'll actually use them in a real production pipeline, not just experiment once and move on.

## Where to think twice

If you need a fully free, ongoing tool with no credit ceiling, Runway isn't it — the free plan is a one-time 125-credit trial, not a renewing free tier, and even Standard's 625 monthly credits disappear quickly if you're iterating on prompts the way most people naturally do when a first generation doesn't look right. If your team needs enterprise compliance (SSO, SOC 2) but doesn't have Enterprise-tier budget, there's a real gap between Max and Enterprise pricing with nothing in between. And if you need offline or on-prem generation for data-sensitivity reasons beyond Runway's "we don't train on your data" policy, this is a cloud-only product — there's no local/on-prem deployment at the self-serve tiers.

## Bottom line

Runway is one of the more capable AI video platforms available right now, and the gap between it and a basic prompt-to-clip generator shows up clearly once you use Act-One or Aleph on a real project rather than a novelty test. It's not the cheapest way to dabble in AI video — the credit system rewards planning your generations rather than brute-forcing dozens of re-rolls — but for anyone producing video as part of actual creative or marketing work, the control on offer at Pro and Max tiers is hard to match with a cheaper, more casual tool. Test the free plan's 125 credits first to see whether Gen-4.5's output and Act-One's workflow actually fit how you work before committing to a monthly plan.
