title: Kinsta Review 2026: Pricing, Plans, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Kinsta's managed WordPress hosting reviewed: real pricing tiers, overage fees, migration, support and who should — and shouldn't — pay the premium.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Kinsta worth it in 2026?

Kinsta is a premium managed WordPress host built on Google Cloud Platform, starting at $35/month for one site with 35,000 monthly visits. It's a strong pick if you want a fast, fully managed stack with real support and unlimited free migrations — but it's priced and metered like a business tool, not a $3/month shared host, and overage fees are real.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $35/month (monthly billing), ~$30/month billed annually |
| Renewal price | Pricing is largely flat — no promo-to-high-renewal jump like budget shared hosts |
| Entry-plan limits | 1 site, 35,000 visits/month, 10GB storage |
| Control panel | Proprietary MyKinsta (no cPanel) |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days (first-time customers only) |
| Free migration | Yes, unlimited, done by Kinsta's team |
| Best for | WordPress sites that need managed performance and can absorb premium pricing |

## What Kinsta actually is

Kinsta is a managed WordPress-only host — it doesn't sell generic shared hosting, email hosting, or cPanel accounts. Every site runs on Google Cloud Platform's infrastructure, with Kinsta handling server management, caching, security patching and backups so you never touch a terminal or a control panel in the traditional sense. Instead, everything — site creation, staging, backups, analytics, billing — goes through Kinsta's own dashboard, MyKinsta.

This matters for who should even consider it: if you want a $2-a-month starter site for a hobby blog, Kinsta isn't built for that use case and will feel expensive. If you're running a client site, a WooCommerce store, or a WordPress install where uptime and page speed directly affect revenue, the managed layer is the actual product being sold.

## Pricing table

Pricing as of this post's publish date (September 2026); Kinsta's rates can change, so confirm current numbers on its pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Price (monthly billing) | Price (annual billing) | Sites | Monthly visits | Storage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Single Site (entry) | $35/mo | ~$30/mo | 1 | 35,000 | 10GB |
| Single Site (next tier) | $50/mo | ~$42/mo | 1 | 65,000 | 10GB |
| Business (WP 2) | $70/mo | ~$59/mo | 2 | 70,000 | 20GB |
| Business (WP 5) | $115/mo | ~$96/mo | 5 | 125,000 | 30GB |
| Business (WP 10) | $225/mo | ~$188/mo | 10 | 315,000 | 40GB |
| Business (WP 20) | $340/mo | ~$284/mo | 20 | 500,000 | 50GB |
| Business (WP 40) | $450/mo | ~$375/mo | 40 | 750,000 | 60GB |

Agency and Enterprise tiers exist above WP 40 for larger operations managing dozens to hundreds of client sites, priced individually rather than off a fixed public table.

## The real cost breakdown

The headline price is close to what you'll actually pay long-term, which is a meaningful difference from budget hosts that quote a 48-month introductory rate and quietly renew at 3-4x that number. Kinsta's annual billing simply knocks off roughly two months' worth of cost compared to paying monthly — there's no bait-and-switch renewal cliff to budget around.

What can inflate the bill is overage usage, and it's worth taking seriously before signing up:

- **Visits over your plan limit:** $0.50 per extra 1,000 visits
- **Disk space over your plan limit:** $2 per GB per month, prorated daily
- **CDN bandwidth over your plan limit:** $0.05 per GB

None of these hard-stop your site — Kinsta bills the overage rather than taking you offline — but a traffic spike (a viral post, a seasonal sale) can add a real line item to your invoice if you're running close to your tier's visit ceiling. MyKinsta's usage dashboard shows you where you stand before it becomes a surprise, so check it periodically rather than assuming the plan you bought will always cover you.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose the Single Site entry plan** if you're running one WordPress site — a business site, a portfolio, a small store — with modest traffic under 35,000 visits/month.
- **Choose the next Single Site tier ($50/mo)** if that one site is growing past the entry visit ceiling but you don't need more than one install.
- **Choose a Business plan (WP 2 and up)** if you manage multiple WordPress sites, such as a freelancer or small agency handling a handful of client builds, and want them consolidated under one MyKinsta account.
- **Choose Agency or Enterprise** only once you're managing a large roster of client sites or need dedicated infrastructure — these aren't self-serve starter tiers.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Built on Google Cloud Platform — fast, reliable infrastructure | Meaningfully pricier than budget shared hosting from the first bill |
| Unlimited free migrations handled by Kinsta's team | No cPanel — MyKinsta is the only interface, which is a switching cost if you're used to cPanel |
| 24/7 WordPress-specialized support | Visit/storage/bandwidth overages bill separately and can add up on traffic spikes |
| Pricing stays largely flat instead of a promo-then-high-renewal model | Money-back guarantee applies only to first-time customers |
| Daily automated backups and staging environments included at every tier | WordPress-only — not a fit if you need to host non-WordPress sites too |

## Support

Kinsta advertises 24/7 support staffed by engineers who specialize in WordPress hosting specifically, reachable through MyKinsta's live chat rather than a generic ticket queue. This is one of the more consistently cited strengths in independent reviews and in its own Trustpilot feedback — support quality is part of what the premium price is paying for, not an afterthought bolted onto cheap infrastructure.

## Migration

Every Kinsta plan includes unlimited free site migrations, done by Kinsta's own migration team rather than left to a self-service plugin. If you're moving an existing WordPress site over from another host, you submit the request through MyKinsta and Kinsta's team handles the transfer — a meaningful convenience if you're not comfortable manually migrating a database and file structure yourself.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Client and agency WordPress work where downtime or slow pages have a real cost.
- WooCommerce stores that need consistent performance during traffic spikes (with overage costs budgeted for).
- Teams that want managed infrastructure and don't want to administer a server or a cPanel account themselves.

## Where to think twice

- Hobby blogs, personal sites, or anyone price-sensitive — the entry price alone ($35/mo) is many multiples of budget shared hosting.
- Sites that aren't built on WordPress — Kinsta doesn't host anything else.
- Anyone who specifically wants or needs cPanel, since MyKinsta is the only option.
- Highly traffic-variable sites without headroom in the budget for visit overage charges.

## Bottom line

Kinsta earns its premium price with genuinely fast Google Cloud infrastructure, a clean proprietary dashboard, unlimited free migrations and WordPress-specialized support — and unlike many budget hosts, what you pay on day one is close to what you'll keep paying, rather than a low teaser rate that jumps at renewal. The trade-off is the metered pricing model: exceeding your plan's visits, storage or CDN bandwidth bills extra, so it rewards knowing your traffic before you commit rather than just picking the cheapest tier. For agencies, WooCommerce stores and any WordPress site where performance matters commercially, it's a defensible choice. For a low-traffic hobby site, it's more hosting than you need at several times the price.

Check the [Kinsta coupon page](/coupons/kinsta) for current offers, or browse [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) to compare it against budget alternatives.

## FAQs

**Does Kinsta offer shared hosting?**
No. Kinsta only offers managed WordPress hosting on cloud infrastructure — there's no traditional cPanel shared hosting tier at any price point.

**What happens if I go over my Kinsta plan's visit limit?**
Kinsta bills an overage fee of $0.50 per extra 1,000 monthly visits rather than suspending your site, so a traffic spike adds a cost rather than taking you offline.

**Does Kinsta have a free trial?**
Kinsta doesn't run an open-ended free trial; instead it backs new Managed WordPress Hosting signups with a 30-day money-back guarantee for first-time customers.

**Can I use cPanel with Kinsta?**
No — Kinsta replaced the traditional control panel entirely with its own MyKinsta dashboard, which covers site management, backups, staging, analytics and billing.

**Does Kinsta include free migrations?**
Yes, unlimited free migrations are included on every plan, carried out by Kinsta's own migration team rather than a self-service tool only.

**Is Kinsta good for WooCommerce stores?**
Yes — its Google Cloud Platform infrastructure and CDN are commonly used for WooCommerce stores that need consistent performance, though store owners should watch visit and bandwidth usage against their plan's limits during sales spikes.

**How does Kinsta's pricing compare to renewal-trap budget hosts?**
Differently — Kinsta's rates stay largely flat rather than following a steep introductory-to-renewal price jump, so the price you sign up at is a more reliable guide to your long-term cost than with many budget shared hosts.

**Is the 30-day money-back guarantee no-questions-asked?**
It's available only to first-time customers, doesn't reset if you switch plans during the window, and any overage or add-on fees incurred are deducted from the refund rather than returned in full.

title: KnownHost Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: KnownHost review 2026: cPanel shared/VPS hosting with a 99.9% uptime SLA, real pricing, renewal costs, pros/cons and who it fits best.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## KnownHost Review 2026: Is This cPanel Host Worth It?

KnownHost is a cPanel-based shared and VPS host built around a formal 99.9% uptime SLA with service credits, 24/7 support, and NVMe/LiteSpeed infrastructure. It's a solid pick for site owners who want cPanel familiarity and a documented uptime guarantee, though its lowest prices require a 3-year commitment and renew noticeably higher.

## At a glance

| Fact | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | $6.71/month (Basic, 3-year term) |
| Renewal price | $8.95/month (Basic) |
| Control panel | cPanel |
| Uptime guarantee | 99.9%, with SLA service credits |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days |
| Best for | Site owners who want cPanel plus a credit-backed uptime SLA |

## What KnownHost actually is

KnownHost is a web hosting company offering shared hosting, managed VPS, unmanaged VPS, and dedicated servers, all running through the standard cPanel control panel rather than a custom dashboard. Its shared hosting stack uses LiteSpeed web servers with LSCache and NVMe storage, and every plan ships with free SSL certificates and Imunify360 malware/security scanning. The company leans on its Service Level Agreement as a differentiator: rather than a marketing claim of "guaranteed uptime," it publishes specific service-credit tiers tied to actual measured uptime each month.

Beyond shared hosting, KnownHost also sells managed VPS (KnownHost handles server maintenance, security patching, and support) and unmanaged VPS (root access, self-managed) for site owners who outgrow shared resources — a growth path that budget hosts building only shared tiers don't offer.

## Pricing table

Pricing below reflects the 3-year billing term, which carries KnownHost's lowest advertised rate. Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check KnownHost's current pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Intro price/mo | Renewal price/mo | Storage | Websites |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Basic | $6.71 | $8.95 | 10 GB NVMe | 1 |
| Standard | $9.71 | $12.95 | 25 GB NVMe | 5 |
| Professional | $14.96 | $19.95 | Unlimited NVMe | Unlimited |
| Premium | $29.96 | $39.95 | Unlimited NVMe | Unlimited |

## Real cost breakdown: intro vs. renewal

KnownHost's advertised per-month prices assume you pay for a full 3-year term upfront — that's the commitment length required to unlock the lowest headline rate. On the Basic plan, that's roughly $241.56 charged at checkout for three years of service. Once that term ends, the plan renews at $8.95/month rather than $6.71/month — a jump of about 33%. The gap is proportionally similar across every tier: Professional goes from $14.96 to $19.95/month at renewal, a roughly 33% increase as well.

If you're not ready to commit to three years, shorter terms are typically available but at a higher effective monthly rate than the headline number quoted above. Either way, budget for the renewal price, not the intro price, when comparing KnownHost against other hosts long-term.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Basic** if you're launching a single small site (a blog, a portfolio, a local-business page) and don't need room to grow beyond one domain.
- **Choose Standard** if you're running up to five websites — a small agency managing a handful of client sites, or someone consolidating a couple of side projects onto one account.
- **Choose Professional** if you want unlimited websites and storage without paying for Premium's extra resource headroom — KnownHost itself flags this as the recommended tier for most buyers.
- **Choose Premium** if you're running resource-heavier sites (more traffic, larger media libraries, more concurrent visitors) and need the highest resource allocation shared hosting offers before stepping up to VPS.
- **Consider VPS instead** if a single shared-hosting site is already straining Professional or Premium — KnownHost's managed VPS (from roughly $43/month) or unmanaged VPS (from roughly $5/month, root access, no managed support) are the next step up.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Formal 99.9% uptime SLA with tiered service credits, not just a marketing claim | Lowest advertised price requires a 3-year upfront commitment |
| Standard cPanel control panel — no new dashboard to learn | Renewal prices run 30%+ above intro pricing across every tier |
| NVMe storage and LiteSpeed/LSCache on every shared tier | Entry Basic tier caps out at a single website |
| Clear growth path into managed or unmanaged VPS on the same account structure | Free domain inclusion isn't clearly advertised on the current shared-hosting pricing page |
| Daily backups and Imunify360 security bundled in | Money-back guarantee is voided by exceeding bandwidth limits or on repeat package purchases |

## Support

KnownHost advertises 24/7 support and is frequently praised in customer reviews for support responsiveness and technical depth — its 4.3-out-of-5 Trustpilot rating (96 reviews) leans heavily on comments about support staff resolving issues quickly. Unmanaged VPS customers should note that additional hands-on support beyond basic hardware/network management is billed separately (KnownHost's published unmanaged-VPS terms cite an hourly rate for extra support), so the "24/7 support" promise applies differently depending on which product line you're on.

## Migration

Shared-hosting migrations to KnownHost run through the standard cPanel-to-cPanel transfer process, which is generally more straightforward than moving between hosts that use different (custom) control panels, since account structures, email, and databases map over more directly. If you're coming from another cPanel host, expect the migration to be comparatively low-friction; if you're moving off a host with a custom panel (like Hostinger's hPanel), plan for more manual reconfiguration of DNS, email, and any custom settings that don't have a direct cPanel equivalent.

## Where it's a strong fit

- You specifically want cPanel rather than a host's custom-built dashboard.
- You care about a documented, credit-backed uptime SLA rather than an unqualified uptime claim.
- You expect to outgrow shared hosting and want a VPS upgrade path within the same provider.
- You're comfortable committing to a multi-year term to get the lowest rate.

## Where to think twice

- You want the lowest possible starting price without a long-term commitment — shorter terms cost more per month here.
- You need a free domain bundled in — KnownHost doesn't clearly advertise one on its current shared-hosting pricing page, unlike some competitors.
- You're on Basic and expect to run more than one website — you'll need to upgrade tiers.
- You want unmanaged VPS with hands-on support included at no extra charge — support beyond hardware/network issues is billed hourly on that product line.

## Bottom line

KnownHost is a credible pick for anyone who wants standard cPanel hosting paired with an unusually explicit uptime guarantee — the tiered SLA credit structure is more substantive than the vague "99.9% guaranteed" language most budget hosts use without backing it up. The tradeoff is the same one most long-term-discount hosts ask for: the advertised price assumes a 3-year commitment, and renewal rates jump by roughly a third once that term ends. If cPanel, SLA transparency, and a built-in VPS upgrade path matter more to you than the single lowest possible sticker price, KnownHost is worth shortlisting alongside other established cPanel hosts.

## FAQs

**Is KnownHost good for beginners?**
It's approachable if you're comfortable with cPanel, which has a larger base of tutorials and familiarity than some hosts' custom dashboards, though it doesn't hold a beginner's hand as much as page-builder-first hosts do.

**What control panel does KnownHost use?**
cPanel, the industry-standard control panel, across its shared hosting and VPS lines.

**Does KnownHost offer a free trial?**
KnownHost doesn't advertise a free trial for shared hosting; instead it backs new shared-hosting signups with a 30-day money-back guarantee.

**How much does KnownHost shared hosting cost?**
Introductory pricing on a 3-year term runs $6.71-$29.96/month depending on tier, renewing at $8.95-$39.95/month afterward.

**Does KnownHost have a money-back guarantee?**
Yes, 30 days for new shared-hosting customers, with exceptions if you exceed your bandwidth allowance in that window or are refunding an additional package beyond your first.

**What is KnownHost's uptime guarantee?**
99.9%, backed by an SLA that issues service credits on a sliding scale if actual uptime falls below that in a given month.

**Can I upgrade from shared hosting to VPS later?**
Yes — KnownHost sells both managed and unmanaged VPS as a next step for sites that outgrow shared hosting resources.

**Is KnownHost's advertised price the price I'll always pay?**
No — the lowest rate requires a 3-year upfront term and renews at a meaningfully higher monthly rate afterward; check the renewal price for your plan before buying.

Ready to compare pricing? Check the [KnownHost coupon page](/coupons/knownhost) for current offers, or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) to see how it stacks up against other providers.

title: Linode Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Honest Verdict
excerpt: Linode (Akamai) review: real VPS pricing from $5/mo, hourly billing, no cPanel, developer-focused setup, and honest pros and cons.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Linode good for hosting?

Linode is good for developers who want raw cloud compute, not for anyone expecting a beginner-friendly website control panel. It's a virtual private server platform — now branded "Akamai Connected Cloud" after Akamai's 2022 acquisition — billed hourly with a monthly cap starting at $5/month for 1 GB RAM. There's no cPanel, no one-click WordPress dashboard, and no phone support on the base plan.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $5/month (1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, 25 GB SSD) |
| Billing model | Hourly, capped at the monthly rate |
| Control panel | None bundled (bare VPS) |
| Uptime guarantee | Not a fixed advertised SLA on shared compute tiers |
| Money-back guarantee | No traditional refund window — usage-based billing |
| Best for | Developers, sysadmins, self-managed app/server deployments |

## What Linode actually is

Linode isn't a shared-hosting company in the sense that Hostinger or Namecheap are. It sells raw compute — virtual machines you provision, configure, and maintain yourself. There's no default install of WordPress, no drag-and-drop site builder, and no cPanel or custom beginner dashboard bundled with a plan. What you get is a Linux server (Ubuntu, Debian, AlmaLinux, and others are supported at deploy time), SSH access, and Linode's own Cloud Manager for spinning instances up and down, attaching storage, and managing networking.

That makes Linode a fit for people who already know how to run a web server, or who are deploying an application stack (a Node app, a database, a Docker host, a small Kubernetes cluster) rather than a static brochure site. If the goal is "point-and-click WordPress hosting," this is the wrong category of product — a shared or managed WordPress host will get there faster with far less setup work.

**Akamai and the "Linode" name.** Akamai acquired Linode in 2022, and the cloud division now operates as "Akamai Connected Cloud." In practice, the Linode brand, the Cloud Manager interface, and the compute product lineup are all still in active use — pricing pages and documentation live at both linode.com and akamai.com, with linode.com redirecting to Akamai's cloud pricing hub. It's worth knowing the company behind it is now a much larger CDN/edge-infrastructure business rather than an independent VPS shop.

## Pricing

Pricing below is for Shared CPU compute instances, verified as of this post's publish date (September 2026); check Linode/Akamai's current pricing page before buying, since cloud pricing changes periodically and can vary slightly by data center region.

| Plan | RAM | vCPU | Storage | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nanode 1 GB | 1 GB | 1 | 25 GB SSD | $5/month |
| Linode 2 GB | 2 GB | 1 | — | $12/month |
| Linode 4 GB | 4 GB | 2 | — | $24/month |
| Linode 8 GB | 8 GB | 4 | — | $48/month |

## The real cost breakdown

Linode doesn't work like shared hosting's "cheap intro rate that jumps at renewal" model — there's no multi-year promotional pricing here. Instead, billing is hourly and capped at the monthly rate: Akamai's own documentation states pricing "starts at $5 for a Shared CPU Linode with 1 vCPU core, 1 GB of memory, and 25 GB of SSD storage," charged per hour of actual use up to that $5 monthly ceiling. Spin up a $5 instance for a two-week test and tear it down, and the bill is roughly half of $5 — not the full month.

The tradeoff is that nothing is bundled in that headline price the way it is with shared hosting. There's no free domain, no included email hosting, no automatic daily backups (sold as a separate add-on), and no CDN thrown in — those are things you provision and often pay for separately. Budget for the base compute cost plus whatever storage, backup, and bandwidth add-ons your setup needs, rather than comparing the $5 headline figure directly against a shared-hosting plan's all-in price.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose the **Nanode 1 GB ($5/month)** if you're running a single lightweight app, a personal project, a test/staging environment, or a low-traffic API — 1 GB of RAM is tight for anything beyond that.

Choose the **Linode 2 GB ($12/month)** if you're hosting a small production site or app with a database on the same box and want more headroom than the Nanode tier gives you.

Choose the **Linode 4 GB ($24/month)** or higher if you're running multiple services, a CMS with moderate traffic, or a small team's shared development/staging server that needs more consistent CPU allocation.

For anything with unpredictable spikes or a need for horizontal scaling, Linode's higher tiers and dedicated-CPU line are the next step up — but at that point you're evaluating cloud infrastructure the way you would AWS or DigitalOcean, not comparing it to shared hosting anymore.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Transparent, hourly-capped billing with no bait-and-switch renewal pricing | No control panel or website dashboard included |
| Straightforward $5/month entry tier with real specs (1 GB RAM, 25 GB SSD) | Not beginner-friendly — assumes server administration knowledge |
| Backed by Akamai's larger infrastructure and network footprint | Trustpilot rating sits at 2.5/5 across 207 reviews, notably lower than typical shared-hosting scores |
| Flexible instance sizing for scaling compute independently of storage | No bundled backups, domain, or email — priced as add-ons |

## Support

Linode's support is oriented toward technical users: a ticketing system, extensive self-serve documentation (techdocs.akamai.com), and community/Q&A resources rather than the live-chat-first model shared hosts lean on. There's no beginner-facing chat agent walking a non-technical customer through fixing a broken WordPress install — support assumes you can describe a server-level problem precisely. Higher-tier managed/enterprise support plans exist for organizations that need faster response guarantees, sold separately from base compute pricing.

## Migration

Moving into Linode means provisioning a fresh instance and migrating the site or app yourself (or via a hired admin) — there's no "enter your old host's login and we'll move it for you" migration tool the way some shared hosts offer for WordPress. Typical approaches are rsync/SFTP file transfer, a database dump and restore, and DNS cutover once the new server is verified working. StackScripts (pre-built deployment scripts) can shortcut common setups like LAMP or WordPress-on-a-VPS, but it's still a server migration, not a one-click import.

## Where it's a strong fit

Linode makes sense for developers deploying custom applications, teams wanting infrastructure-as-code-style control over their server environment, and anyone avoiding shared hosting's constraints (shared resources, restricted server access, host-imposed limits). Hourly-capped billing is also genuinely useful for short-lived test environments or irregular-usage projects.

## Where to think twice

If the goal is "get a WordPress site online with minimal setup," Linode is the wrong tool — there's no control panel, no included site-building tools, and every piece of the stack (web server, PHP, database, TLS certificates, backups) has to be configured. The 2.5/5 Trustpilot score from 207 reviews is also worth weighing against shared hosts in this category that post markedly higher review volumes and scores — read a sample of the actual reviews rather than the star average alone before deciding.

## Bottom line

Linode is a competent, transparently-priced cloud VPS platform for people who know what a VPS is for. The $5/month entry tier is real and hourly-capped billing avoids the renewal-price traps common in shared hosting, but this isn't a substitute for managed hosting — no control panel, no bundled backups or email, and a support model that expects technical fluency. If that describes your project, evaluate it against DigitalOcean or Vultr at a similar price point. If you want a dashboard and one-click WordPress installs, choose a shared or managed host instead.

## FAQs

**Does Linode include a free domain?**
No. Linode sells compute instances, not domain registration bundles — you'd register a domain separately and point its DNS at your instance.

**Can I install WordPress on Linode?**
Yes, but you'd install and configure it yourself (or use a StackScript/marketplace app template) — there's no automatic WordPress installer built into a plain shared-hosting-style dashboard, because Linode doesn't include one.

**What happened to Linode after the Akamai acquisition?**
Akamai acquired Linode in 2022 and now brands the cloud division "Akamai Connected Cloud." The Linode name, Cloud Manager, and compute product lineup are still active under that umbrella.

**Is Linode cheaper than shared hosting?**
The $5/month entry tier is priced similarly to budget shared hosting, but shared hosting typically bundles a control panel, free domain, and sometimes email or backups that Linode prices separately — compare the full stack of what you need, not just the headline number.

**Does Linode offer a money-back guarantee?**
Linode's billing is hourly and usage-based rather than a prepaid term with a refund window — there's a limited-time signup credit for new accounts in some promotions, but it doesn't function like a shared host's 30-day money-back guarantee.

**Is Linode good for beginners?**
Not particularly. It's aimed at developers and technical users comfortable managing a server via SSH; there's no simplified control panel to fall back on.

**What is Linode's Trustpilot rating?**
2.5 out of 5 based on 207 reviews as of this review's research date — noticeably lower than the ratings typical budget shared hosts post, so it's worth reading a sample of the actual reviews for context.

**Does Linode support Docker or Kubernetes?**
Yes — Linode/Akamai offers both standard compute instances (where you can run Docker yourself) and a managed Kubernetes product (LKE) for container orchestration.

Compare it against other budget options on our [Linode coupon page](/coupons/linode), or browse more options on our [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) page.

| Money-back guarantee | 30 days |
| Control panel | OVHcloud Control Panel (Manager); cPanel/Plesk paid add-ons on VPS/dedicated |
| Best for | Budget sites, EU-based hosting needs, developers comfortable without cPanel |

Pricing was accurate as of September 2026 and can change — check OVHcloud's live pricing page before buying.

## What OVHcloud actually is

OVHcloud started as a dedicated-server and data-center company and is still one of the larger players in raw compute and cloud infrastructure in Europe. That history matters because it means OVHcloud isn't purely a shared-hosting brand or purely a VPS/cloud brand — it's both, plus dedicated servers and public cloud, sold from the same account and control panel.

For someone shopping for a coupon site or small business site, the relevant tier is shared web hosting, split into three ranges:

- **Eco** — the cheapest tier, aimed at single sites, portfolios and small personal projects.
- **Business** — more storage, databases and email accounts, aimed at growing sites.
- **Agencies** — built for freelancers/agencies running many client sites on one account, with the highest resource ceilings.

Anyone who actually needs raw compute instead can step up to VPS (from about $4.54/month for 2 vCores/4GB RAM) or dedicated servers, without switching providers.

## Pricing table

| Plan | Range | Intro price | Renewal price | Storage | Sites |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | Eco | $1.89/mo | $3.09/mo | 1GB SSD | 1 |
| Personal | Eco | $3.59/mo | $7.09/mo | 100GB SSD | 15 |
| Startup | Business | $3.59/mo | $7.09/mo | 100GB SSD | 15 |
| Pro | Business | $2.39/mo | $11.79/mo | 250GB SSD | 100 |
| Performance | Business | $8.29/mo | $23.59/mo | 500GB SSD | 150 |
| VPS-1 | VPS | $4.54/mo | — | 40GB NVMe, 2 vCores, 4GB RAM | — |

## Real cost breakdown

The advertised price is a first-term promotional rate, and OVHcloud is explicit that the discount gets deeper the longer you commit — 24-month terms save several months versus paying annually, and 48-month terms save even more. That structure only pays off if you're confident you'll keep the site running for the full term, because the renewal jump is steep: the Pro plan, for instance, intros at $2.39/month but renews at $11.79/month — roughly a 5x increase. Factor the renewal rate, not the teaser price, into any multi-year cost comparison against Hostinger or Namecheap.

Add-on costs to budget for separately: a domain is typically free for the first year on qualifying plans, backups are included on some tiers but not others, and cPanel/Plesk licensing is a paid extra if you want it instead of the native Manager panel.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Starter (Eco)** if you're launching one small personal site or a landing page and don't need multiple mailboxes.
- **Choose Personal or Startup** if you're running up to 15 sites and want more storage and databases without paying for the Business range's higher-end resources.
- **Choose Pro** if you manage many small sites (up to 100) and want SSH/Git access for a more developer-oriented workflow.
- **Choose Performance or the Agencies range** if you're running a higher-traffic site or many client sites and want a CDN included and dedicated-style resources.
- **Choose VPS** instead of shared hosting if you need root access, a specific software stack, or predictable resources that aren't shared with other tenants.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Three product lines (shared, VPS, dedicated) under one account | Native panel isn't cPanel — a real switching cost for cPanel-trained admins |
| European data centers, useful for EU-based audiences and compliance | Renewal prices rise sharply (2-5x) after the first term |
| VPS entry pricing is competitive for the specs offered | cPanel/Plesk are paid add-ons, not included by default |
| 30-day money-back guarantee | Trustpilot rating (3.9/5) is solid but well behind top-rated budget hosts |

## Support

OVHcloud offers ticket-based support and phone support on most plans, plus an extensive self-service documentation library (docs.ovhcloud.com) that covers control panel tasks, VPS setup and troubleshooting in detail. It doesn't lean on 24/7 live chat as heavily as some budget competitors — if round-the-clock chat is a priority, compare directly against Hostinger or Namecheap before committing.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to OVHcloud shared hosting means manually migrating files and databases through the OVHcloud Control Panel or via FTP/SSH, since there's no universal one-click migration plugin baked into every plan the way some competitors advertise. Developer-oriented plans (Pro and above) include SSH and Git access, which makes migrating a site from the command line more straightforward than on the entry-level Eco tier.

## Where it's a strong fit

- You want EU-based data centers for latency or data-residency reasons.
- You're comfortable managing sites without cPanel, or you actively prefer a cleaner custom panel.
- You might outgrow shared hosting and want to move to VPS or dedicated without switching providers.
- You're price-sensitive on the first term and plan your budget around the renewal rate in advance.

## Where to think twice

- You specifically need cPanel included in the base price — you'll pay extra for it here, and only on VPS/dedicated tiers.
- You want 24/7 live chat as your primary support channel.
- You're not going to track renewal dates — the multi-year renewal jump can catch budget-conscious buyers off guard.

## Bottom line

OVHcloud earns its place among budget hosts on breadth: it's one of the few providers that credibly covers shared hosting, VPS and dedicated servers from the same account, backed by real European infrastructure and a 3.9/5 Trustpilot rating from over 8,500 reviews. The catch is the same one that applies to most low-cost hosts — the intro price is not the real price, and the jump to the OVHcloud Control Panel instead of cPanel is a genuine adjustment if you've only ever managed sites through cPanel. If you're price-sensitive but willing to plan around the renewal rate and skip cPanel, it's a reasonable pick; if cPanel or 24/7 chat are non-negotiable, look elsewhere first.

## FAQs

**Is OVHcloud good for beginners?**
It's workable but not the most beginner-polished option — the OVHcloud Control Panel is functional but less guided than Hostinger's hPanel, and there's no universal one-click migration tool across every plan.

**Does OVHcloud offer a free trial?**
OVHcloud backs most hosting and VPS plans with a 30-day money-back guarantee rather than a free trial, so you can get a refund if you cancel within that window.

**What's the difference between OVHcloud's Eco, Business and Agencies ranges?**
Eco is the cheapest tier for single sites and small projects; Business adds more storage, databases and email accounts for growing sites; Agencies is built for freelancers and agencies managing many client sites on higher resource ceilings.

**Can I get cPanel on OVHcloud?**
Not on shared hosting by default — shared hosting and VPS plans run on the native OVHcloud Control Panel. cPanel (and Plesk) are available as paid add-ons only on VPS and dedicated server plans.

**How much does OVHcloud VPS cost?**
Entry-level VPS-1 starts around $4.54/month for 2 vCores, 4GB RAM and 40GB NVMe SSD, scaling up through VPS-2, VPS-3 and VPS-4 tiers with more cores, RAM and storage.

**Will my OVHcloud hosting price increase after the first year?**
Yes. Like most budget hosts, OVHcloud's lowest prices are first-term promotions. Renewal rates on Business-range shared hosting run roughly $7.09-$23.59/month depending on the plan, which can be 2-5x the intro rate — check the specific renewal price for your plan before signing up.

**Does OVHcloud include a free domain?**
Some plans include a free domain for the first year — check the specific plan's terms, since this varies by range and promotion.

**Is OVHcloud reliable?**
OVHcloud holds a 3.9/5 rating on Trustpilot from over 8,500 reviews (rated "Great"), and shared hosting plans are backed by a 99.9% observed availability figure — solid, though not the highest-rated budget host on review aggregators.

title: Pagely Review 2026: Pricing, Features, and Verdict
excerpt: Pagely offers premium AWS-based managed WordPress hosting for enterprise sites. See real pricing, features, pros/cons and who it's actually built for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Pagely Review 2026: Is Premium Managed WordPress Hosting Worth It?

Pagely is a good fit if you run a high-traffic or mission-critical WordPress site and want AWS-backed infrastructure with a dedicated managed-hosting team behind it. It's not built for small, budget-conscious sites — entry pricing starts at $99/month, several times what mainstream shared hosts charge, with no cPanel option.

## At a glance

| Fact | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | $99/month (StartPress, list price; promotional pricing sometimes lower) |
| Entry-tier renewal | $99-$199/month depending on active promotion |
| Control panel | Proprietary "Atomic" panel (no cPanel) |
| Infrastructure | Amazon Web Services (AWS) |
| Visitor/pageview caps | None on any plan |
| Money-back guarantee | Not published on the pricing page — confirm with sales |
| Free migration | Yes |
| Best for | High-traffic, enterprise or mission-critical WordPress sites |

## What Pagely actually is

Pagely is a managed WordPress hosting provider that runs entirely on Amazon Web Services rather than its own bare-metal servers or a shared-hosting stack. It positions itself squarely at the enterprise and high-traffic end of the market — the kind of WordPress installs where uptime, security isolation and dedicated support matter more than shaving a few dollars off the monthly bill. Everything runs through Pagely's own control panel, called Atomic, built specifically around managing WordPress apps on their AWS setup rather than a general-purpose panel like cPanel or Plesk.

This matters for who should consider it: Pagely isn't trying to compete with $3/month shared hosting, and its plans, support model and infrastructure choices reflect that. If your reference point for "hosting" is a budget host's control panel and pricing, Pagely will look unusually expensive and unusually specialized by comparison — because it's solving a different problem.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and is subject to change — always check Pagely's current pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Price | Sites | Storage | Bandwidth | CDN |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| StartPress | $99/mo | 5 | 30GB SSD | 50GB | 150GB |
| DevPress | $199/mo | 10 | 30GB SSD | 100GB | 350GB |
| LitePress | $299/mo | 15 | 50GB SSD | 150GB | 500GB |
| ProPress | $499/mo | 35 | 50GB SSD | 200GB | 1TB |
| PowerPress | $999/mo | 60 | 50GB SSD | 300GB | 2TB |
| ScalePress | Custom | Custom | Custom | Custom | Custom |

All plans include PressCACHE (Pagely's caching layer), a global WordPress CDN, advanced network security, and security/performance analytics dashboards. Notably absent from lower tiers: PressTHUMB (automatic image optimization) and WordPress Multisite support are not included on LitePress or below, and Elasticsearch is limited to Pro-tier plans (ProPress) and above. If your site needs any of those specifically, check the tier requirement before choosing a plan by price alone.

## Real cost breakdown

The entry-level StartPress plan lists at $99/month, though Pagely runs promotional pricing periodically that can bring the effective rate down — treat $99/month as the number to budget around rather than assuming a permanent discount. Unlike shared hosts that lure buyers with a steep multi-year discount that jumps at renewal, Pagely's pricing structure is flatter and more transparent tier-to-tier, but it starts from a much higher baseline. There's no cheap "just to get started" tier the way there is with commodity hosts — the cheapest plan is already priced for a business that depends on its site staying up.

Migrations onto Pagely are free, which offsets some of the switching cost for a site moving from another managed host. Beyond the listed plan price, there don't appear to be mandatory add-on fees baked into the base tiers based on available documentation, though enterprise-tier (ScalePress) pricing is fully custom and quote-based, so it's worth getting an explicit quote rather than assuming a number.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **StartPress** if you're running a handful of WordPress sites (up to 5) that need reliable, AWS-backed hosting but don't need heavy storage or bandwidth — a good starting point for an agency managing a small client portfolio.

Choose **DevPress or LitePress** if you're scaling past a handful of sites (10-15) or need more storage headroom — LitePress's 50GB SSD tier is double StartPress's allowance.

Choose **ProPress or PowerPress** if you're running a larger portfolio (35-60 sites), need Elasticsearch for search-heavy WordPress builds, or require WordPress Multisite support, since both are gated to this tier and above.

Choose **ScalePress (Enterprise)** if you're a large publisher, SaaS company or brand with custom infrastructure, compliance or uptime requirements that a standard tier can't cover — this is a quote-based conversation with Pagely's sales team, not a self-serve signup.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| No visitor/pageview caps on any plan | Entry price ($99/mo) is far above mainstream hosts |
| Built on AWS with dedicated security/network layers | No cPanel — must learn Pagely's own Atomic panel |
| Free migrations included | Money-back guarantee not clearly published |
| Scales cleanly from small agency use to enterprise | Some features (Multisite, Elasticsearch, PressTHUMB) gated above entry tiers |
| Strong support responsiveness (ticket + live chat) | Overkill and poor value for small, low-traffic sites |

## Support

Pagely offers ticket-based and live chat support across all plans rather than reserving live channels for higher tiers. Independent reporting on Pagely's support responsiveness cites roughly 79% of tickets answered within an hour and a customer satisfaction rating around 99% over a recent six-month period, though these figures come from third-party review aggregation rather than Pagely's own published stats, so treat them as directional rather than exact.

## Migration

Pagely includes free site migrations for new customers moving an existing WordPress site onto its platform. Given that Pagely's stack is AWS-based and runs through its own Atomic panel rather than cPanel, having the migration handled by Pagely's team is more valuable here than it would be moving between two cPanel-based hosts, where a plugin-based migration is often straightforward to do yourself.

## Where it's a strong fit

- High-traffic WordPress sites that would get throttled or hit overage fees on visitor-capped budget hosting
- Agencies or businesses running a portfolio of WordPress sites that want AWS-grade infrastructure without managing AWS directly
- Enterprise and publisher-scale sites where uptime and dedicated support justify a premium price
- Teams that specifically want to avoid vendor lock-in to cPanel-based workflows and are comfortable learning a new panel

## Where to think twice

- Solo bloggers, small local business sites, or anyone comparing hosting purely on lowest monthly price
- Sites that need cPanel specifically, for compatibility with existing scripts, staff familiarity, or migration tooling
- Buyers who want a clearly stated, guaranteed refund window before committing, since Pagely's pricing page doesn't spell one out
- Anyone needing WordPress Multisite or Elasticsearch on a tight budget, since both require stepping up past the entry tiers

## Bottom line

Pagely earns its premium positioning by building specifically for WordPress sites that can't afford downtime — AWS infrastructure, no visitor caps, and a support team responsive enough to back up the price. It's a legitimate option for agencies and enterprise WordPress operations, but it is not, and doesn't try to be, a fit for small or budget-sensitive sites; StartPress at $99/month is the cheapest way in, and that's still a different market entirely from the $3-10/month shared-hosting tier most small sites shop in.

## FAQs

**Is Pagely good for beginners?**
Not particularly — Pagely is built for teams and businesses that already understand managed WordPress hosting and need enterprise-grade infrastructure. Its Atomic control panel and AWS-based setup have a learning curve, and its pricing isn't aimed at first-time site owners.

**Does Pagely support cPanel?**
No. Pagely uses its own proprietary control panel, Atomic, across all plans. There's no cPanel option.

**What's the cheapest Pagely plan?**
StartPress, at $99/month list price, is the entry-level plan, covering up to 5 WordPress sites, 30GB SSD storage and 50GB bandwidth.

**Does Pagely cap traffic or pageviews?**
No — none of Pagely's plans cap visitors or pageviews. Plans are differentiated by number of sites, storage and bandwidth/CDN allowance instead.

**Is migration to Pagely free?**
Yes, Pagely includes free migrations for new customers moving an existing WordPress site onto the platform.

**Does Pagely offer a money-back guarantee?**
Pagely doesn't publish a specific money-back guarantee window on its pricing page. Confirm current refund terms directly with Pagely's sales team before purchasing.

**What's Pagely's customer rating?**
Pagely holds a 4.5-out-of-5 rating on Trustpilot, though based on a small sample of 15 reviews with no new reviews logged in the past 12 months — worth noting as a limited data point rather than a high-volume signal.

**Who are Pagely's plans built for?**
Pagely targets high-traffic WordPress sites, agencies managing multiple client sites, and enterprise/publisher-scale operations — its ScalePress enterprise tier is custom-quoted for large deployments with bespoke infrastructure needs.

Ready to compare pricing? Check the [Pagely coupon page](/coupons/pagely) for current offers, or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) across other providers.

title: Pantheon Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: An evidence-based look at Pantheon's managed WordPress/Drupal hosting, its Dev/Test/Live workflow, real pricing tiers, and who it's actually built for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Pantheon good hosting for WordPress or Drupal?

Pantheon is a solid choice if you're a developer or agency that wants a structured Dev/Test/Live workflow with Git version control baked in, but it's overkill and expensive for a simple personal site. It's built for teams managing WordPress or Drupal sites professionally, not budget shared hosting.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $41/month (Basic, annual prepay) |
| Renewal/monthly-billed price | $55/month (Basic, billed monthly) |
| Control panel | Proprietary dashboard (no cPanel) |
| Uptime guarantee | 99.9% SLA on Performance plans and above |
| Money-back guarantee | None published — free trial before going live instead |
| Best for | Agencies and developers running WordPress/Drupal sites |

Pricing above was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check [Pantheon's pricing page](https://pantheon.io/plans/pricing) for current rates before buying.

## What Pantheon actually is

Pantheon is a managed WebOps platform for WordPress and Drupal, not a general-purpose web host. It doesn't sell email hosting, domain registration bundles, or a cPanel-style file manager the way budget shared hosts do. Instead, every site gets three separate environments — Dev, Test and Live — each running in its own container, with integrated Git version control for moving code between them. The pitch is aimed squarely at developers and agencies who need a repeatable way to build, test and ship changes to a WordPress or Drupal site without touching production directly.

That focus shows up in who Pantheon markets to: consultants managing one client site, agencies running dozens, and internal teams at larger organizations running Drupal at scale. It is not positioned as a first host for someone who just wants to point a domain at a blog and forget about it.

## Pricing

| Plan | Price | Monthly visits | What's included |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic | $41/month (annual) or $55/month (monthly billing) | 25K-35K | 20GB SSD storage, 125K pages served, Dev/Test/Live workflow |
| Performance Small | Starts around $200/month | 25K | 99.9% uptime SLA, New Relic Pro monitoring, Solr search |
| Performance Medium | Starts around $350/month | 50K | Same as Small, higher traffic allowance |
| Performance Large | Starts around $700/month | 150K | Same as Small, higher traffic allowance |
| Performance XL | Starts around $1,150/month | 300K | Same as Small, higher traffic allowance |
| Elite | Custom pricing | Unlimited | Dedicated infrastructure, 4+ application containers, replica database, concierge support |

## Real cost breakdown

Pantheon's headline number is the Basic plan at $41/month, but that rate requires annual prepayment — billed monthly, Basic runs $55/month instead. There's no long-term promotional-then-renewal trap like you'd see on budget shared hosting (Pantheon's list prices are what you pay from day one), but the jump from Basic to Performance Small is steep: from roughly $41-55/month to around $200/month, mainly to unlock the 99.9% uptime SLA and performance monitoring. Elite tier pricing isn't published at all and requires a sales conversation, which is typical for platforms selling into agencies and enterprises rather than individual site owners.

There's no traditional money-back guarantee. Instead, Pantheon lets you build and test a site for free and only starts billing once you connect a custom domain and go live — functionally similar to a free trial, but open-ended rather than a fixed refund window.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Basic** if you're a freelancer or small agency hosting a single low-traffic WordPress or Drupal site and mainly want the Dev/Test/Live workflow without paying for uptime SLAs you don't need yet.
- **Choose a Performance plan** if the site is customer-facing and traffic-sensitive — an ecommerce storefront, a marketing site tied to campaigns, or anything where downtime has a real cost — since this tier is where the uptime SLA and New Relic monitoring kick in.
- **Choose Elite** if you're running Drupal or WordPress at genuine enterprise scale and need dedicated infrastructure, replica databases, or concierge-level support that a self-serve plan won't cover.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Dev/Test/Live workflow with Git integration on every plan | Trustpilot rating is low (2.5/5 from 18 reviews) |
| Free trial — no charge until you go live with a custom domain | No traditional money-back guarantee once live |
| Purpose-built for WordPress and Drupal, not a generic all-purpose host | Meaningfully pricier than shared hosting once past Basic |
| Uptime SLA and performance monitoring on Performance tier and above | No cPanel — requires comfort with a code-driven deployment workflow |
| Elite tier scales to dedicated infrastructure for large deployments | Elite pricing isn't published; requires a sales call |

## Support

Pantheon's support is oriented toward technical users rather than live chat for general questions — expect ticket-based support with response times that scale by plan tier, and dedicated/concierge support reserved for Elite customers. It is not built around the 24/7 live-chat model that budget shared hosts lean on; the assumption is that a developer or agency using Pantheon already has the technical context to work through documentation and structured support channels.

## Migration

Pantheon doesn't advertise a blanket free-migration service the way some budget hosts bundle one in. It provides migration guides and tooling for moving WordPress and Drupal sites onto the platform, and offers paid professional migration services for more complex builds. If you're moving a straightforward WordPress site, the self-serve tooling is generally enough; a large or heavily customized Drupal site is more likely to need the paid migration path.

## Where it's a strong fit

Pantheon makes sense for agencies managing multiple client sites who want a consistent, repeatable deployment workflow across all of them, and for teams running Drupal specifically — a CMS Pantheon has deep roots in. It's also a reasonable fit for any WordPress team that wants proper staging environments and Git-based deployments without building that infrastructure themselves.

## Where to think twice

If you're hosting a single small site on a tight budget, Pantheon's pricing structure doesn't compete with budget shared hosting — you're paying for workflow infrastructure you may not need. It's also not the right pick if your team wants a point-and-click cPanel experience rather than a Git-driven deployment process, or if you need hosting for anything other than WordPress or Drupal, since that's the entire focus of the platform.

## Bottom line

Pantheon does one thing well: giving WordPress and Drupal teams a proper Dev/Test/Live workflow with version control built in, and it backs that with real infrastructure (uptime SLAs, monitoring) once you move past the entry plan. That focus comes at a real price gap versus shared hosting, and the public Trustpilot reviews skew negative, so it's worth weighing that alongside the platform's technical strengths before committing — especially for anything beyond a single low-traffic site. For an agency or developer who values the workflow model over drag-and-drop simplicity, it's a legitimate option; for a budget-conscious single-site owner, it's likely more platform than you need.

Check the [Pantheon coupon page](/coupons/pantheon) for current offers, or browse [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) for budget-friendly alternatives if Pantheon's pricing doesn't fit.

## FAQs

**Does Pantheon use cPanel?**
No. Pantheon runs a proprietary dashboard centered on Dev/Test/Live environments and Git version control, not cPanel.

**How much does Pantheon cost?**
The Basic plan starts at $41/month paid annually (or $55/month billed monthly). Performance plans start around $200/month and scale up based on traffic allowance, with Elite pricing custom-quoted.

**Does Pantheon offer a free trial?**
Yes. You can build and test a site on Pantheon for free and aren't charged until you connect a custom domain and take the site live.

**Is there a money-back guarantee?**
Pantheon doesn't publish a traditional money-back guarantee. The free-trial-before-going-live model serves a similar risk-reducing purpose instead.

**What is the Dev/Test/Live workflow?**
It's three separate environments per site — Dev, Test and Live — each in its own container, letting you push code changes up the chain and pull content down without ever editing production directly.

**Does Pantheon offer free migration?**
Not as a blanket free service. Pantheon provides migration guides and tooling for self-serve moves, with paid professional migration services available for complex sites.

**Is Pantheon good for a small personal blog?**
Generally not the best fit. Its pricing and Git-driven workflow are built for developers and agencies; a small personal blog will likely find better value on budget shared hosting.

**Does Pantheon support WordPress and Drupal equally?**
Yes, both are first-class citizens on the platform, with Pantheon having particularly deep roots in the Drupal community alongside its WordPress hosting product.

title: Pressable Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Pressable is Automattic's managed WordPress host, priced by monthly visits. Here's how its plans, pricing and support actually hold up.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Pressable Review 2026: Is Managed WordPress Hosting Worth It?

Pressable is a managed WordPress host owned by Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com and Jetpack. It's a solid fit if you run one or more WordPress sites and want dedicated resources, unlimited free migrations and hands-on WordPress support — but its visit-metered pricing means it's a poor match for a low-tier plan with unpredictable traffic spikes, since overages get billed per extra visit and per extra GB of storage.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $20.83/month (billed $250/year), $25/month on monthly billing |
| Entry plan limits | 1 site, 30,000 visits/month, 20GB storage |
| Control panel | Custom Pressable dashboard (not cPanel) |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days |
| Free migration | Yes, unlimited WordPress site migrations |
| Best for | WordPress-only sites and agencies that want managed support over raw control-panel access |

## What Pressable actually is

Pressable is not a general-purpose shared host — it hosts WordPress exclusively, and it's owned by Automattic, the same company that runs WordPress.com and develops Jetpack. That ownership shows up in the product: every Signature plan bundles Jetpack Security (Pressable lists this as a $239/year value) and the infrastructure is built around WordPress-specific performance features rather than a generic LAMP stack.

There's no cPanel on any plan. Site management happens through Pressable's own dashboard, which is purpose-built for WordPress — creating sites, managing backups, and handling staging environments rather than the general server-administration tools cPanel exposes. If you're coming from a cPanel host, expect a different (narrower, WordPress-focused) set of controls, not a like-for-like swap.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of September 2026 and can change — check Pressable's current pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Sites | Monthly visits | Storage | Price (annual) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Signature 1 | 1 | 30,000 | 20GB | $20.83/month ($250/year) |
| Signature 3 | 5 | 75,000 | 35GB | Higher tier, priced on Pressable's site |
| Signature 5 | 20 | 400,000 | 80GB | Higher tier, priced on Pressable's site |
| Signature 8 | 100 | 2,000,000 | 325GB | Higher tier, priced on Pressable's site |

Pressable also sells Premium Site Plans for enterprise needs, which add a 100% uptime SLA — not offered on the standard Signature tiers.

## Real cost breakdown

The headline $20.83/month rate for Signature 1 requires paying $250 upfront for a full year. Paying month to month instead costs $25/month with no annual commitment — a real, non-trivial premium for flexibility, but a smaller gap than the multi-year lock-in discounts common at budget shared hosts.

The bigger cost variable isn't the base plan — it's overages. Every Signature tier has a hard visit and storage allowance, and going over either one triggers metered charges: roughly $1.20 per extra 1,000 monthly visits and $1.00 per extra GB of storage. A site that occasionally spikes past 30,000 visits on Signature 1 will get billed for the overage rather than throttled, so the real monthly cost of a growing or spiky site can run noticeably higher than the advertised entry price. Size your plan for your typical traffic, not your average traffic, if spikes are a regular pattern for your site.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Signature 1** if you're running a single WordPress blog, brochure site or small WooCommerce store comfortably under 30,000 monthly visits.
- **Choose Signature 3** if you manage a handful of client or personal sites (up to 5) with moderate combined traffic.
- **Choose Signature 5** if you're an agency managing around 20 sites, or a single higher-traffic WordPress property pushing several hundred thousand visits a month.
- **Choose Signature 8 or a Premium Site Plan** if you're hosting a large portfolio (up to 100 sites) or need the 100% uptime SLA that only the Premium tier offers.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Unlimited free WordPress migrations on every plan | No cPanel — custom dashboard only |
| Dedicated PHP workers per site (5 vCPUs) | Visit/storage overage fees can raise real cost |
| Jetpack Security bundled in | WordPress-only — no other CMS or general hosting |
| 24/7 support with fast first response | 100% uptime SLA reserved for Premium plans, not Signature tiers |
| Hourly and daily backup options | Entry plan's 30,000-visit cap is easy to outgrow |

## Support

Pressable offers 24/7 support, and the company advertises an average first-response time of around four minutes — fast for a managed host. Because Pressable is Automattic-owned, support staff are working within a WordPress-specific stack all day, which tends to mean deeper WordPress troubleshooting knowledge than a generalist shared-hosting support team, though it also means support won't help with non-WordPress server questions since the platform doesn't host anything else.

## Migration

Every Signature plan includes unlimited free WordPress site migrations, handled by Pressable's own team rather than left to a plugin or a DIY export/import. This is a genuine differentiator versus hosts that charge per-migration or cap free migrations to a single site — if you're moving several client sites over, this alone can offset switching-cost friction that would otherwise apply per site.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Agencies or freelancers managing multiple WordPress client sites who want migrations handled for them.

## Where to think twice

- Non-WordPress projects — Pressable doesn't host other CMS platforms or general-purpose sites.
- Budget shoppers comparing against multi-year discounted shared hosting, where Pressable's per-visit metered model is priced differently and won't look competitive on a simple sticker-price basis.

## Bottom line

Pressable is a capable, WordPress-only managed host backed by Automattic's WordPress expertise, with real advantages for agencies and multi-site operators: unlimited free migrations, dedicated resources per site, and bundled Jetpack Security. It earns a strong 4.6-star Trustpilot rating across 302 reviews, suggesting most customers are satisfied with the support and reliability. The trade-off is the visit-metered pricing model — it rewards accurately sizing your plan to actual traffic and penalizes guessing low, so it's worth confirming your typical monthly visits before committing to a tier.

Check the current [Pressable coupon page](/coupons/pressable) for available offers, or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) to compare against other managed and shared hosting options.

title: RackNerd Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: RackNerd offers budget KVM VPS hosting with rotating flash-sale pricing and no default cPanel. Here's the real pricing, specs and verdict.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## RackNerd Review 2026: Is This Budget VPS Host Worth It?

RackNerd is a budget VPS provider built around rotating flash-sale pricing rather than a fixed rate card — you can get a 1GB KVM VPS for well under $2/month during a promotion. It does not include cPanel by default; plans ship with SolusVM instead, and cPanel only shows up occasionally as a paid add-on on specific deals.

## At a glance

| Fact | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Entry price | ~$21.99/year for 1GB RAM, 1 vCPU, 20GB SSD, 3TB bandwidth (deal pricing, rotates) |
| Billing | Primarily annual, deal-driven; rates change between promotions |
| Control panel | SolusVM included; cPanel not bundled by default, occasionally a paid add-on |
| Data centers | ~20 locations, including Los Angeles, Dallas, New York, Chicago, Atlanta, Ashburn, Amsterdam, London, Frankfurt, Dublin, Singapore |
| Trustpilot rating | 4.1/5 from 377 reviews |
| Best for | Developers and sysadmins comfortable managing a server without a bundled control panel |

## What RackNerd actually is

RackNerd is not a shared-hosting company with a polished dashboard aimed at beginners — it's a VPS and dedicated-server provider whose entire go-to-market is aggressive, time-limited deal pricing. Its own specials page runs an active countdown timer on plan pricing, and the specific dollar figure for a given RAM/CPU/storage combination shifts from one promotion to the next rather than sitting on a static price list.

That model has upside and a real catch. The upside: genuinely cheap compute if you catch a good promo and don't need hand-holding. The catch: because pricing is deal-based, the number you see today may not be the number available next month, and different customers can end up paying different amounts for functionally the same VPS depending on which sale they bought into.

On the software side, every plan is a KVM-based VPS with full root access, managed through SolusVM rather than a web-hosting control panel like cPanel or Plesk. This makes RackNerd a fit for people who are going to SSH in and configure their own stack (Docker, a LAMP/LEMP setup, a game server, a VPN, etc.), not people who want to click around a dashboard to install WordPress in two minutes.

## Pricing table

Pricing was accurate as of September 2026 and pulled from RackNerd's own specials page — because RackNerd runs flash-sale pricing, treat these as a snapshot rather than a guaranteed rate, and check the live specials page before buying.

| Plan | RAM | vCPU | SSD | Bandwidth | Price (annual) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 GB | 1 GB | 1 | 20 GB | 3 TB/mo | $21.99/yr |
| 2 GB | 2 GB | 2 | 35 GB | 5 TB/mo | $35.99/yr |
| 4 GB | 4 GB | 3 | 60 GB | 7 TB/mo | $59.99/yr |
| 6 GB | 6 GB | 6 | 100 GB | 12 TB/mo | $89.99/yr |
| 8 GB | 8 GB | 7 | 150 GB | 20 TB/mo | $119.99/yr |

## Real cost breakdown

Unlike shared-hosting hosts that lure you in with a low intro rate and a much higher renewal, RackNerd's model is different: it's the sale price itself that's the moving part, not a bait-and-switch between year one and year two. In practice that still means the same discipline applies — don't assume the price you screenshot today will still be on the page tomorrow, and don't assume your renewal will match your first invoice, since it depends on whatever promotion is live when the plan comes up for renewal or whether RackNerd's standard (non-promo) rate applies instead.

There's no bundled domain, no bundled email hosting, and no bundled cPanel license in the base price — a VPS is raw compute, so anything beyond the OS image (a control panel, a mail server, a CDN) is either self-managed or an added line item if RackNerd offers it as an add-on on a given deal.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose the 1GB plan if you're running a single lightweight service — a personal VPN, a small Node/Python app, a Minecraft-adjacent hobby server, or a testing box you don't mind rebuilding.

Choose the 2GB or 4GB plan if you're self-hosting something with a database attached — a small WordPress site you're managing yourself via SSH, a Nextcloud instance, or a couple of low-traffic sites sharing one VPS.

Choose the 6GB or 8GB plan if you're running multiple sites/services on one box, a CI runner, or something with real memory pressure (search indexing, a cache layer, a small game server cluster).

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Frequent deep-discount VPS deals | Pricing is deal-based, not a stable published rate |
| Full root access with KVM virtualization | No cPanel bundled by default |
| Wide spread of data center locations (~20) | Better suited to technical users than beginners |
| Solid Trustpilot standing (4.1/5, 377 reviews) | Support depth varies by ticket volume during sale rushes |

## Support

RackNerd offers ticket-based support through its client area, and Trustpilot data shows the company replies to essentially all reviews, including negative ones, typically within about two weeks — a sign of active engagement, though that response window also suggests support isn't always same-day. There's no live chat positioned as the primary support channel the way some shared hosts advertise; expect a support-ticket workflow rather than instant chat.

## Migration

Because RackNerd VPS plans are unmanaged by default, migrating an existing site or app to RackNerd generally means handling the move yourself: spinning up the new VPS, installing whatever stack you need (LAMP, LEMP, Docker, etc.), and manually transferring files/databases or restoring a backup — there's no white-glove cPanel-to-cPanel migration tool baked into the base plan the way some shared hosts offer. If you rely on a control panel for migrations, factor in either buying that add-on where available or doing the migration at the command line.

## Where it's a strong fit

RackNerd works well for developers, sysadmins, and hobbyists who know their way around a terminal and want cheap, reasonably capable compute without paying for a bundled control panel or managed-support layer they won't use. It's also a reasonable pick for anyone who wants to place a workload in a specific region, given the wide geographic spread of data centers.

## Where to think twice

If you want a beginner-friendly, one-click-install hosting experience — install WordPress, manage backups, and never touch a terminal — RackNerd's unmanaged, SolusVM-based VPS is the wrong shape of product. Shared hosting with cPanel (like Namecheap) or a hosting-specific control panel (like Hostinger's hPanel) will get you there with far less setup work. Also think twice if price stability matters more to you than price minimums — RackNerd's deal-driven model means the rate you lock in isn't guaranteed to look the same on your next renewal cycle.

## Bottom line

RackNerd earns its reputation as a budget VPS option for people who don't need a control panel handed to them — the specs-per-dollar on its flash-sale pricing are hard to beat if you're comfortable managing a server yourself, and its Trustpilot record (4.1/5 across 377 reviews) suggests it delivers on that narrow promise reasonably reliably. Just go in knowing this is unmanaged infrastructure with rotating pricing, not turnkey web hosting, and check the live specials page rather than trusting any single quoted price to still be current.

## FAQs

**Is RackNerd good for beginners?**
Not particularly. RackNerd's VPS plans don't include a hosting control panel like cPanel by default, so you're expected to manage the server yourself via SSH and SolusVM. Beginners who want a point-and-click experience are usually better served by shared hosting.

**Does RackNerd offer cPanel?**
Not as a standard inclusion. RackNerd's base VPS plans use SolusVM for VPS-level management. cPanel is occasionally offered as a paid add-on or bundled into specific promotional deals, but it isn't part of the default plan.

**Why does RackNerd's pricing keep changing?**
RackNerd markets primarily through time-limited flash sales rather than a fixed price list, so the rate for a given RAM/CPU/storage combination can differ between promotions. Always check the live specials page for the current price before buying.

**What virtualization does RackNerd use?**
RackNerd's VPS plans run on KVM, which provides full virtualization and root access, as opposed to container-based virtualization with more limited isolation.

**How many data center locations does RackNerd have?**
Roughly 20, spanning North America (including Los Angeles, Dallas, New York, Chicago, Atlanta and Ashburn) and international locations such as Amsterdam, London, Frankfurt, Dublin and Singapore.

**What's RackNerd's Trustpilot rating?**
4.1 out of 5 stars from 377 reviews as of this writing, with RackNerd responding to a high share of reviews including negative ones.

**Does RackNerd help migrate my existing site?**
Not with an automated built-in tool on standard plans — since the VPS is unmanaged, moving an existing site typically means manually setting up the stack and transferring files/databases yourself, or paying for a managed migration if RackNerd offers one on a given deal.

**Is RackNerd billed monthly or annually?**
RackNerd's best-known deals are typically annual, though billing terms can vary by specific promotion — check the term length on whichever deal you're considering before checkout.

Ready to compare pricing? Check the [RackNerd coupon page](/coupons/racknerd) for current offers, or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting).

title: Rocket.net Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
