body:
## Is Microsoft Azure good for website hosting?

This review covers Azure strictly as a website-hosting option — Azure App Service, Microsoft's PaaS for web apps, plus a brief look at Virtual Machines — not Azure's full cloud catalog. App Service is solid for developers already on Microsoft's stack, with a real free tier, but its pricing and setup assume cloud familiarity, not beginner-friendliness.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $0/month (F1 Free tier) |
| Entry paid tier | ~$13/month (B1 Basic, Linux) |
| Autoscaling tier | ~$57/month (S1 Standard) |
| Uptime guarantee | 99.95% SLA (Standard tier and above) |
| Money-back guarantee | None published — usage-based billing, case-by-case refunds |
| Best for | Developers deploying app-based sites who already use Azure/Microsoft tooling |

## What Azure actually is (for hosting purposes)

Azure is Microsoft's full cloud computing platform — spanning databases, AI services, networking, identity management and hundreds of other products. That's far outside what this review covers. For website hosting specifically, the relevant product is **Azure App Service**, a managed platform-as-a-service (PaaS) that runs your code (Node.js, Python, .NET, Java, PHP, or a custom container) without you managing the underlying server, OS patching, or web server config.

The other option comparable to a traditional host is **Azure Virtual Machines** — a self-managed VM where you install and run your own stack (Nginx, Apache, whatever you want), billed by compute time. VMs give more control but none of App Service's managed conveniences: no built-in deployment slots, no one-click autoscale rules, no managed OS patching.

Most people evaluating Azure against a conventional web host should be thinking about App Service, not the rest of Azure's catalog — and definitely not the full platform. This review sticks to that scope.

## App Service pricing

| Tier | Specs | Price (Linux, approx.) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 Free | Shared CPU, 1GB RAM, 1GB storage | $0/month | 60 CPU min/day cap, no custom domain |
| B1 Basic | 1 vCPU, 1.75GB RAM, 10GB storage | ~$13/month | Custom domain + SSL, manual scaling only |
| S1 Standard | 1 vCPU, 1.75GB RAM, 10GB storage | ~$57/month | Autoscaling, staging slots, daily backups |
| P1v3 Premium v3 | 2 vCPU, 8GB RAM, 250GB storage | ~$110-125/month | Faster autoscale, network isolation options |

Pricing was accurate as of this review's publish date and varies by region, currency and purchase option — reserved instances or savings-plan commitments can cut the pay-as-you-go rate noticeably. Confirm current numbers on Azure's own App Service pricing page before budgeting.

## Real cost breakdown

There's no long-term "intro price that renews higher" model here the way there is with shared hosts — Azure bills pay-as-you-go by the hour/second for whatever tier you're running, with no minimum term. That means the entry cost is genuinely $0 (F1 Free) if your site fits inside the free tier's 60 CPU minutes/day, but any real production site with sustained traffic needs at least Basic (~$13/month) for a custom domain, and Standard (~$57/month) if you want autoscaling or staging slots — a meaningfully higher jump than a $3-5/month shared-hosting plan. Add-ons like a custom domain's SSL certificate are typically free (Azure-managed certs), but bandwidth, storage and any attached database (Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, etc.) are billed separately on top of the App Service plan itself.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose F1 Free** if you're testing a small app, prototyping, or running a personal project with negligible traffic — it's genuinely free, not a time-limited trial.
- **Choose B1 Basic** if you're launching a small production site with a custom domain and steady (not spiky) traffic, and you're comfortable resizing manually if traffic grows.
- **Choose S1 Standard** if you need autoscaling, staging/deployment slots for testing before going live, or automated backups — this is the realistic floor for a business site that can't tolerate manual intervention during traffic spikes.
- **Choose Premium v3** if you're running a higher-traffic app that needs more compute headroom, faster autoscale response, or VNet integration for security/compliance requirements.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Real permanent free tier (F1), not a time-limited trial | Pricing and setup assume cloud/DevOps familiarity, not beginner-friendly |
| Managed PaaS — no OS patching or server admin | No published money-back guarantee on consumed usage |
| Deep integration with Azure SQL, Active Directory, and other Microsoft services | Meaningfully pricier than shared hosting once you need autoscaling (Standard tier) |
| Autoscaling and deployment slots on Standard tier and above | Trustpilot sentiment for azure.microsoft.com skews negative, driven mostly by billing/support complaints rather than App Service itself |
| 99.95% SLA on Standard tier and above | Multi-region/Isolated tiers can get expensive fast for high-traffic sites |

## Support

Azure support is tiered by plan: free Basic support (billing/subscription help only) is included with every account, while technical support for App Service issues requires a paid support plan (Developer, Standard, or Professional Direct), each with its own response-time SLA. There's no live chat for free-tier users the way many budget hosts offer — expect ticket-based support unless you're paying for a support plan, plus extensive self-serve documentation on Microsoft Learn and an active developer community on Stack Overflow and Microsoft Q&A.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to App Service isn't a one-click import like cPanel-to-cPanel migrations on shared hosts. For a code-based app (Node, Python, .NET, PHP, Java), you typically connect a Git repo or set up CI/CD (GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps) and deploy from there, or push a container image if you're already using Docker. There's no drag-and-drop file manager migration path for a static HTML site the way traditional hosts offer — App Service expects an app deployment, not an FTP upload, which is the biggest adjustment for anyone coming from shared hosting.

## Where it's a strong fit

Azure App Service makes sense if you're already building on Microsoft's stack — .NET apps, Azure SQL, Active Directory integration — or need a managed PaaS that scales without managing servers yourself, with predictable per-second billing and genuine enterprise SLAs at the Standard tier and above.

## Where to think twice

This isn't for beginners who want a drag-and-drop website builder or a cheap shared-hosting bill. If you just need to publish a WordPress site or a simple brochure site, App Service's pricing model and deployment workflow are overkill compared to a $3-5/month shared host — and Azure's own Trustpilot presence (a low 1.4/5 average across 57 reviews) reflects real frustration, concentrated in billing and support experiences rather than App Service's technical reliability specifically.

## Verdict

Azure App Service is a capable, genuinely scalable PaaS for hosting code-based web apps, with a real free tier and solid uptime SLAs once you're on Standard or above — but it's built for developers, not for someone who wants the simplicity of a traditional shared host. If your project is a standard website rather than an app needing Microsoft's cloud ecosystem, a dedicated web host will likely be cheaper and far less setup work. Check the [Microsoft Azure coupon page](/coupons/azure) for current offers, or browse [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) for simpler alternatives.

## FAQs

**Is Azure App Service free?**
There's a genuine Free (F1) tier — 60 CPU minutes/day, 1GB RAM, 1GB storage, no custom domain — that doesn't expire on a trial clock. It's separate from the broader $200/30-day Azure free-account credit new sign-ups get.

**How much does Azure App Service cost for a real website?**
Expect roughly $13/month for Basic (custom domain, manual scaling) or roughly $57/month for Standard (autoscaling, staging slots, backups) on Linux, billed pay-as-you-go with no minimum term.

**Does Azure App Service have a money-back guarantee?**
No published blanket guarantee — you're billed for compute already used, and refund requests go through Microsoft billing support case-by-case rather than a fixed refund window.

**Can I host a WordPress site on Azure?**
Technically yes, via App Service's PHP support or a WordPress-specific Azure Marketplace image, but it's more setup than a WordPress-optimized shared host and isn't the product's strong suit.

**Is Azure good for beginners?**
Not particularly. App Service assumes some familiarity with Git-based deployment, cloud pricing models and (for anything beyond Free/Basic) autoscale configuration — it's built for developers, not first-time website owners.

**What's the difference between App Service and Azure Virtual Machines for hosting?**
App Service is managed PaaS — Microsoft handles the OS and patching, you deploy code. Virtual Machines are self-managed — you install and maintain your own web server stack, with more control but more admin overhead.

**Does Azure App Service support autoscaling?**
Yes, but only from the Standard (S1) tier upward — the Basic tier requires manual scaling.

**How reliable is Azure App Service?**
Standard tier and above carries a 99.95% SLA. Independent review sentiment for Azure's broader site (Trustpilot) skews negative, but that largely reflects billing/account-support complaints rather than App Service uptime specifically.

title: BigRock Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: BigRock review: cPanel shared hosting pricing, renewal costs, free SSL, support and migration — is India's top domain registrar worth hosting with?
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is BigRock good for hosting a website?

BigRock is a solid, budget-friendly pick if you're already buying an Indian domain there and want cPanel hosting without shopping around — it's cheap on the first term, includes free SSL, and support is generally responsive. It's a weaker pick if you want a bundled free domain or the lowest possible renewal cost, since renewals run well above the promo rate.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | ~₹69–159/mo (longest prepaid term) |
| Renewal price | Roughly 2–3x the intro rate |
| Control panel | cPanel (Linux) / Plesk-style panel (Windows) |
| Free SSL | Yes |
| Free domain | No, not bundled with hosting |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days (first-time accounts, hosting fees only) |
| Best for | Indian domain owners wanting a familiar cPanel host |

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check BigRock's live rate card before buying.

## What BigRock actually is

BigRock is one of India's largest domain registrars, and its hosting business runs alongside that — cPanel-based Linux shared hosting, a Windows/Plesk equivalent, reseller hosting, and unmanaged VPS. It's part of the same corporate family as other Indian-market hosts under the Endurance/Newfold umbrella, which is why its plan structure and support tooling will feel familiar if you've used a sibling brand before. The pitch is straightforward: register your domain and host it in one place, on infrastructure aimed at Indian small businesses and freelancers rather than global enterprise buyers.

Linux shared hosting comes in four tiers — Starter, Advanced, Business and Pro — moving from a single-site entry plan up to multi-site plans with more storage, email accounts and database limits. Windows hosting mirrors that structure with Essential, Premium, Business and Pro tiers for sites that specifically need ASP.NET or MSSQL.

## Pricing

| Plan | Best for | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Starter | One small site | cPanel, SSD storage, free SSL, limited email accounts |
| Advanced | A growing single site | More storage/bandwidth headroom, more email accounts |
| Business | A few sites | Multiple domains, higher resource limits |
| Pro | Freelancers/agencies | Highest resource ceiling on shared infrastructure |

BigRock's cheapest advertised rate requires paying for the longest available term — up to five years upfront — which is how the per-month figure gets pushed down toward the ₹69–159 range. Shorter one-year terms cost noticeably more per month from the outset.

## Real cost breakdown: intro vs. renewal

The number BigRock puts in front of you at checkout is a promotional first-term rate, not a fixed monthly cost. Like most Indian budget hosts, BigRock's renewal pricing is meaningfully higher than the intro rate — commonly cited at two to three times the promotional figure once your prepaid term ends. Because the lowest headline price is tied to the longest commitment, you're effectively locking in years of hosting before you find out what the renewal actually costs.

Two things to check before you buy:
- The exact renewal price shown at checkout for the term length you're picking (it varies by term — 1-year, 2-year, 3-year and 5-year commitments each have different intro and renewal figures).
- Whether a free domain is included — BigRock hosting plans generally do **not** bundle a free domain the way some competitors do, so factor in domain registration as a separate line item.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Starter** if you're launching a single small site — a portfolio, a local business page, a simple blog — and don't need multiple domains or heavy email use.
- **Choose Advanced** if your one site is growing and you're starting to bump into storage or bandwidth limits, or you want more mailboxes.
- **Choose Business** if you're running two or three separate sites (personal + a side project, for example) and want them on one account.
- **Choose Pro** if you're a freelancer or small agency hosting several client sites on shared infrastructure and want the highest resource ceiling before stepping up to VPS.
- **Skip shared hosting entirely** and look at BigRock's unmanaged VPS if you need root access or your site's traffic has outgrown what shared cPanel hosting can comfortably handle.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| cPanel — familiar, well-documented control panel | No free domain bundled with hosting |
| Free SSL certificate on hosting plans | Renewal pricing runs 2–3x the intro rate |
| Optional CodeGuard backups, Cloudflare CDN, Varnish caching | Lowest price requires the longest prepaid term |
| Well-known Indian brand, easy to pair with a BigRock-registered domain | Refund process reported as slower/more involved than some competitors |
| 30-day money-back guarantee on hosting fees | Storage limits vary by promotion/tier — confirm exact allowance before buying |

## Support

BigRock offers the support channels typical of an Indian budget host — a ticket system and phone support tied to your account dashboard, plus a help-center knowledge base for common setup and troubleshooting tasks. User feedback is mixed but leans positive: several reviewers specifically call out support staff as patient and able to walk through account or DNS issues in detail, though — as with most budget hosts — response quality can vary by issue complexity and time of day.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to BigRock is a manual, cPanel-to-cPanel style process for most users: export your site files and database from your current host, then import them through BigRock's cPanel dashboard (or have their support team assist, which is common for first-time movers unfamiliar with cPanel migration tools). If your previous host also used cPanel, the process is usually straightforward since file structures and database export/import tools are standardized. Point your domain's nameservers or DNS records to BigRock only after confirming the new hosting environment works correctly.

## Where BigRock is a strong fit

- You're already registering or renewing a domain through BigRock and want hosting in the same account.
- You want a standard cPanel environment rather than a custom-built dashboard.
- You're price-sensitive on the first term and comfortable planning around a higher renewal rate.
- You run one to a handful of smaller Indian-market sites and don't need enterprise-grade infrastructure.

## Where to think twice

- You want a free domain bundled with your hosting plan — BigRock generally doesn't include one.
- You want the lowest possible long-term cost — the renewal jump means shopping around at renewal time (or negotiating) is often worthwhile.
- You need guaranteed unlimited storage with no fair-use caveats — confirm the exact allowance for your chosen tier before committing, since it varies by promotion.

## Verdict

BigRock is a reasonable, no-frills choice for anyone already anchored to the brand through domain registration — cPanel is familiar, SSL is free, and the entry price is genuinely cheap if you're willing to commit to a multi-year term. The catch is the same one that applies across most Indian budget hosts: the price that gets you in the door isn't the price you'll pay at renewal, and a bundled free domain — a perk many competitors offer — isn't part of the deal here. Compare BigRock's renewal rate against a current [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) listing before committing to the longest term, and check the [BigRock coupon page](/coupons/bigrock) for any live promotional pricing.

## FAQs

**Does BigRock use cPanel?**
Yes — BigRock's Linux shared hosting runs on cPanel, a standard, widely documented control panel. Windows hosting plans use a comparable Windows-based panel rather than cPanel itself.

**Is BigRock's advertised price what I'll always pay?**
No. The advertised rate is a promotional price tied to your prepaid term length, and it renews at a higher rate — commonly two to three times the promo price — once that term ends.

**Does BigRock include a free domain with hosting?**
Generally no. Unlike some competitors that bundle a free domain for the first year, BigRock hosting plans typically don't include one, so budget for domain registration separately.

**Does BigRock offer a money-back guarantee?**
Yes — a 30-day money-back guarantee covers shared hosting, reseller hosting, cloud hosting and unmanaged VPS for first-time accounts. It doesn't apply to renewals, auto-renewals, or dedicated servers, and only covers hosting fees, not add-ons.

**Does BigRock include a free SSL certificate?**
Yes, hosting plans include a free SSL certificate so your site can run over HTTPS by default.

**How do I migrate my existing site to BigRock?**
You export your site files and database from your current host and import them via BigRock's cPanel dashboard, or ask BigRock's support team to assist — the process is smoothest when your previous host also used cPanel.

**Is BigRock good for beginners?**
It's workable for beginners familiar with — or willing to learn — cPanel, and BigRock's support has generally received positive feedback for walking new users through setup issues.

**How do I get the best price on BigRock hosting?**
Compare term lengths at checkout rather than defaulting to the longest one, check the exact renewal price shown for your chosen term, and look for current promotional pricing on the [BigRock coupon page](/coupons/bigrock).

title: BuyVM Review 2026: Budget KVM VPS Pricing & Verdict
excerpt: BuyVM offers cheap, dedicated KVM VPS and storage plans with unmetered bandwidth — see real pricing, pros, cons, and whether it fits your workload.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is BuyVM a good VPS host?

BuyVM is a good fit if you're a developer who wants cheap, unmetered-bandwidth KVM VPS resources and doesn't need a control panel or hand-holding. Plans start at $25/year, storage-heavy tiers reach 4TB, and DDoS protection is a $3/month add-on — but there's no bundled cPanel and support skips phone calls entirely.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $25/year (KVM 128) |
| Monthly entry plan | $5/mo (KVM 256, 2 cores / 256MB RAM / 30GB) |
| Control panel | None bundled — Stallion (in-house) + billing portal |
| Money-back guarantee | None advertised; refunds handled per-ticket |
| Data centers | Las Vegas, Piscataway (NJ), Luxembourg |
| Best for | Developers, self-hosters, storage/Plex/backup boxes |

## What BuyVM actually is

BuyVM is the retail VPS brand of FranTech Solutions, a Canadian hosting company that's been selling budget KVM slices since the early 2010s. It has built a loyal following in self-hosting and homelab communities for a fairly simple reason: real dedicated cores and RAM, unmetered or very high bandwidth allowances, and prices that undercut most competitors — in exchange for skipping the polish. There's no drag-and-drop website builder, no bundled cPanel license, and no live chat sales funnel pushing upsells. You get a KVM virtual machine, a billing portal, and BuyVM's own Stallion panel for power/reinstall/console access.

That trade-off is deliberate. BuyVM markets itself with a blunt, no-nonsense tone rather than typical hosting-brochure language, and its customer base skews toward people running VPNs, small web apps, game servers, Seedboxes, and backup/storage nodes rather than WordPress blogs.

## Pricing (accurate as of September 2026 — check BuyVM's site for current rates)

**Standard KVM plans:**

| Plan | CPU | RAM | Storage | Bandwidth | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| KVM 128 | 1 core | 128MB | 15GB SATA | 500GB | $25/year |
| KVM 256 | 2 cores | 256MB | 30GB SATA | 1TB | $5/month |
| KVM 512 | 2 cores | 512MB | 50GB SATA | 2TB | $10/month |
| KVM 1024 | 4 cores | 1024MB | 100GB SATA | 5TB | $20/month |

**High-volume plans:**

| Plan | CPU | RAM | Storage | Bandwidth | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plan 2048 | 4 cores | 2GB | 150GB SATA | 10TB @ 1Gbps | $40/month |
| Plan 4096 | 8 cores | 4GB | 200GB SATA | 15TB @ 1Gbps | $80/month |

**Storage VPS plans** (unlimited bandwidth, built for media/backup workloads):

| Plan | CPU | RAM | Storage | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Storage 250 | 1 core | 1GB | 250GB | $7/month |
| Storage 500 | 2 cores | 2GB | 500GB | $15/month |
| Storage 1000 | 4 cores | 4GB | 1000GB | $30/month |
| Storage 2000 | 4 cores | 2GB | 2000GB | $60/month |
| Storage 3000 | 8 cores | 12GB | 3000GB | $90/month |
| Storage 4000 | 8 cores | 16GB | 4000GB | $120/month |

## The real cost breakdown

There's no bait-and-switch renewal pricing here the way there is with a lot of shared hosts — BuyVM's monthly plans renew at the same rate you signed up at, and the KVM 128 annual plan renews at $25/year again. The costs to actually watch for are add-ons: a DDoS-protected IP runs $3/month per IP (not included by default on standard plans), extra IPv4 addresses cost extra, and automated backups are billed separately rather than bundled free. None of the standard KVM tiers include DDoS filtering out of the box, so if you're running anything public-facing that could get attacked, budget for that add-on from day one.

Because BuyVM runs on a strict no-overselling policy, a specific plan/location combination can simply be sold out — you may need to check back or pick a different data center to actually get the tier you want.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose KVM 128** if you want the cheapest possible always-on box for a lightweight VPN, DNS server, or single small script — 128MB RAM is tight but workable for minimal Linux workloads.
- **Choose KVM 256 or KVM 512** if you're running a small web app, Discord bot, or personal project and want some headroom without committing to a big monthly bill.
- **Choose KVM 1024 or the high-volume plans** if you're running something with real traffic or multiple services on one box and need 4-8 cores.
- **Choose a Storage VPS tier** if the workload is about disk space rather than CPU — Plex media servers, Seedboxes, backup targets, or file storage where you need hundreds of gigabytes to multiple terabytes more than raw compute.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely cheap entry pricing ($25/year, $5/month) | No bundled cPanel or mainstream control panel |
| Unmetered/high bandwidth allowances on most tiers | No advertised money-back guarantee |
| Dedicated (non-oversold) CPU and RAM | Popular plan/location combos often sell out |
| DDoS protection available cheaply ($3/mo per IP) | Support is ticket/community-based, not phone |
| Storage VPS line is excellent value for storage-heavy use | Steeper learning curve for hosting beginners |

## Support

BuyVM's support runs through its ticketing system in the my.frantech.ca portal and an active community forum where staff and experienced users answer questions. There's no phone support and no live-chat sales team pushing upgrades — this fits the developer-focused, self-service audience BuyVM targets, but it means beginners without Linux server experience will be doing more of their own troubleshooting than they would with a beginner-oriented shared host.

## Migration

BuyVM doesn't advertise a white-glove, free migration service the way some managed hosts do. Moving an existing site or app onto BuyVM typically means either restoring from a backup/image on the old server, or manually re-provisioning the app stack on the new VPS — standard practice for any unmanaged KVM host. If you're coming from shared hosting with no server administration experience, plan for either learning the process or hiring outside help for the migration.

## Where BuyVM is a strong fit

- You're comfortable administering a Linux (or Windows) server yourself and don't need a bundled control panel.
- You want cheap, dedicated, non-oversold VPS resources for a VPN, small app, bot, or dev/test box.
- You need a storage-heavy box — Plex, Seedbox, backups — where the Storage VPS line's price-per-GB is hard to beat.
- You value transparent, flat pricing without renewal-rate surprises.

## Where to think twice

- You're new to servers and want a hosting company that walks you through setup with cPanel and phone support.
- You need guaranteed stock on a specific plan/location combination right away — BuyVM's no-overselling model means popular configs can be sold out.
- You want a blanket refund guarantee locked in before you buy.

## Verdict

BuyVM earns its reputation in self-hosting circles by being straightforward about what it is: cheap, dedicated KVM resources with unmetered bandwidth, no upsells, and no pretense of being beginner software. For developers, VPN users, and anyone running storage-heavy workloads like Plex or backups, its pricing and Storage VPS lineup are hard to beat. If you need a polished dashboard, guaranteed availability, or phone support, look elsewhere — but if you know your way around a terminal, BuyVM is one of the better budget VPS values around.

## FAQs

**Does BuyVM include a control panel like cPanel?**
No — BuyVM doesn't bundle cPanel or any mainstream control panel. Server management runs through Stallion, BuyVM's own in-house panel, alongside the my.frantech.ca billing portal.

**What data center locations does BuyVM offer?**
BuyVM operates in Las Vegas (Nevada), Piscataway (New Jersey), and Luxembourg.

**Does BuyVM offer a money-back guarantee?**
BuyVM doesn't advertise a blanket money-back guarantee. Refund requests are handled case-by-case through a support ticket, so check current terms before purchasing if that matters to you.

**Is DDoS protection included with BuyVM plans?**
Not by default. BuyVM offers DDoS-protected IPs as a $3/month per-IP add-on rather than bundling it free with standard plans.

**What's the cheapest BuyVM plan?**
The KVM 128 plan is $25/year (1 core, 128MB RAM, 15GB storage, 500GB bandwidth). The cheapest monthly-billed option is KVM 256 at $5/month.

**Is BuyVM good for beginners?**
Not especially — there's no bundled control panel and support is ticket/forum-based rather than phone or live chat, so it suits people already comfortable managing a Linux or Windows server.

**What is BuyVM's Storage VPS good for?**
Storage VPS plans pair modest CPU/RAM with large, unmetered-bandwidth disk allocations (250GB up to 4TB), making them well suited to Plex media servers, Seedboxes, and backup targets rather than compute-heavy apps.

**Why does a BuyVM plan sometimes show as out of stock?**
BuyVM runs a strict no-overselling policy, so once a specific plan/data-center combination's capacity is allocated, it can't be oversold to more customers until more hardware is added — check back later or try a different location.

Compare current offers on the [BuyVM coupon page](/coupons/buyvm), or browse more options across providers on our [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) page.

title: ByetHost Review 2026: Free Hosting Pros, Cons and Cost
excerpt: ByetHost gives you free ad-free hosting with real limits, plus paid NVMe cPanel plans from $29.99/year — here's what's honestly worth it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is ByetHost worth using?

ByetHost is a genuinely free web host — 5 GB storage, unlimited (fair-use capped) bandwidth, no forced ads — that also sells paid NVMe cPanel plans starting at $29.99/year. It's a solid pick for a small test site or hobby project at zero cost, but the free tier's single FTP account and 10MB file-upload cap make it a poor fit for anything you depend on.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (paid plans from $29.99/year) |
| Renewal price | Paid plans renew at the same listed annual rate |
| Uptime guarantee | Not published for the free tier; no formal SLA found |
| Money-back guarantee | None — free tier has no payment; paid-tier refund terms vary, check at checkout |
| Best for | Test projects, learning PHP/MySQL, small no-budget sites |

## What ByetHost actually is

ByetHost is a free hosting brand that's been running since the mid-2000s as part of the Byet Internet Services group, the same family behind a cluster of other free-hosting brands. Its pitch is simple: host a small site for free, with no banner ads forced onto your pages — a real differentiator, since plenty of "free" hosts pay for their infrastructure by injecting ads you can't remove.

The free plan gives you 5 GB of NVMe storage, unlimited bandwidth with a roughly 50,000-hits-per-day fair-use ceiling, PHP 8.3, MySQL 8, free SSL, FTP access, cron jobs and Softaculous with over 400 one-click app installs (WordPress included). You can point your own domain at it or use a ByetHost subdomain. The account doesn't expire on its own, but stays alive only if you log in periodically — free hosts routinely reclaim dormant accounts.

The catch is real: you get a single FTP account, a hard 10MB per-file upload limit, and the older VistaPanel control panel instead of cPanel. None of that matters for a static portfolio or a small WordPress blog with light traffic. It matters a lot if you're running e-commerce, uploading large media files, or need more than one person with FTP access.

For anyone who outgrows those limits, ByetHost sells paid shared hosting on cPanel — a meaningfully different, more capable product than the free tier.

## Pricing

*Pricing was accurate as of September 2026 and can change — verify current rates on ByetHost's own site before buying.*

| Plan | Price | Storage | Bandwidth | Domains | Panel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 5 GB NVMe | Unlimited (fair-use capped) | 1 (subdomain or your own) | VistaPanel |
| Starter | $29.99/year | 10 GB NVMe | 250 GB/month | 1 addon + 1 free domain | cPanel |
| Super Premium | $56.78/year | Unlimited NVMe | 250 GB/month | 20 addon + 1 free + 20 bonus extensions | cPanel |
| Ultimate Premium | $85.22/year | Unlimited NVMe | Unlimited | Unlimited addon + 1 free + 20 bonus extensions | cPanel |

## Real cost breakdown

The free tier costs nothing upfront and nothing at renewal — there's no billing cycle to track. The trade-off is the 10MB file cap, single FTP account, and no guaranteed uptime SLA.

The paid tiers are billed annually rather than monthly, so the sticker price is the actual charge at checkout: $29.99 for Starter's first year, $56.78 for Super Premium, $85.22 for Ultimate Premium. ByetHost lists these as flat annual rates rather than a discounted intro term that jumps at renewal, but always confirm the renewal price shown in your cart before paying, since promotional pricing on hosting sites changes often.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose the **free plan** if you're learning PHP/MySQL, testing a small script, or hosting a low-traffic personal page and don't want to spend anything.

Choose **Starter** if you've outgrown the free tier's 10MB file cap and single FTP account but only need one real domain and modest storage.

Choose **Super Premium** if you're running a small agency or personal network of sites — unlimited storage and 20 addon domains cover most multi-site needs.

Choose **Ultimate Premium** if bandwidth is a real constraint (media-heavy site, growing traffic) or you're hosting an unpredictable number of addon domains.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free tier with no forced ads | Free tier uses dated VistaPanel, not cPanel |
| Free plan never expires with activity | Single FTP account and 10MB upload cap on free tier |
| Paid tiers use NVMe storage and cPanel | No published uptime SLA on the free tier |
| Softaculous with 400+ apps on all tiers | Trustpilot reviews are mixed, skewing negative |
| Paid annual pricing is transparent, no surprise renewal jump found | Support is community/ticket-based, not live chat |

## Support

ByetHost's free tier relies on a community forum and ticket system rather than live chat or phone support — response times can be slow, which is typical for free hosting where support isn't the revenue driver. Paid plans get access to a dedicated support ticket queue described as 24/7, plus complimentary migration assistance for moving an existing site over. If fast support matters more than saving money, weigh that against paid mainstream hosts that offer 24/7 live chat.

## Migration

Moving a site onto ByetHost's free tier is manual: you upload files over the single FTP connection and import your database through the provided phpMyAdmin, working around the 10MB file-size ceiling if any assets are larger. Paid plans include free migration assistance from the support team, which removes most of that manual work — a meaningful reason to go paid if you're bringing over an existing WordPress site with a media library.

## Where it's a strong fit

ByetHost is a strong fit for students, hobbyists and developers who want a real, ad-free host to learn on or park a small side project without spending money. It's also reasonable for testing a script or app before committing budget to a paid host elsewhere.

## Where to think twice

Think twice if you're running anything business-critical, need guaranteed uptime, upload large media files regularly, or need more than one FTP login. The free tier's limitations and the site's mixed Trustpilot feedback both point toward treating ByetHost as a starting point rather than a permanent home for anything that matters.

## Bottom line

ByetHost delivers on its core promise — free hosting without forced ads — better than most in the category, and its paid NVMe/cPanel tiers are reasonably priced if you outgrow the free plan. But the free tier's hard limits (10MB uploads, one FTP account, no SLA) and inconsistent user feedback mean it's best treated as a testing ground or budget starting point, not a long-term home for a site you depend on.

Compare it against other budget options on our [ByetHost coupon page](/coupons/byethost), or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) before deciding.

## FAQs

**Is ByetHost really free forever?**
Yes — the free plan has no time limit, but ByetHost can suspend accounts that go inactive for an extended period, so log in occasionally to keep it alive.

**Does ByetHost put ads on free websites?**
No — ByetHost's free plan doesn't force ads or banners onto your site, which is one of its main selling points over many other free hosts.

**What control panel does ByetHost use?**
The free plan uses VistaPanel, a simpler custom panel. Paid plans switch to the industry-standard cPanel with Softaculous.

**Can I upload large files on the free plan?**
Not easily — the free tier caps individual file uploads at 10MB, which can be a real obstacle for media-heavy sites or large WordPress themes/plugins.

**How much do ByetHost's paid plans cost?**
Paid shared hosting starts at $29.99/year for Starter, rising to $56.78/year for Super Premium and $85.22/year for Ultimate Premium, all billed annually.

**Does ByetHost help migrate an existing site?**
Paid plans include complimentary migration assistance from support. On the free plan, you'll need to move files and databases manually over FTP.

**Is ByetHost good for WordPress?**
It can host a small WordPress site via Softaculous's one-click installer, but the 10MB upload cap and single FTP account on the free tier can complicate installing larger themes or plugins — the paid tiers are a better fit for a serious WordPress site.

**What do ByetHost's reviews look like?**
Trustpilot feedback for ByetHost is mixed and skews toward lower ratings, so read recent reviews and weigh them against your own risk tolerance before relying on it for anything important.

title: Cloudflare Pages Review 2026: Free Static Site Hosting
excerpt: Cloudflare Pages review: free static & Jamstack hosting, real pricing, limits, and why it's not a fit for WordPress or PHP-based sites.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Cloudflare good for hosting a website?

This review covers Cloudflare Pages specifically — Cloudflare's free static-site and Jamstack hosting product — not Cloudflare as a whole. Cloudflare's core business is CDN, DNS and web security, not traditional hosting. Pages is a strong, free fit for static sites and Jamstack frontends, but it does not run PHP, MySQL or WordPress.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free |
| Renewal price | Free (paid Workers plan starts at $5/month) |
| Uptime guarantee | Not separately published for Pages |
| Money-back guarantee | Not applicable — free tier, no credit card required |
| Best for | Static sites, Jamstack frontends, documentation, blogs built with a static-site generator |

## What Cloudflare actually is

Cloudflare runs one of the largest content-delivery and DNS networks on the internet, plus a broad security product line — DDoS protection, a web application firewall, bot management, and Zero Trust access tools. Most of what Cloudflare is known for sits in front of other companies' websites and infrastructure rather than hosting sites itself.

Cloudflare Pages is the exception worth reviewing here: a free platform for deploying static and Jamstack sites straight from a Git repository to Cloudflare's edge network. Push to your connected branch and Cloudflare builds and deploys automatically, with a unique preview URL generated for every pull request. It pairs with Cloudflare Workers (edge compute/serverless functions) through Pages Functions when a site needs a bit of dynamic logic, but the platform as a whole is not designed to replace a shared-hosting cPanel stack.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check Cloudflare's own pricing page before committing.

| Plan | Price | Builds | Concurrent builds | Files per deployment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/month | 500 builds/month | 1 | Up to 20,000 |
| Workers Paid | $5/month | 5,000 builds/month | 5 | Up to 100,000 (with config) |

Static asset bandwidth and requests are unmetered on both tiers — Cloudflare doesn't bill Pages by traffic volume the way most hosts bill by bandwidth cap. What the paid tier actually buys is more build capacity and a larger Pages Functions request allowance for sites that run serverless logic at the edge, not more bandwidth.

## Real cost breakdown

The free tier is genuinely free with no time limit and no credit card requirement — this isn't an introductory-price-then-renewal-hike situation like a lot of shared hosts run. If a site outgrows 500 builds a month (unlikely for most individual sites and small teams — that's roughly 16 deploys a day) or needs more than one build running at once, the $5/month Workers Paid plan removes that ceiling and also raises the Pages Functions request allowance beyond the free Workers plan's daily limit. There's no separate "Pages plan" bill — the $5/month charge is the Workers Paid plan, which happens to also lift Pages' build limits.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose the Free plan if you're deploying a personal site, a documentation site, a small business's static marketing pages, or a blog built with a static-site generator — the build and file limits are generous enough that most single-site projects never hit them.

Choose Workers Paid ($5/month) if you're deploying frequently across a team (multiple builds triggered per hour), running several Pages projects that share the 500-build pool, or building a Jamstack site whose Functions layer does real work — API routes, form handling, edge-side personalization — that could bump against the free Workers request ceiling.

## Is Cloudflare Pages right for your site type?

Pages is built to serve static output — HTML, CSS, JS and other compiled assets, plus whatever a Pages Function can do at request time. It's a strong fit for:

- Static-site-generator output (Hugo, Eleventy, Astro, Jekyll)
- Modern JS framework builds (Next.js static export, Vite, Gatsby)
- Documentation sites and marketing pages
- Jamstack frontends that call external APIs for their data

It is not a fit for a traditional dynamic CMS stack. Cloudflare Pages does not run PHP or host a MySQL database, so WordPress, standard PHP applications, and anything expecting a classic LAMP/cPanel environment need a different host entirely — pair Pages with Cloudflare as your DNS/CDN layer in front of that host if you still want Cloudflare's edge network involved.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free tier with no time limit and no card required | Not a fit for WordPress, PHP or database-driven CMS sites |
| Unmetered bandwidth on static assets at every tier | Free tier caps at 500 builds/month and 1 concurrent build |
| Deploys run on Cloudflare's global edge network | No traditional cPanel/email/hosting-account experience |
| Automatic preview URLs on every pull request | Support is community/docs-first unless on a paid Enterprise plan |

## Support

Free and Workers Paid customers get Cloudflare's community forum and documentation as their primary support channels — there's no phone line or dedicated account manager at this tier. Cloudflare's docs for Pages are thorough and cover most build and deployment issues directly. Faster, prioritized support is reserved for Cloudflare's Business and Enterprise contracts, which are a different product tier entirely from what a typical Pages site needs.

## Migration

Moving a static site onto Pages is a Git-connect operation, not a file-transfer migration in the traditional hosting sense: point Cloudflare at your GitHub or GitLab repository, set the build command and output directory for your framework, and Cloudflare handles the rest on every push. There's no database or email to migrate because Pages doesn't host either. Moving away from Pages is equally simple — the site's source lives in your own repository, so redeploying it elsewhere is a matter of pointing a different static host at the same repo.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Developers and teams already building with a static-site generator or a Jamstack framework
- Projects that want free, unmetered bandwidth regardless of traffic spikes
- Sites that benefit from deploy previews on every branch or pull request
- Anyone who wants Cloudflare's edge network without paying for hosting

## Where to think twice

- WordPress, Drupal, or any PHP/MySQL-driven site — Pages simply doesn't run that stack
- Teams that need phone support or a dedicated account contact at low cost
- Projects needing more than 500 builds/month without moving to a paid plan
- Anyone expecting a conventional hosting-account experience (file manager, email hosting, cPanel)

## Verdict

Cloudflare Pages is a genuinely useful, genuinely free option for static and Jamstack site hosting — the unmetered bandwidth and global edge deployment are hard to beat at zero cost. But it's worth being clear-eyed about scope: Cloudflare's core business is CDN, DNS and security, and Pages is a narrow, static-only hosting product bolted onto that platform. If your site is static or Jamstack, it's worth serious consideration. If it's WordPress or another PHP-based CMS, look elsewhere for the actual hosting and consider routing it through Cloudflare's CDN separately.

## FAQs

**Does Cloudflare Pages host WordPress sites?**
No. Pages only serves static output — it doesn't run PHP or host a MySQL database, so WordPress and similar CMS platforms need a traditional host instead.

**Is Cloudflare Pages really free?**
Yes, the free tier has no time limit and requires no credit card. It's capped at 500 builds/month and one concurrent build, not a trial that expires or auto-upgrades.

**What's the difference between Cloudflare Pages and Cloudflare Workers?**
Pages is the static-site hosting and deployment platform; Workers is Cloudflare's serverless compute product. Pages Functions bridges the two, letting a Pages-hosted static site run small pieces of server-side logic backed by Workers.

**Does Cloudflare Pages charge for bandwidth?**
No — static asset bandwidth and requests are unmetered on both the free and paid tiers, which is unusual compared to most hosting providers' bandwidth caps.

**Can I use a custom domain with Cloudflare Pages for free?**
Yes, custom domains and automatic HTTPS are included on the free tier at no extra cost.

**How do I migrate an existing site to Cloudflare Pages?**
Connect your Git repository (GitHub or GitLab), set your framework's build command and output directory, and Cloudflare builds and deploys automatically on every push — there's no file-transfer-style migration involved.

**What kind of support does Cloudflare offer free Pages users?**
Community forums and documentation are the primary channels on the free and Workers Paid tiers; prioritized support is reserved for Business and Enterprise contracts.

**Is Cloudflare Pages a good replacement for shared hosting?**
Only for static or Jamstack sites. It doesn't replace shared hosting for PHP/database-driven sites like WordPress — those still need a conventional host.

Looking for other hosting options? Check the [Cloudflare coupon page](/coupons/cloudflare) for current deals, or browse [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) for more providers.

title: CloudSigma Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: CloudSigma review: Swiss cloud IaaS with independently sized CPU, RAM and storage, usage-based billing, and no bundled control panel by default.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is CloudSigma good hosting?

CloudSigma is a solid pick if you want raw cloud infrastructure you configure yourself — CPU, RAM and storage set independently, billed by the resource. It's not good hosting for beginners who want a one-click website builder or bundled control panel, since neither is included by default.

| Detail | CloudSigma |
|---|---|
| Starting price | ~$14/month (configuration-dependent) |
| Typical range | $14–$677/month |
| Billing model | Pay-per-resource (subscription or burst) |
| Uptime SLA | 100%, with time credits for outages over 15 minutes |
| Free trial | ~7 days (confirm current terms) |
| Best for | Developers, agencies, custom infrastructure |

## What CloudSigma actually is

CloudSigma is a Swiss-founded cloud infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) provider. It doesn't sell shared hosting plans or WordPress-optimized tiers the way consumer hosts do. Instead, every server is built resource by resource: you pick the number of CPU cores, the amount of RAM, and the SSD storage size independently, rather than choosing from a fixed list of "small/medium/large" VM bundles.

That structure makes CloudSigma closer to a boutique alternative to AWS EC2 or Google Compute Engine than to a Hostinger or Bluehost. It's aimed at developers, agencies and businesses running specific workloads — a database server that needs heavy RAM but light CPU, for instance — rather than someone launching a first blog.

Data centers are spread across a wide international network, including locations in Switzerland, other parts of Europe, North America and Asia, which is useful if data residency or latency to a specific region matters for your project.

## Pricing breakdown

CloudSigma bills per resource rather than per bundled plan. CPU, RAM, storage and bandwidth are each metered and charged separately, either as a prepaid subscription (with volume-style discounts for longer commitments) or as pay-as-you-go "burst" usage charged in short cycles once you exceed what you've subscribed to.

- Entry-level configurations start around $14/month; fully specced servers can run into the hundreds depending on CPU/RAM/storage chosen — published figures put the range around $14 to $677/month.
- Annual commitments carry a reported subscription discount (roughly 10%), with steeper discounts for multi-year terms.
- Burst pricing applies when usage exceeds your subscribed capacity — useful for handling spikes without over-provisioning permanently, but it means your bill isn't perfectly fixed month to month if traffic or load varies.

Pricing was accurate as of September 2026 and can change — always check CloudSigma's current pricing page before committing, since utility-billed infrastructure shifts more often than flat hosting plans.

## The no-control-panel reality

This is the detail that catches people off guard: CloudSigma does not bundle cPanel, hPanel, Plesk or any consumer-style dashboard by default. Server management runs through CloudSigma's own web console and a documented API. That's a feature if you're comfortable scripting deployments and want full control — it's a real obstacle if you were expecting to point-and-click install WordPress the way you would on shared hosting.

If your workflow depends on a familiar cPanel-style interface, budget time to either install one yourself on top of a CloudSigma instance or look at a host that bundles a panel out of the box.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose a minimal CPU/RAM/storage build** if you're running a single lightweight application, API, or test environment and want to keep costs near the $14–$30/month range.
- **Choose a RAM-heavy configuration** if you're running a database, cache layer, or memory-intensive service — CloudSigma's per-resource billing lets you scale RAM without paying for CPU you don't need.
- **Choose a higher-CPU build with burst headroom** if your workload has unpredictable traffic spikes — burst billing covers overflow without requiring you to permanently provision for peak load.
- **Look elsewhere** if you want a bundled control panel, one-click app installs, or predictable flat monthly pricing regardless of usage.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| CPU/RAM/storage configured independently | No bundled control panel by default |
| Pay only for resources actually used | Usage-based billing means less predictable bills |
| 100% uptime SLA with downtime credits | Not beginner-friendly |
| Wide international data center footprint | Small public review presence (limited Trustpilot volume) |
| Subscription discounts for longer commitments | No shared hosting or domain registration |

## Support

CloudSigma offers 24/7 live chat and email support according to independent reviews. There's no phone-first, hand-holding support model here — it's oriented toward technical users who can describe an infrastructure issue precisely, which fits the platform's developer-focused positioning.

## Migration

Moving an existing site or application onto CloudSigma means provisioning a server yourself (choosing CPU, RAM, storage, and OS image) and handling the migration manually or via your own scripts/API calls — there's no built-in one-click site migration tool aimed at non-technical users. Teams already comfortable with infrastructure-as-code or manual server setup will find this straightforward; anyone coming from shared hosting should expect a steeper first migration.

## Where CloudSigma is a strong fit

- Developers and agencies who want to size infrastructure precisely instead of over-paying for bundled VM tiers.
- Workloads with an unusual CPU-to-RAM ratio that standard cloud VM sizes don't fit well.
- Projects that need a specific European (Swiss) data residency option alongside broader global locations.
- Teams comfortable managing servers via API/console rather than a GUI control panel.

## Where to think twice

- First-time website owners wanting a simple, guided setup.
- Anyone expecting a bundled cPanel/hPanel-style dashboard.
- Budgets that need a fixed, predictable monthly bill rather than usage-based charges.
- Projects wanting built-in one-click app installers or a website builder.

## Verdict

CloudSigma delivers on a specific promise: pay for exactly the CPU, RAM and storage you configure, with a 100% uptime SLA and a genuinely international footprint of data centers. That's valuable for developers who know what they need and don't want to pay for a bundled VM tier that's oversized in one dimension and undersized in another. It's a poor fit if you want a beginner-friendly panel, one-click installs, or fully flat pricing — this is infrastructure for people who are comfortable configuring it themselves. Check current [CloudSigma coupon page](/coupons/cloudsigma) offers before signing up, and compare against other options on our [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) page.

## FAQs

**Does CloudSigma include a control panel?**
No — there's no bundled cPanel, hPanel or Plesk-style dashboard by default. Management happens through CloudSigma's own web console and API.

**How does CloudSigma pricing work?**
CPU, RAM, storage and bandwidth are billed separately and metered by actual usage, either as a prepaid subscription or as pay-as-you-go burst charges once you exceed your subscribed capacity.

**Is there a free trial?**
CloudSigma has offered a trial period (around 7 days in independent reviews) — confirm the current length and terms directly on CloudSigma's site before signing up.

**What's CloudSigma's uptime guarantee?**
CloudSigma publishes a 100% uptime SLA, with time credits issued for outages that exceed 15 minutes.

**Where are CloudSigma's data centers located?**
CloudSigma operates a broad international network of data centers spanning Switzerland and other parts of Europe, North America, and Asia.

**Is CloudSigma good for beginners?**
Not really — there's no shared hosting, no domain registration, and no bundled control panel, so it suits developers and technically comfortable users more than first-time site owners.

**Does CloudSigma offer support?**
Yes, 24/7 live chat and email support are available according to independent reviews, oriented toward technical questions rather than beginner hand-holding.

**How does CloudSigma compare to AWS or Google Cloud?**
CloudSigma occupies a similar per-resource billing niche but as a smaller, more boutique European provider — it can suit projects wanting Swiss/European data residency or a simpler pricing model than hyperscaler cloud consoles, though it lacks the breadth of managed services the hyperscalers offer.

title: DomainRacer Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Is DomainRacer worth it? An honest look at DomainRacer's cPanel hosting plans, real renewal pricing, support and Trustpilot record.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is DomainRacer worth it?

DomainRacer is a budget Indian host that sells standard cPanel shared, reseller, VPS and cloud hosting on LiteSpeed servers with NVMe SSD storage. It's cheap and technically capable, but its Trustpilot record is mixed — a 3.2/5 average across 104 reviews, with a notable share of 1-star complaints — so it fits price-driven, low-traffic sites better than businesses that can't tolerate support friction.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | ~₹58/month (Basic, intro rate) |
| Renewal price | ~₹82/month (Basic, 1-year term) |
| Control panel | cPanel (Plesk on Windows plans) |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days |
| Trustpilot rating | 3.2/5 (104 reviews) |
| Best for | Budget Indian shared/reseller hosting |

## What DomainRacer actually is

DomainRacer is a web hosting company based in India that sells shared, reseller, VPS and cloud hosting, mostly on cPanel, aimed at price-sensitive customers — freelancers, small local businesses and agencies reselling hosting to their own clients. Its shared plans run on LiteSpeed web servers rather than plain Apache, which is a genuine performance advantage over many budget hosts still using Apache or NGINX-only stacks. Servers use NVMe SSD storage rather than older SATA SSD, and DomainRacer advertises a 99.99% uptime guarantee with service credits if it's missed.

Pricing is quoted in Indian rupees by default, with USD, GBP and EUR billing options for international customers. Payment can be made by card, PayPal or other regional methods depending on currency.

## Shared hosting pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check DomainRacer's own pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Intro price | Storage | Websites | Bandwidth | Free domain |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Basic | ~₹58/mo | 1GB NVMe SSD | 1 | 5GB | No |
| Personal | ~₹88/mo | Unlimited NVMe SSD | 1 | Unlimited | No |
| Silver | ~₹173/mo | Unlimited NVMe SSD | 3 | Unlimited | No |
| Advanced | ~₹238/mo | Unlimited NVMe SSD | Unlimited | Unlimited | Yes (.IN/.COM) |

All four tiers include a free SSL certificate, the Softaculous one-click installer (WordPress, and 450+ other apps), the SitePad drag-and-drop site builder, and JetBackup for self-service restores.

## The real cost breakdown: intro vs. renewal

DomainRacer's headline prices are introductory-term discounts, and the jump at renewal is significant in percentage terms even though the absolute numbers are small. The Basic plan's roughly ₹58/month intro rate renews near ₹82/month — about a 40% increase. The top Advanced tier follows the same pattern: roughly ₹238/month intro renewing near ₹288/month.

None of this is unusual for budget hosting — most low-cost hosts use the same intro-then-renew structure — but it means the plan that looks cheapest on the pricing page isn't necessarily the cheapest plan over two or three years. Locking in a longer prepaid term (2-3 years) reduces the intro rate further, but the same renewal jump still applies once that term ends, so budget for the renewal figure rather than the discount headline.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **Basic** only if you're testing a single very-low-traffic site and are comfortable with just 1GB of storage and 5GB of bandwidth — it's tight for anything beyond a brochure site.

Choose **Personal** if you're running one real website (a blog, portfolio or small business site) and want unlimited storage/bandwidth without paying for multiple websites you don't need.

Choose **Silver** if you're managing up to three sites — a common setup for freelancers running a personal site plus a couple of client or side projects.

Choose **Advanced** if you need unlimited websites on one account, want the free domain bundled in, or you're planning to host multiple client sites without upgrading again later.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| LiteSpeed servers + NVMe SSD storage | Trustpilot rating is mixed (3.2/5) |
| Very low entry price | Renewal price roughly 40% higher than intro |
| 30-day money-back guarantee | Only the top tier includes a free domain |
| Standard cPanel (not a proprietary panel) | Entry Basic plan's storage/bandwidth are limited |
| Free SSL, Softaculous, JetBackup on every tier | Some user reports cite slow pre-sales support |

## Support

DomainRacer offers support through live chat, a ticket system and phone, alongside a self-service knowledge base for common cPanel and setup questions. Independent reviews have flagged pre-sales response times as inconsistent, which is worth testing yourself (via live chat) before committing to a longer prepaid term, since that's harder to walk back once paid.

## Migration

DomainRacer advertises free website migration assistance for new customers moving an existing site over from another host, handled by its support team rather than a fully automated migration tool. If you're moving a site with a custom stack or non-standard configuration, confirm the specifics with support before you cancel your existing host.

## Where DomainRacer is a strong fit

- Budget shared or reseller hosting for a single site or a small handful of client sites
- Buyers who specifically want LiteSpeed performance without paying premium-host prices
- Indian customers who want local-currency billing and support

## Where to think twice

- Businesses that need guaranteed fast pre-sales support before they buy
- Sites that will outgrow the Basic tier's 1GB/5GB limits quickly
- Anyone who wants a free domain bundled on an entry-level plan (only Advanced includes one)

## Bottom line

DomainRacer delivers real technical value for the price — LiteSpeed, NVMe SSD and standard cPanel are a solid combination well below what many competitors charge for the same stack. The tradeoff is a Trustpilot record that's more mixed than the biggest hosting brands, so it suits buyers prioritizing low cost and are willing to test support responsiveness themselves rather than businesses that need a spotless support track record from day one. Compare it against [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) before deciding, and check the [DomainRacer coupon page](/coupons/domainracer) for any active offers.

## FAQs

**Is DomainRacer cPanel or a custom panel?**
DomainRacer uses standard cPanel on its Linux shared and reseller plans, with Plesk offered on Windows hosting plans — not a proprietary custom panel.

**Does DomainRacer's advertised price stay the same at renewal?**
No. DomainRacer's intro pricing is a term-based discount; plans renew at a meaningfully higher rate afterward — roughly 40% higher on the plans checked for this review. Check the renewal price, not just the intro rate, before committing to a long term.

**Does DomainRacer offer a money-back guarantee?**
Yes — DomainRacer backs new hosting purchases with a 30-day money-back guarantee, though refund exclusions (like domain fees) can apply.

**Does DomainRacer include a free domain?**
Only on the Advanced shared hosting tier, which bundles a free .IN or .COM domain. The Basic, Personal and Silver tiers do not include one.

**What is DomainRacer's Trustpilot rating?**
DomainRacer holds a 3.2 out of 5 rating from 104 Trustpilot reviews as of this review's publish date — a mixed record compared to top-tier hosting brands, worth weighing against its low price.

**Does DomainRacer help migrate my existing website?**
DomainRacer offers migration assistance from its support team for new customers switching from another host; confirm the specifics for your site's setup before cancelling your old host.

**Is DomainRacer good for beginners?**
Standard cPanel, Softaculous and the SitePad builder make it usable for beginners, but test live chat support responsiveness during pre-sales before buying, given the mixed review record.

**Can I run multiple websites on one DomainRacer plan?**
Yes, starting from the Silver tier (up to 3 websites) or the Advanced tier (unlimited websites); the Basic and Personal tiers are limited to a single website each.

title: E2E Networks Review 2026: GPU Cloud Pricing & Verdict
excerpt: E2E Networks review: NSE-listed Indian GPU cloud pricing, CPU compute rates, billing model, support and whether it fits AI workloads over shared hosting.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is E2E Networks good for hosting?

E2E Networks isn't a website host — it's an NSE-listed Indian GPU and CPU cloud provider built for AI training, inference and general compute workloads. If you need shared hosting or a control panel, look elsewhere. If you need NVIDIA GPU capacity or Linux/Windows VMs with transparent hourly billing, it's a legitimate option worth comparing.

**At a glance**

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price (CPU) | ~$0.044/hour (~$32/month, E1LC series) |
| Starting price (GPU) | ~$0.57/hour (NVIDIA L4) |
| Billing model | Pay-as-you-go, per-minute; monthly/annual commitments discounted |
| Money-back guarantee | None published — usage-based billing, check your invoice terms |
| Best for | AI/ML teams, developers needing GPU capacity, India-based infrastructure |

## What E2E Networks actually is

E2E Networks is India's only publicly listed pure-play GPU cloud company, trading on the NSE and BSE. It operates its own data centers in Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Bengaluru, and its product lineup centers on two things: NVIDIA GPU cloud instances (B200, H200, H100, L4) for AI training and inference, and standard CPU compute instances for general application workloads.

This matters because it changes what you're evaluating. There's no cPanel, no one-click WordPress installer, no bundled email hosting, and no shared-hosting-style "unlimited websites" plan. Provisioning is instance-based — you spin up a Linux or Windows VM, a container, or a managed Kubernetes node with GPUs attached, and you manage the stack yourself (or through E2E's own TIR/AI platform tooling for ML pipelines). Anyone coming from a budget shared host expecting a drag-and-drop site builder will be looking in the wrong place.

## Pricing

Pricing below is accurate as of this post's date (September 2026) and pulled from E2E's own pricing page — cloud infrastructure pricing changes fairly often, so confirm current rates before buying. E2E updated its published GPU, compute and storage pricing effective July 1, 2026.

| Instance type | Example plan | Hourly | Monthly equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU — E1 series | E1LC-2.6GB | ~$0.044/hr | ~$32/month |
| CPU — E1 series | E1LC-4.12GB | ~$0.089/hr | ~$65/month |
| CPU — C3 series | C3.8GB | ~$0.049/hr | ~$36/month |
| CPU — C3 series | C3.16GB | ~$0.096/hr | ~$70/month |
| GPU — NVIDIA L4 | 24GB vRAM | ~$0.57/hr | usage-based |
| GPU — NVIDIA H100 | 80GB vRAM | ~$2.69/hr | usage-based |
| GPU — NVIDIA H200 | 141GB vRAM | ~$3.99/hr | usage-based |
