## The real cost breakdown

There's no long-term-prepay-then-renew trap here the way there is with shared hosting — E2E bills by the minute on GPU instances and by the hour on CPU instances, so what you pay roughly tracks what you use. The trade-off is the opposite one: costs scale directly with usage, so an H100 or B200 instance left running idle burns money exactly like a running meter. E2E does offer discounted monthly and annual commitment pricing (roughly 10-30% below on-demand rates), which is worth locking in once your workload is predictable, but there's no flat "$X/month forever" price the way a shared host advertises.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose an **E1 or C3 CPU instance** if you're running a standard web application, API backend or database workload with no GPU requirement — these start under $50/month and are the closest thing E2E has to "basic" hosting.

Choose an **L4 GPU instance** if you're doing lighter inference workloads, computer vision, or small-model fine-tuning and don't need a flagship GPU's memory.

Choose an **H100 or H200 instance** if you're training or fine-tuning larger models and need substantial vRAM and throughput.

Choose a **B200 instance**, E2E's top tier, only if your workload genuinely needs the newest generation of NVIDIA silicon — it's priced accordingly.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Transparent per-minute/hourly billing, no long contracts required | No shared hosting or cPanel — not built for standard websites |
| Wide NVIDIA GPU lineup (L4 through B200) at India-competitive rates | Very thin public review record (Trustpilot: 2.3/5 from just 7 reviews) |
| NSE/BSE-listed public company — financials and operations are disclosed | No published money-back guarantee — billing is strictly usage-based |
| India-based data centers (Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru) with local support hours | Pricing has changed mid-year before (July 2026 update) — confirm current rates |

## Support

E2E Networks' support is India-based, operating in local business hours rather than round-the-clock live chat common at consumer hosts. Support is oriented around ticket/account-dashboard channels tied to your cloud console rather than a public help-desk chat widget. If you need guaranteed 24/7 phone support, confirm SLA terms directly with E2E before committing a production workload.

## Migration

There's no "import your WordPress site" migration flow here, because E2E isn't a website host. Migrating to E2E means standing up new VM images or container deployments and moving your application, data and (for ML workloads) model weights and datasets across — the same process you'd follow moving between any two IaaS/GPU cloud providers. Budget real engineering time for this rather than expecting a one-click transfer.

## Where E2E Networks is a strong fit

- Teams in or targeting India that want GPU capacity from a domestically listed, NSE-regulated provider
- AI/ML teams that need transparent, granular hourly billing on H100/H200/B200 GPUs without long-term contracts
- Developers who already run their own infrastructure and just need CPU compute at competitive per-hour rates

## Where to think twice

- Anyone looking for shared hosting, a website builder, or a cPanel-style dashboard — E2E doesn't offer this
- Buyers who want a published money-back guarantee before committing spend
- Anyone relying heavily on public reviews to vet a provider — E2E's Trustpilot presence is too thin (7 reviews) to lean on

## Verdict

E2E Networks is a legitimate, publicly listed Indian cloud infrastructure provider with a real GPU lineup and transparent usage-based pricing — but it's a cloud/GPU compute company, not a hosting company in the shared-hosting sense, and anyone comparing it against a budget host is comparing the wrong category. It's worth shortlisting if you specifically need NVIDIA GPU capacity or general-purpose CPU compute out of India, less so if you want a beginner-friendly website host.

## FAQs

**Does E2E Networks offer shared web hosting?**
No. E2E Networks is a cloud infrastructure and GPU cloud provider — it offers VM instances, containers and managed GPU compute, not cPanel-style shared hosting or website builders.

**What GPUs does E2E Networks offer?**
Its lineup spans NVIDIA L4 up through H100, H200 and B200, priced per hour with per-minute billing granularity.

**Does E2E Networks have a money-back guarantee?**
E2E doesn't publish a blanket money-back guarantee like consumer hosts do. Billing is usage-based, so review the cancellation and refund terms on your specific invoice or contract before committing.

**Is E2E Networks a trustworthy company?**
It's India's only NSE/BSE-listed pure-play GPU cloud company, which brings public financial disclosure most private hosts don't have. That said, its public review footprint is thin — only 7 Trustpilot reviews at a 2.3/5 average — so weigh that limited sample accordingly.

**Where are E2E Networks' data centers?**
Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Bengaluru, India.

**How is E2E Networks billed?**
Pay-as-you-go with per-minute billing on GPU instances and hourly billing on CPU instances; monthly and annual commitments bring discounted rates versus on-demand.

**Can I migrate an existing website or app to E2E Networks?**
Yes, but there's no automated import tool — you provision a new VM or container and move your application and data across manually, the same as migrating between any two cloud/IaaS providers.

**Is E2E Networks good for AI startups?**
It's positioned specifically for AI/ML workloads with a full GPU range and India-based infrastructure, which can be attractive for cost or data-residency reasons — but compare its per-hour GPU rates against other providers for your specific GPU model before committing.

Check current offers on the [E2E Networks coupon page](/coupons/e2enetworks), or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting).

title: Freehostia Review 2026: Free Hosting Tier and Real Costs
excerpt: Freehostia review 2026: what its free ad-free hosting tier really offers, paid Watercircle-Supernatural pricing, Hepsia panel, pros, cons and verdict.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Freehostia worth using?

Freehostia is worth it if you want a genuinely free, ad-free hosting tier for a small site or a test project — its 250MB/6GB Chocolate plan won't run a real WordPress site for long. Its paid Watercircle-to-Supernatural plans ($3.25-$10.50/mo) are reasonably priced but run on Freehostia's own Hepsia panel, not cPanel.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (Chocolate plan) |
| Cheapest paid plan | Watercircle, $3.25/mo |
| Renewal price | Same listed price (no long-term teaser pricing found) |
| Control panel | Hepsia (Freehostia's own, not cPanel) |
| Uptime guarantee | 99.9% target |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days (paid plans) |
| Best for | Small/test sites on the free tier; budget shared hosting on paid tiers |

## What Freehostia actually is

Freehostia is a budget web host operated by LiquidNet, and it has built its identity almost entirely around one thing: a hosting plan that costs nothing and doesn't plaster ads across your site. That's rarer than it sounds — most "free hosting" offers are ad-subsidized or bait for an upsell. Freehostia's free "Chocolate" plan is real, ad-free hosting, but it comes with real limits: 250MB of disk space, 6GB of bandwidth a month, up to 5 hosted domains, a 10MB cap on MySQL database storage, and a 2MB maximum file upload size. That's enough for a static portfolio, a landing page, or a project you're testing — it is not enough to run a WordPress site with any meaningful traffic or plugin footprint.

Past the free tier, Freehostia sells four paid shared plans that scale up disk space, bandwidth, domain slots and email accounts, with the two highest tiers going unlimited on all of those. Every plan — free or paid — is managed through Hepsia, a control panel Freehostia built and maintains itself rather than licensing cPanel. If you've only ever used cPanel, expect a different (though reportedly straightforward) interface, not a like-for-like clone.

## Pricing

Pricing below was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check Freehostia's own pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Price | Disk space | Bandwidth | Domains | Email accounts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chocolate (free) | $0 | 250MB | 6GB/mo | 5 | Limited |
| Watercircle | $3.25/mo | 500GB | 50GB/mo | 10 | 100 |
| Lovebeat | $5.25/mo | 2TB | 1TB/mo | 20 | 300 |
| Wildhoney | $8.25/mo | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |
| Supernatural | $10.50/mo | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |

## The real cost breakdown

Freehostia's paid pricing is refreshingly plain compared to hosts that lure you in with a 48-month teaser rate and triple the renewal price — we didn't find evidence of a separate, lower introductory rate that jumps at renewal; the listed monthly prices above appear to be what you pay both at signup and on renewal. That's a real point in its favor if accurate for your billing term, but always confirm the exact renewal terms shown at checkout for the billing cycle you pick, since longer prepaid terms can still carry different effective rates than month-to-month.

The free Chocolate plan costs nothing, but "free" comes with its own real cost: the 250MB/6GB ceiling means you'll likely need to upgrade to a paid plan — or migrate elsewhere — the moment a site gets real visitors or media files. Treat it as a sandbox, not a permanent home for anything you depend on.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **Chocolate (free)** if you're testing a site idea, building a portfolio you don't expect much traffic on, or need a zero-cost sandbox to learn hosting basics.

Choose **Watercircle** if you're launching one real site — a small business page, a blog, a brochure site — and want headroom past the free tier's limits without paying much for it.

Choose **Lovebeat** if you're running a site with growing media (images, video, larger page counts) or want more email accounts than Watercircle's 100.

Choose **Wildhoney or Supernatural** if you're hosting multiple sites, don't want to think about storage/bandwidth ceilings again, or want the free domain registration bundled with the top two tiers.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely free ad-free tier exists | Free tier's 250MB/10MB MySQL limits are tight |
| No cPanel license cost passed to Hepsia users | Hepsia has a learning curve if you're used to cPanel |
| Paid plans are inexpensive relative to storage/bandwidth offered | Trustpilot presence is thin — very few recent reviews |
| Load-balanced cluster architecture (not one bottleneck server) | Free plan not suited to WordPress at any real traffic |
| 30-day money-back guarantee on paid plans | Free tier has no refund guarantee (no payment taken) |

## Support

Freehostia advertises 24/7 customer support on its plans, including the free tier. As with any budget host, expect ticket-based support to be the primary channel rather than 24/7 live chat with instant human response — check Freehostia's own support page for current channels (live chat, ticket, knowledge base) before you sign up if a specific support format matters to you.

## Migration

Freehostia's Hepsia panel includes a 1-click script installer for common apps, which helps with setting up a fresh site but isn't the same as an automated full-site migration tool. If you're moving an existing site from another host, plan on manually exporting your files/database and reimporting them (or using your CMS's own export/import tools) rather than assuming a one-click "migrate my site" button exists — we didn't find one advertised.

## Where Freehostia is a strong fit

- You want a truly free, ad-free place to host a small static site or a project you're testing before committing money.
- You're price-sensitive and want a paid plan with a flat, predictable rate rather than a steep post-promo renewal jump.
- You don't mind learning a non-cPanel control panel in exchange for lower cost.

## Where to think twice

- You're running (or plan to run) a WordPress site with real traffic — the free tier's 250MB/6GB caps will bite fast.
- You specifically need cPanel because you're used to it or a tool you rely on assumes it.
- You want a host with a large, easily verifiable review base — Freehostia's public review presence is thin, so you're relying more on the provider's own claims than a deep pool of independent feedback.

## Verdict

Freehostia earns its niche by doing something genuinely rare: a free hosting tier that's actually ad-free rather than a bait-and-switch. That tier is legitimately useful for small, low-traffic sites and for testing ideas before you commit real money. Once you need more room, its paid Watercircle-through-Supernatural plans are inexpensive and, notably, don't appear to hide a steep renewal-price jump behind an introductory rate — a rarer trait than it should be in budget hosting. The trade-off is Hepsia instead of cPanel and a thin independent review record, so go in informed rather than assuming Freehostia behaves like a mainstream cPanel host.

## FAQs

**Is Freehostia's free plan really free forever?**
Yes — the Chocolate plan doesn't require payment and doesn't display forced ads, but it's capped at 250MB of storage and 6GB of monthly bandwidth, so it's meant for small or test sites rather than a permanent home for a growing one.

**Does Freehostia use cPanel?**
No. Freehostia manages both its free and paid plans through Hepsia, its own in-house control panel, not cPanel.

**Does Freehostia's paid pricing jump at renewal?**
We didn't find evidence of a separate low introductory rate that increases sharply at renewal — the listed monthly prices appear to apply on an ongoing basis, but always confirm the exact terms for your chosen billing cycle at checkout.

**Is there a money-back guarantee?**
Yes, paid Freehostia plans come with a 30-day money-back guarantee. The free plan has no refund guarantee since no payment is collected.

**Can the free plan run WordPress?**
Technically yes for a very small install, but the 250MB storage cap and 10MB MySQL database limit will constrain it quickly — a real WordPress site with plugins, media and traffic needs a paid plan.

**How many domains can I host on the free plan?**
Up to 5 domains on the Chocolate free plan, scaling to 10, 20, or unlimited domains on the paid Watercircle, Lovebeat, and Wildhoney/Supernatural tiers respectively.

**Does Freehostia have good reviews?**
Its Trustpilot presence is limited — a small number of reviews with mixed scores — so there isn't a large independent review base to lean on. Weigh that against the provider's own claims when deciding.

**How do I migrate an existing site to Freehostia?**
Freehostia doesn't appear to offer a dedicated one-click migration tool; plan on exporting your files and database from your current host and reimporting them through Hepsia, or using your CMS's built-in export/import feature.

Compare current offers on the [Freehostia coupon page](/coupons/freehostia), or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting).

title: FreeHosting.com Review 2026: Free Plan Limits & Verdict
excerpt: FreeHosting.com review: 10GB free hosting with no forced ads, but a 1.8/5 Trustpilot rating. Real limits, pricing and honest verdict inside.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is FreeHosting.com actually free, and is it worth using?

Yes — the free plan is genuinely free for life, with 10GB storage, unlimited bandwidth and no forced ads. But it's a single-site, single-email, single-database plan with no SSH access, and real-world Trustpilot reviews describe a rough support experience and upsell pressure toward a $29.95 SSL add-on. Treat it as a sandbox for testing an idea, not a home for anything that needs to stay online reliably.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (lifetime, 1 site) |
| Paid tier | $7.99/mo (100GB, multi-site) |
| Uptime guarantee | Not publicly stated |
| Money-back guarantee | Not applicable on free plan |
| Trustpilot rating | 1.8 / 5 (41 reviews) |
| Best for | Testing a small hobby site on zero budget |

## What FreeHosting.com actually is

FreeHosting.com is a no-cost web hosting service built for hobby projects, students, and anyone who wants to try a site before paying for hosting anywhere else. The free plan bundles 10GB of disk space, bandwidth that isn't capped by a fixed number (governed instead by a fair-use policy), one MySQL database, one email account, PHP/MySQL support, and a control panel for managing files, domains and mail from a single dashboard. It also includes a drag-and-drop site builder with a large template library and an app installer for common CMS platforms.

Two things separate it from the free hosts that pad their numbers: it doesn't force third-party ads onto hosted sites, and it doesn't run on a trial countdown — the free plan is meant to keep running for as long as the domain attached to it stays registered.

That said, "free" comes with real boundaries. You need your own registered domain to sign up — there's no free subdomain to get started with immediately. The free tier is capped at one website, one email inbox and one database, and it has no SSH access or cron job scheduling, both of which sit behind the paid plan. Independent reviews are also considerably harsher than the marketing copy: FreeHosting.com sits at 1.8 out of 5 on Trustpilot across 41 reviews, with recurring complaints about being pushed toward a $29.95 SSL certificate purchase, slow or unanswered support tickets, and sites getting rate-limited or knocked offline without much warning. Read that as a signal to keep expectations modest, not as a dealbreaker for a throwaway test site.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this article's publish date and can change — verify current figures on FreeHosting.com's own site before signing up.

| Plan | Price | Storage | Sites | Email/DB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/mo | 10GB | 1 | 1 email, 1 database |
| Paid | $7.99/mo | 100GB | Multiple | Unlimited email, unlimited databases |

## What "free" actually costs you

The free plan isn't hiding a subscription fee, but it isn't cost-free either — the cost shows up as limitations and friction instead of a bill:

- **One site, one email, one database.** Anything beyond a single small project means either juggling workarounds or upgrading.
- **No SSH, no cron jobs.** Anyone wanting server-level control or scheduled tasks has to move to the paid tier.
- **Bring your own domain.** There's no free subdomain, so you're paying a domain registrar even if hosting itself is free.
- **SSL upsell pressure.** Multiple Trustpilot reviewers report being steered toward a $29.95 SSL certificate to get a fully working, secure site — worth confirming whether a free SSL option is actually available before you commit time to building on the platform.
- **Support and reliability are the real gap.** Reviewers describe ignored tickets and intermittent rate-limiting that can take a site offline; for anything beyond a low-stakes hobby page, that's the cost that matters most.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose the **free plan** if you're testing an idea, building a portfolio page, or learning web development and don't need guaranteed uptime or fast support turnaround.

Choose the **$7.99/mo paid plan** if you've outgrown one site, one email account or one database, or if you need multi-site hosting without juggling multiple free accounts.

Consider skipping FreeHosting.com entirely if you're hosting anything business-critical — the Trustpilot complaint pattern around support responsiveness and site interruptions makes it a hard sell for a site that needs to stay up.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely free for life, no trial clock | Trustpilot rating of 1.8/5 across 41 reviews |
| No forced third-party ads on your site | Free tier limited to 1 site, 1 email, 1 database |
| Unmetered bandwidth under fair-use policy | Requires your own domain — no free subdomain |
| Site builder and app installer included | No SSH access or cron jobs on the free plan |
| Straightforward $7.99/mo upgrade path | Reviewers report SSL upsell pressure and slow support |

## Support

FreeHosting.com offers ticket-based support alongside its help documentation, but reviewer feedback is a consistent weak point — multiple Trustpilot reviews describe tickets going unanswered for extended periods, including from paying customers. If responsive support matters for your project, budget extra patience or lean on the self-serve help articles and community resources before opening a ticket.

## Migration

Moving an existing site onto FreeHosting.com typically means exporting your files and database from wherever they currently live and importing them through the control panel's file manager and database tools, since there's no mention of a dedicated white-glove migration service. Reviewers note some friction connecting a personalized domain, so it's worth testing DNS propagation and domain connection on a low-stakes project before moving anything that can't afford downtime.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Learning HTML/CSS/PHP or testing a static site with zero budget
- A short-lived portfolio, resume site, or class project
- Prototyping a site's structure before choosing a paid host

## Where to think twice

- Any site where uptime or fast support matters
- E-commerce, client work, or anything handling payments
- Multi-site setups — the free tier caps you at one

## The bottom line

FreeHosting.com delivers on the basic promise of free, ad-free hosting with a real control panel — that alone puts it ahead of hosts that plaster your site with banner ads. But the gap between the marketing page and the Trustpilot reviews is wide enough to matter: a 1.8-out-of-5 rating built on support and reliability complaints means this is a tool for low-stakes experimentation, not a platform to build anything you depend on. If you outgrow the free tier or need guarantees around uptime and support, it's worth comparing FreeHosting.com's $7.99/mo plan against established budget hosts before committing. See the [FreeHosting.com coupon page](/coupons/freehostingcom) for current offers, or browse [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) more broadly.

## FAQs

### Is FreeHosting.com really free forever?

Yes, the free plan has no trial countdown and is designed to keep running for as long as the domain attached to it stays registered and active — though reviewers report accounts can be rate-limited or suspended without much warning.

### Does FreeHosting.com put ads on my site?

No. FreeHosting.com states it doesn't force third-party advertising onto hosted sites, which is a real point in its favor compared to many other free hosts.

### Do I need to buy a domain separately?

Yes. The free plan requires your own registered domain — there's no free subdomain option to get started with immediately.

### What are the free plan's limits?

10GB storage, unlimited bandwidth under a fair-use policy, one website, one email account and one MySQL database. There's no SSH access or cron job scheduling on the free tier.

### Is FreeHosting.com good, based on reviews?

Independent reviews are mixed-to-poor: FreeHosting.com holds a 1.8-out-of-5 rating on Trustpilot from 41 reviews, with common complaints about SSL upsell pressure, slow support responses and intermittent site interruptions.

### How much does the paid plan cost?

The paid tier is $7.99/month and includes 100GB storage, multi-site hosting, and unlimited email accounts and databases.

### Can I migrate an existing website to FreeHosting.com?

Yes, using the control panel's file manager and database import tools, though there's no dedicated migration service — some reviewers note friction when connecting a personalized domain.

### Is FreeHosting.com good for beginners?

It's reasonable for learning or a first small project thanks to the included site builder and app installer, but the support and reliability complaints in reviews mean beginners shouldn't expect much hand-holding if something goes wrong.

title: GlowHost Review 2026: cPanel Hosting Pricing & Verdict

author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is GlowHost worth it in 2026?

GlowHost is a solid pick if you want standard cPanel hosting from a US-based host with a genuinely long refund window and reseller/WHMCS tools built in — it suits web design agencies and freelancers managing several client sites more than a first-time blogger. Its downsides are limited data center choice (US-only on shared plans) and pricing that isn't the cheapest in the category.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Under $4/mo (Unlimited Single Domain, intro term) |
| Renewal price | From around $4.87/mo, higher on upper tiers |
| Control panel | cPanel / WHM |
| Money-back guarantee | 91 days |
| Best for | Agencies, resellers, and cPanel-familiar site owners |

## What GlowHost actually is

GlowHost is a privately held US hosting company that has run cPanel-based shared, reseller, VPS and dedicated hosting for small businesses and agencies for years. Unlike budget hosts that build a proprietary dashboard, GlowHost sticks with the industry-standard cPanel/WHM stack layered on CloudLinux OS — which matters if you or your developer already know cPanel and don't want to relearn a custom interface. It leans into the web-agency/reseller crowd specifically: WHMCS-compatible reseller plans let an agency resell hosting to clients under its own branding rather than routing every client through one shared account.

## Pricing by plan

| Plan | Intro price | Storage | Bandwidth | Sites |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unlimited Single Domain | ~$3.47/mo | Unlimited (SATA) | Unlimited | 1 |
| Unlimited Multi-Domain | ~$6.27/mo | Unlimited (SATA) | Unlimited | Unlimited |
| Personal Hosting | ~$6.97/mo | 10 GB SSD | 100 GB | Unlimited |
| Professional Hosting | ~$12.57/mo | 20 GB SSD | 250 GB | Unlimited |

Reseller hosting starts around $24.95/mo for the entry Level I package, running up through higher storage/bandwidth tiers for agencies hosting more client sites. Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — always confirm the current rate on GlowHost's own pricing page before checking out.

## The real cost breakdown

GlowHost's headline numbers look competitive, but as with most hosts, the intro price only applies to your first billing term. The Unlimited Single Domain plan's advertised rate climbs to roughly $4.87/mo on renewal, and the pattern holds across the lineup — Multi-Domain, Personal and Professional all renew somewhat higher than their intro rate. None of the jumps are dramatic compared to some budget competitors, but you should still check the exact renewal figure shown at checkout for your billing term before committing, since GlowHost (like nearly every host) charges the full term upfront rather than month to month at the advertised rate.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **Unlimited Single Domain** if you're hosting exactly one personal or small-business site and don't need SSD-tier storage speed.

Choose **Unlimited Multi-Domain** if you're running several low-traffic sites and want unlimited storage without the reseller price jump.

Choose **Personal Hosting** if you want SSD storage for a single more demanding site and 10GB is enough for your media/database footprint.

Choose **Professional Hosting** if you're running multiple sites that need faster SSD storage and more bandwidth headroom than the Personal tier gives you.

Choose a **Reseller plan** if you're an agency or freelancer hosting client sites under your own brand and need WHMCS billing integration and full cPanel account creation for each client.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Standard cPanel/WHM — no proprietary dashboard to learn | Shared servers are US-only, no international data centers |
| 91-day money-back guarantee, longer than most competitors' 30 days | Entry storage (10-20GB on SSD tiers) is modest next to some rivals |
| WHMCS-compatible reseller plans built for agencies | Unlimited-storage tiers run on SATA rather than SSD drives |
| CloudLinux OS and Softaculous one-click app installs included | Not the cheapest intro pricing in the shared-hosting category |

## Support

GlowHost advertises 24/7 support through live chat and ticketing, alongside a knowledge base covering common cPanel and account-setup questions. Because it runs standard cPanel rather than a custom panel, general cPanel documentation and tutorials from outside GlowHost also apply directly to its accounts — a practical advantage if you ever need to troubleshoot something the support team hasn't answered yet.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to GlowHost is more straightforward than on hosts with a proprietary panel, since cPanel-to-cPanel migrations are a well-worn path: you (or GlowHost's team) can use cPanel's own account-transfer tools to pull your files, databases and email over directly from your old cPanel host. If your current host doesn't use cPanel, you'll be looking at a manual migration — export your database, copy files over FTP/SFTP, and re-point DNS once everything is verified on the new account.

## Where GlowHost is a strong fit

GlowHost fits web agencies and freelance developers who need a reseller account to host multiple clients under WHMCS billing, and anyone who specifically wants a real cPanel/WHM environment rather than a simplified custom dashboard. The 91-day refund window also makes it a lower-risk trial than most hosts if you're not sure it'll work for your setup.

## Where to think twice

If you need a data center outside the US, or you're comparing purely on the lowest possible intro price, GlowHost isn't the cheapest option in the shared-hosting space — budget-focused hosts undercut its entry pricing. Its unlimited-storage plans also run on SATA drives rather than SSD, so a storage-speed-sensitive site is better matched to the Personal or Professional SSD tiers.

## Verdict

GlowHost earns its place for a specific audience — cPanel loyalists and hosting resellers — rather than as a blanket recommendation for every type of site owner. The 91-day guarantee and standard cPanel/WHM stack are genuinely useful differentiators, but the US-only data center and mid-pack pricing mean shoppers who just want the absolute cheapest beginner plan should compare it against other options first. Check the current [GlowHost coupon page](/coupons/glowhost) for active offers, or browse more [web hosting deals](/category/hosting) to compare.

## FAQs

**Does GlowHost use cPanel?**
Yes — every shared, reseller, VPS and dedicated plan runs standard cPanel/WHM on top of CloudLinux OS, rather than a proprietary control panel.

**How long is GlowHost's money-back guarantee?**
GlowHost offers a 91-day money-back guarantee on its hosting plans, longer than the 30-day window most competitors offer.

**Does GlowHost's advertised price stay the same after renewal?**
No. Like most hosts, GlowHost's lowest advertised prices apply to the initial term only and renew at a higher monthly rate — check the renewal figure at checkout before committing.

**Is GlowHost good for web design agencies?**
Yes — GlowHost's WHMCS-compatible reseller plans are built specifically for agencies and freelancers hosting multiple client sites under one branded account.

**Where are GlowHost's servers located?**
GlowHost's shared hosting servers are US-based only. Customers needing other regions should look at GlowHost's VPS or dedicated server options, or a different provider.

**Can I migrate my existing site to GlowHost?**
Yes. Because GlowHost uses standard cPanel, migrating from another cPanel host is typically handled through cPanel's own account-transfer tools; non-cPanel migrations require a manual file/database transfer.

**Does GlowHost include a free SSL certificate?**
Yes — GlowHost includes a free private SSL certificate on its shared and reseller hosting packages.

**What's the difference between GlowHost's Personal and Professional plans?**
Professional Hosting doubles the SSD storage (20GB vs 10GB) and raises the bandwidth allowance (250GB vs 100GB) compared to Personal Hosting, at a higher monthly price.

## What Go4hosting actually is

Go4hosting is a hosting and data-center company headquartered in India, running its own facilities rather than reselling capacity from a third party. Alongside shared and reseller hosting, it sells Linux/Windows VPS, dedicated servers, colocation and multi-cloud hosting on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. The company leans on India-specific credentials — ISO 20000-1, HIPAA and PCI DSS compliance — and advertises 24/7 support with sub-30-minute response targets, aiming at businesses that want (or are required) to keep data in Indian data centers.

Pricing on this page was accurate as of September 2026 and is quoted in Indian rupees, since that's Go4hosting's primary listed currency — expect it to change over time, so check the live pricing page before buying.

## Shared hosting pricing

Go4hosting's shared hosting comes in three tiers, all built around unlimited storage and bandwidth, differing mainly in support level and domain count:

| Plan | 3-year term | 1-year term (renewal-level rate) | Domains | Support |

| Home | ₹97.50/mo | ₹147.50/mo | Single domain | Unlimited email support |

Committing to just 1 year instead pushes the effective monthly rate up by roughly 50% across all three plans — Home goes from ₹97.50 to ₹147.50/mo, Basic from ₹147.50 to ₹197.50/mo, and Value from ₹172.50 to ₹247.50/mo. ## Which plan should you choose

Choose **Home** if you're hosting a single small site on a tight budget and don't need phone support. Choose **Basic** if you're running more than one domain and want chat support alongside email. Choose **Value** if you're migrating an existing site — the free migration and phone support make the extra cost worthwhile for anyone who doesn't want to move files manually. For anything beyond a basic brochure site, or if you need resources outside India, it's worth comparing Go4hosting's VPS/dedicated tiers or a more globally-distributed host against these shared plans.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| India-based data centers and compliance certifications | Monthly rate jumps significantly on shorter terms |
| Unlimited storage/bandwidth advertised on all shared tiers | Add-ons (cPanel, Softaculous, SSL) can bill separately |
| Free migration included on the Value tier | Refund guarantee reportedly applied narrowly in practice |
| Broad product range (shared to VPS to multi-cloud) in one account | Limited independent review volume to verify support quality |

## Support

Go4hosting advertises 24/7 support across phone, email and chat, with claimed response times under 30 minutes, plus WhatsApp support and a published knowledge base for self-service troubleshooting. Support channel access varies by plan — the entry-level Home tier is limited to email support, while Basic adds chat and Value adds phone support, so pick a tier accordingly if live support access matters to you.

## Migration

Free migration is only explicitly included on the Value shared hosting tier; Home and Basic customers should confirm migration costs before signing up if they're moving an existing site rather than starting fresh. Go4hosting's knowledge base covers manual setup topics like configuring cPanel and SSL, which is useful context if you end up handling parts of the move yourself.

## Where it's a strong fit

Go4hosting makes sense for businesses that specifically need India-hosted infrastructure — lower latency to Indian visitors, or a data-residency requirement — and for teams that value its compliance stack (HIPAA, PCI DSS, ISO 20000-1) for regulated workloads. Its product range also means you can start on shared hosting and move up to VPS, dedicated or multi-cloud without switching providers.

## Where to think twice

If you're not specifically targeting India, most global hosts offer more transparent all-in pricing and a larger independent review base to gauge real-world reliability against. The steep 1-year vs 3-year price gap and reports of add-on costs and a narrowly-applied refund guarantee mean it pays to read the fine print carefully — and to budget for a longer commitment if you want the advertised rate.

## Verdict

Go4hosting is a reasonable pick specifically for India-hosted or compliance-driven projects, less so as a default choice if you have no geographic requirement. Its shared plans are inexpensive on paper, but the true cost depends heavily on term length and which extras you need — verify the full checkout total, not just the lowest advertised monthly figure, before you commit.

**Is Go4hosting good for migrating an existing website?**

title: Google Cloud Review 2026: Compute Engine Hosting Costs
excerpt: An honest look at Google Cloud's Compute Engine for website hosting — VM pricing, free tier, support, migration and whether it fits beginners.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Google Cloud good for website hosting?

This review covers Google Cloud narrowly as a website-hosting option — specifically Compute Engine virtual machines (with a brief note on App Engine) — not GCP's full 100+ service enterprise catalog. As a VM host, it's capable and cheap at entry level, but it's built for engineers, not a beginner site owner wanting a one-click setup.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | ~$6.11/month (e2-micro) |
| Free tier | 1 e2-micro VM/month, always free (select US regions) |
| Renewal price | Same pay-as-you-go rate — no promo/renewal gap |
| Uptime guarantee | 99.5-99.99% SLA depending on config |
| Money-back guarantee | None — usage-based billing, no fixed refund window |
| Best for | Developers comfortable managing a Linux server |

## What Google Cloud actually is (for hosting purposes)

Google Cloud Platform is Google's enterprise cloud — data warehousing, machine learning, Kubernetes, networking, and dozens of other services most site owners will never touch. For hosting a website, the relevant piece is Compute Engine: raw virtual machines you provision, configure, and manage yourself, billed per second with no contract. App Engine sits one layer up as a more managed platform-as-a-service option (you deploy code, Google handles the server), but it costs more and is less flexible than a plain VM for a typical site.

There's no cPanel, no bundled domain, no one-click WordPress installer, and no support team that will SSH in and fix your server for you. You're choosing Google Cloud because you want direct control over a Linux box at commodity-cloud pricing, not because you want a turnkey hosting panel.

## Compute Engine pricing (entry-level VMs)

Pricing was accurate as of September 2026 and can change — always confirm current rates on Google Cloud's own pricing page before budgeting.

| Machine type | vCPU | RAM | Price/hour | Price/month (730 hrs) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| e2-micro | 2 (shared, up to 1/8 core) | 1 GB | ~$0.0084 | ~$6.11 |
| e2-small | 2 (shared) | 2 GB | ~$0.0168 | ~$12.23 |
| e2-medium | 2 (shared) | 4 GB | ~$0.0335 | ~$24.46 |

These are on-demand list prices for the us-central1 region before sustained-use or committed-use discounts, which can lower the effective rate further for VMs left running continuously.

## The real cost breakdown

There's no teaser price and no renewal cliff here — Compute Engine is metered per second from day one, so the number above is the number you keep paying, not an introductory rate that jumps later. That said, the sticker price is only the compute cost: persistent disk storage, network egress beyond the free allowance, static IP reservations, snapshots, and load balancing are all billed separately and add up quickly once a site gets real traffic. Google's Always Free tier covers one e2-micro instance per month (in us-west1, us-central1 or us-east1 only), 30 GB of standard persistent disk, and 1 GB of network egress — genuinely free indefinitely for a small static site or low-traffic blog, but easy to exceed without noticing.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **e2-micro** (free tier eligible) if you're hosting a personal blog, a portfolio, or a low-traffic static site and want to stay at $0.

Choose **e2-small** if e2-micro's 1 GB RAM starts causing out-of-memory issues — a WordPress install with a handful of plugins, or a small Node/Python app, typically needs this tier.

Choose **e2-medium** or larger if you're running a CMS with a database on the same box, expect meaningful traffic, or need headroom for background jobs alongside the web server.

Choose **App Engine** instead of a raw VM if you'd rather deploy code and let Google manage scaling and patching, and you're comfortable paying more for that convenience.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely free e2-micro tier, indefinitely | No cPanel, no one-click installers — you configure everything |
| Pay-per-second billing, no long contract | No bundled domain, email or free SSL panel like traditional hosts |
| Scales to any size without switching providers | Storage, egress and IPs are billed separately from compute |
| Global data center footprint and strong network | No phone support on lower tiers; steep learning curve |
| Sustained/committed-use discounts reward steady workloads | Easy to rack up unexpected charges without close monitoring |

## Support

Google Cloud's support is tiered and paid — the free "Basic" tier gets you documentation, community forums (Stack Overflow, Google Cloud Community) and billing support only, with no technical support channel. Paid support plans (Standard, Enhanced, Premium) add case-based technical support with response-time SLAs, starting at a flat monthly fee plus a percentage of usage. There is no live chat or phone line included by default the way many hosting providers offer out of the box — budget for a support plan if you'll need hands-on help, or be prepared to self-serve through documentation and community channels.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to Compute Engine means standing up a new VM, installing your stack (web server, database, language runtime) yourself or via a startup script, and migrating files and databases manually — there's no automated "import my WordPress site" wizard. Google does offer a Migrate to Virtual Machines tool aimed at moving existing server workloads into Compute Engine, which can ease a lift-and-shift from another VM host, but for a typical shared-hosting site the more common path is a manual rebuild: export your database, copy files over, reconfigure DNS to point at the new VM's static IP.

## Where it's a strong fit

Google Cloud makes sense if you're a developer who wants full root access to a Linux server, expects to scale well beyond what shared hosting can handle, or is already using other Google Cloud services and wants everything under one account. The free e2-micro tier is also a legitimately good way to host a small personal project at zero ongoing cost, provided you're comfortable with basic server administration.

## Where to think twice

This is not for beginners. If you want to point-and-click a WordPress site into existence, get a bundled domain and free SSL without configuring anything, or call a support line when something breaks, a traditional shared or managed host will get you there faster and with far less risk of a surprise bill. The lack of guardrails — no spending cap by default, granular per-resource billing — means it's possible to rack up real costs without realizing it until the invoice arrives.

## Verdict

Google Cloud's Compute Engine is a solid, fairly priced option for hosting a website if you already know your way around a Linux server and want cloud-scale flexibility with a genuinely free entry point. It is not a replacement for a beginner-friendly host — there's no control panel, no bundled extras, and support requires a paid plan. Treat it as infrastructure you manage, not a hosting product you subscribe to.

## FAQs

**Is Google Cloud free for hosting a website?**
One e2-micro VM is free indefinitely under the Always Free tier in select US regions, along with 30 GB of disk and 1 GB of egress per month — enough for a small static site or low-traffic blog, but anything beyond those limits starts billing.

**Does Google Cloud offer a money-back guarantee?**
No. Billing is usage-based per second rather than a subscription, so there's no fixed refund window like a traditional host's 30-day guarantee. New accounts may receive promotional credit, which simply expires unused rather than being refunded.

**Do I need technical skills to use Google Cloud for hosting?**
Yes. Compute Engine gives you a bare virtual machine — you install and configure the web server, database, and any CMS yourself, typically over SSH. There's no cPanel or one-click WordPress installer built in.

**How does Compute Engine pricing compare to shared hosting?**
Entry-level VMs start around $6/month (e2-micro) with no renewal price hike, but storage, IP addresses, and network egress are billed separately, so the effective monthly cost is usually higher than the headline compute price alone.

**Can I run WordPress on Google Cloud?**
Yes, either by installing it manually on a Compute Engine VM or via Google Cloud Marketplace's pre-configured WordPress images, but you're still responsible for ongoing server maintenance, unlike managed WordPress hosting.

**Does Google Cloud include free SSL?**
Not automatically the way shared hosts bundle Let's Encrypt. You can configure SSL yourself (e.g. via Certbot) on a VM, or use Google-managed certificates if you front the site with a Google Cloud load balancer.

**What support does Google Cloud offer for hosting issues?**
Free-tier accounts get documentation and community forums only; case-based technical support with SLA response times requires a paid support plan on top of your usage costs.

**Is Google Cloud better than DigitalOcean or Vultr for hosting?**
It depends on your comfort level — DigitalOcean and Vultr are generally considered simpler for straightforward VM hosting with more predictable flat-rate droplets, while Google Cloud offers deeper enterprise features and a genuinely free micro instance, at the cost of a steeper learning curve and less predictable itemized billing.

Check the [Google Cloud coupon page](/coupons/googlecloud) for current offers, or browse [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) for beginner-friendlier alternatives.

## What HostingRaja actually is

HostingRaja is an Indian web hosting company running its own data centers within India, built around the pitch that a locally hosted site loads faster for an Indian audience than a US- or Europe-based host, backed by support that understands the local market. Its core product line is cPanel-based shared hosting, split into WordPress Hosting, Web Hosting and Premium Hosting tiers, with separate reseller, VPS, dedicated server and cloud hosting products for higher-traffic or agency use cases.

Softaculous comes bundled with the shared plans for one-click WordPress and other CMS installs, and the higher tiers add a free domain, dedicated IP and automatic backups that the cheapest tier doesn't include. HostingRaja doesn't publish its exact renewal pricing as prominently as the intro rate on its marketing pages, which makes it easy to anchor on the ₹49 or ₹104 headline figure without seeing what the plan actually costs at your next billing cycle.

Before you check out, open the cart or order summary and look for the renewal price explicitly — most Indian hosts in this price bracket roughly double or more at renewal versus the first-term promotional rate. Choose **Web Hosting** if you need more headroom than the WordPress-only tier — unmetered bandwidth and free SSL without yet needing a dedicated IP or bundled domain.

Choose **Premium Hosting** if you want the free domain, dedicated IP and automatic backups bundled in, or if you're running a small business site where backups shouldn't be an afterthought.

Choose **Reseller Hosting** if you're managing hosting for multiple clients and want a white-label cPanel setup rather than separate individual accounts.

Choose **VPS Hosting** if a shared plan's resource limits are becoming a bottleneck and you need dedicated CPU/RAM with root-level control.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Low entry-level pricing across shared tiers | Renewal pricing isn't clearly shown upfront |

## Support

HostingRaja advertises 24/7 customer support, which for an India-focused host is a genuine advantage if your own team or audience operates in Indian time zones — you're not waiting on a support queue that's asleep during your business hours. Support is reachable through the usual channels (ticket, chat, phone) listed on HostingRaja's own contact page; response quality for more advanced technical issues varies by review source, so it's worth checking recent independent feedback for your specific plan tier before assuming parity with larger global hosts.

If your current site isn't on cPanel already, ask support directly about the migration path before signing up, since that detail isn't spelled out in the marketing pages we reviewed.

## Where it's a strong fit

HostingRaja makes the most sense if your audience is primarily in India and you want a host with servers physically located there, if you're comfortable with cPanel, and if your budget is the primary constraint on a small WordPress or brochure site. The combination of low entry pricing and a large, mostly positive Trustpilot review base (4.7 out of 5 across over 1,000 reviews) suggests a reasonably solid track record for its core shared-hosting audience.

If you need transparent, published renewal pricing before you commit, or you want an ironclad no-questions-asked refund window, read HostingRaja's actual terms closely first — some user reports describe refund eligibility being tied to demonstrating a technical fault rather than a pure change-of-mind guarantee. ## Verdict

HostingRaja is a credible, budget-friendly choice for India-targeted websites that want local infrastructure and cPanel familiarity, backed by a large and largely positive Trustpilot track record. The tradeoffs are typical of budget hosting in this price bracket — renewal pricing needs to be checked manually, and the money-back guarantee has fine print worth reading rather than assuming it's unconditional. For small business and personal sites focused on an Indian audience, it's worth shortlisting; for a global audience with no India-specific need, compare it against wider-reach hosts before deciding. ### How does HostingRaja compare to international hosts like Hostinger?

HostingRaja's main differentiator is its India-based data centers and local support hours; international hosts like Hostinger have broader global name recognition and infrastructure but no India-specific latency advantage.
