| Resource | Always Free allowance | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro (AMD) | Up to 2 instances, 1/8 OCPU + 1 GB RAM each | 50 GB boot volume each |
| Ampere A1 (Arm) | 1,500 OCPU-hrs + 9,000 GB-hrs/month | ≈ 2 OCPU / 12 GB run continuously |
| Block storage | 200 GB combined | Shared across boot + block volumes |
| Outbound data transfer | 10 TB/month | Across the whole tenancy |
| Load balancer | 1 flexible LB, 10 Mbps | Optional, also free |
| Paid x86 Compute (E4.Flex) | — | $0.0255/OCPU-hr + $0.0015/GB-hr |
| Paid Ampere A1 (over free allowance) | — | $0.01/OCPU-hr + $0.0015/GB-hr |

The Ampere A1 free allowance is worth flagging honestly: Oracle quietly cut it in mid-2026 from 4 OCPU/24 GB down to the current 2 OCPU/12 GB, without a public announcement — existing instances above the new limit were subject to reclamation. It's still a genuinely free-forever tier, just smaller than it used to be, and worth double-checking on Oracle's docs before you plan capacity around it.

### Real cost breakdown

There's no promotional-then-renewal pricing model here like typical shared hosting — OCI is pure pay-as-you-go beyond the free allowance, billed monthly in arrears for actual usage. A small low-traffic site can realistically run entirely inside the Always Free tier at $0/month indefinitely. Step outside it (more OCPU, more RAM, extra storage, a database service) and costs scale linearly with the rates above — there's no bundled "plan price" to point to, so budget based on the resources you'll actually consume. New accounts also get $300 in trial credit for 30 days, separate from the permanent free resources, useful for testing paid services before deciding to pay for them.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose the VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro Always Free instance** if you're hosting a tiny static site, a personal blog, or a low-traffic API and want $0 cost with minimal resource needs — 1 GB RAM is tight but workable for lightweight workloads.
- **Choose the Ampere A1 Always Free allowance** if you want more headroom — 2 OCPU/12 GB is enough for a small WordPress install, a Node/Python app, or a couple of lightweight services, still at $0/month.
- **Choose paid Compute (E4.Flex or A1 beyond the free allowance)** if your site outgrows free-tier limits — traffic spikes, more RAM-hungry software, or you need dedicated OCPUs rather than shared micro capacity.
- **Skip OCI entirely** if you're not comfortable managing a Linux server yourself — there's no managed hosting layer, and no support safety net on the free tier if something breaks.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Always Free tier is genuinely free forever, not a time-limited trial | No managed/shared-hosting product — self-administer everything |
| Ampere A1 free allowance is real usable compute for small workloads | Free-tier Ampere allowance was quietly cut in half in 2026 |
| 10 TB/month outbound transfer even on the free tier | No beginner-friendly control panel or one-click installs |
| Pay-as-you-go paid tiers scale precisely with actual usage | Documentation and console are built for enterprise IT, steep learning curve |
| $300 trial credit to test paid services before committing | No meaningful consumer support presence for hosting-scale users |

## Support

OCI's support structure is built around enterprise support tiers and paid plans; Always Free and pay-as-you-go accounts get access to Oracle's documentation, community forums, and a basic support ticketing option, but there's no phone/live-chat safety net comparable to consumer web hosts. If you need hands-held troubleshooting when your site goes down, factor that gap into your decision — you're expected to debug your own VM.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to OCI means treating it like any VPS migration: provision a Compute instance, install your stack, move files/database over manually (or via your own backup tooling), point DNS at the new instance's public IP, and validate before cutting over. There's no automated site-migration tool bundled with the free tier — plan for manual work or scripting it yourself.

## Where it's a strong fit

If you're a developer, hobbyist, or budget-conscious technical user who wants real compute at zero ongoing cost — a personal project, a side API, a low-traffic app, or a testbed — the Always Free tier is one of the more generous offers among major cloud providers, even after the 2026 Ampere cut. It's also a reasonable low-cost option if you outgrow the free allowance and want precise pay-as-you-go billing instead of a flat monthly plan.

## Where to think twice

This is not for beginners. If you want to upload files and have a working WordPress site in ten minutes with support on hand if something breaks, OCI Compute is the wrong tool — there's no managed layer, no control panel, and no hand-holding. It's also not the pick if you need guaranteed uptime SLAs or fast support response on a free-tier account.

## Verdict

Scoped correctly — as self-managed Compute VM hosting, not Oracle's full enterprise platform — OCI's Always Free tier is a legitimately notable option for technically capable users who want real, permanent free compute rather than a 12-month trial. The 2026 cut to Ampere A1 limits is a fair reason for some caution, and this is squarely a DIY option with no consumer support net, but for the right technical user it's hard to beat $0/month for genuine VM capacity.

Compare it against managed alternatives on our [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) page, or check current offers on the [Oracle Cloud coupon page](/coupons/oraclecloud).

## FAQs

**Is Oracle Cloud's Always Free tier actually free forever?**
Yes — Always Free resources don't expire or convert to a paid trial as long as usage stays within the published limits. This is separate from the $300, 30-day trial credit new accounts also receive for testing paid services.

**What do I get on the Always Free tier?**
Up to two VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro AMD instances (1/8 OCPU, 1 GB RAM each), plus Ampere A1 Arm compute currently capped at 1,500 OCPU-hours and 9,000 GB-hours per month (about 2 OCPU/12 GB run continuously), 200 GB combined block storage, and 10 TB/month outbound transfer.

**Did Oracle reduce the free tier?**
Yes — in mid-2026 Oracle cut the Ampere A1 Always Free allowance from 4 OCPU/24 GB down to 2 OCPU/12 GB without a public announcement, and reclaimed instances that exceeded the new limit. The AMD micro instances and storage allowance were unaffected.

**Is Oracle Cloud good for beginners?**
No. There's no managed hosting product, control panel, or one-click installer — you provision and administer the VM yourself. It suits developers and technically comfortable users, not first-time site owners.

**How much does Oracle Cloud Compute cost beyond the free tier?**
Standard x86 Compute runs $0.0255 per OCPU-hour plus $0.0015 per GB-memory-hour. Ampere A1 usage beyond the free allowance is $0.01 per OCPU-hour plus $0.0015 per GB-hour. Both are pure pay-as-you-go with no fixed monthly plan price.

**Does Oracle Cloud offer a money-back guarantee?**
Not in the traditional hosting sense — there's no prepaid term to refund. You only pay for what you use beyond the free allowance, billed monthly in arrears.

**What support does Oracle Cloud offer free-tier users?**
Documentation, community forums, and basic ticketing — there's no phone or live-chat support comparable to consumer hosting providers for free-tier or pay-as-you-go accounts.

**How do I migrate an existing site to Oracle Cloud?**
Treat it as a standard VPS migration: provision a Compute instance, install your stack, move files and databases manually, then repoint DNS. There's no bundled automated migration tool.

title: ResellerClub Review 2026: Reseller Hosting Pricing
excerpt: ResellerClub review: white-label reseller hosting plans, WHM/cPanel vs Plesk pricing, 30-day guarantee, and who this agency-focused host actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is ResellerClub good for reseller hosting?

ResellerClub is a solid pick if you're reselling hosting to your own clients under your own brand — it gives you WHM/cPanel (or Plesk on Windows), unlimited branded cPanel accounts, and a white-label storefront. It's a poor fit if you just want to host one personal or business website, since everything here is built around managing other people's accounts.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Best for | Agencies, freelancers and IT resellers hosting multiple client sites |
| Starting price | Entry-tier Linux reseller plans (R1) typically start around $10-15/month on promotional pricing |
| Renewal price | Renews meaningfully higher after the first term — confirm the current rate at checkout |
| Control panel | WHM/cPanel (Linux plans), Plesk (Windows plans) |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days, first hosting account only |
| Not designed for | Single-site owners who don't need to resell hosting to others |

## What ResellerClub actually is

ResellerClub isn't a typical end-user host, and that distinction matters before you sign up. It's part of the same corporate group as BigRock, and its whole product is built around letting a designer, developer or agency buy bulk server capacity and portion it back out to their own clients — each with their own branded control panel — while ResellerClub's name stays invisible to the end customer.

That reseller-first design shows up everywhere in the product. Instead of one hosting account, you get a WHM master account that lets you spin up unlimited individually branded cPanel accounts for clients (Linux plans), or a Plesk-based equivalent for Windows/ASP.NET clients. There's a "SuperSite" storefront you can brand as your own, plus a domain-reseller program covering a large number of TLDs so you can bundle domains, hosting, SSL and security add-ons into your own packages at your own markup. If what you actually need is hosting for a single website, this add-on complexity is wasted overhead — a standard shared-hosting plan from a consumer-focused host will be simpler and usually cheaper.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this review's publish date and can change — ResellerClub, like most reseller hosts, runs region- and currency-specific promotions, so confirm the live number at checkout.

| Plan | Platform | Approx. entry pricing | What scales up |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Linux (WHM/cPanel) | Lowest reseller tier | Base disk space and bandwidth allowance |
| R2 | Linux (WHM/cPanel) | Mid-low tier | More storage, more bandwidth |
| R3 | Linux (WHM/cPanel) | Mid tier | Larger allowances for growing client bases |
| R4 | Linux (WHM/cPanel) | Top Linux tier | Highest storage/bandwidth in the Linux lineup |
| Windows R1-R4 | Plesk | Priced separately from Linux tiers | Same scaling pattern, aimed at ASP.NET clients |

All tiers advertise unlimited hosted websites per account, unlimited email accounts, and a free SSL certificate bundled in — the difference between tiers is disk space, bandwidth and how many client accounts you can comfortably run before needing to upgrade.

## The real cost breakdown

The number on the pricing page is a first-term promotional rate, not what you'll pay indefinitely. As with most reseller and shared hosting providers, the lowest headline price requires prepaying a longer term, and the plan renews at a noticeably higher monthly-equivalent rate once that term ends. Before committing to the cheapest-looking tier on the longest term, check the renewal price shown at checkout and multiply it out over a year or two — that's the number that actually matters if you plan to keep reselling long-term. Domain-reseller pricing, SSL, and security add-ons are all separate line items you layer on top of the base hosting plan as you build out your own product catalog.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose R1 if you're just starting out reselling hosting and have a handful of small client sites — it's the cheapest way to test whether the reseller model works for your business before committing to a bigger tier.

Choose R2 or R3 if you already manage a growing roster of client accounts and are running into storage or bandwidth ceilings on R1 — the jump in allowances is designed to buy you headroom without switching platforms.

Choose R4 (or the equivalent Windows tier) if you're operating at agency scale with many active client sites, or if your clients specifically need more storage-heavy or higher-traffic hosting than the lower tiers comfortably support.

Choose the Windows/Plesk line specifically if your client base builds on ASP.NET rather than PHP — trying to force ASP.NET clients onto the Linux/cPanel tiers doesn't work.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuine white-label branding — clients never see ResellerClub's name | Overkill and unnecessarily complex if you just need hosting for one site |
| Unlimited branded client (cPanel) accounts per reseller plan | Entry pricing is promotional and renews higher |
| Both Linux (WHM/cPanel) and Windows (Plesk) options available | 30-day money-back guarantee only covers your first account, not renewals |
| Bundled domain-reseller program across many TLDs | You're the one fielding client support tickets — ResellerClub backs the infrastructure, not your customer relationships |
| Free SSL included across reseller tiers | Third-party pricing listings vary by region/currency, so the checkout number needs its own verification |

## Support

ResellerClub provides support to you, the reseller — not directly to your end clients, since as far as they're concerned you are the hosting company. That means you're responsible for first-line client support, while ResellerClub's own support channels (ticketing, live chat, phone) back you up on server-level and platform issues. This is standard for the reseller-hosting model, but it's a meaningfully different support relationship than a typical end-user host, where the provider talks directly to the site owner.

## Migration

Moving existing client sites into ResellerClub's reseller platform is handled through cPanel-to-cPanel migration tooling on the Linux plans, which can import existing client accounts, email and databases from another WHM-based host. Migrations from non-cPanel platforms, or from Windows/Plesk environments, typically need more manual handling. If you're bringing over a large existing client base, it's worth confirming migration support for your specific source platform before you commit a full roster of clients to the switch.

## Where it's a strong fit

ResellerClub makes sense if you're a web designer, developer or small agency that already builds sites for clients and wants to bundle hosting into your own service without standing up your own server infrastructure. The white-label storefront and unlimited branded accounts let you look like a full-service hosting company to your clients while ResellerClub handles the underlying WHM/Plesk infrastructure.

## Where to think twice

If you only need hosting for your own single website or small business, ResellerClub is the wrong tool — you'll be paying for reseller infrastructure (branding, client-account management, domain-reseller tooling) you'll never use. A standard shared-hosting plan aimed at end users will be simpler to set up and typically cheaper for that use case.

## Verdict

ResellerClub earns its strong Trustpilot rating largely from the audience it's actually built for: resellers who want to run a white-label hosting business without owning servers. The WHM/cPanel and Plesk foundations are proven, the branding tools are genuinely useful for agencies, and the domain-reseller bundle rounds out a real business-in-a-box offering. Just go in with clear eyes about the pricing structure — confirm the renewal rate before you lock in a term — and about the support model, since you'll be your clients' first line of support, not ResellerClub.

## FAQs

**Is ResellerClub good for hosting a single personal website?**
Not really — it's built for reselling hosting to clients under your own brand. If you just need to host one site, a standard shared-hosting plan will be simpler and likely cheaper.

**What control panel does ResellerClub use?**
Linux reseller plans use WHM/cPanel; Windows reseller plans use Plesk.

**Does ResellerClub offer a money-back guarantee?**
Yes — a 30-day money-back guarantee, but per ResellerClub's own terms it applies only to a customer's first hosting account, not to renewals or additional accounts.

**Is ResellerClub's advertised price what I'll actually pay?**
The advertised price is typically a first-term promotional rate. Confirm the renewal price at checkout before committing to a long prepaid term.

**Can my clients tell they're hosted through ResellerClub?**
No — the platform is designed for white-label reselling, so clients interact with your own branded control panel and storefront rather than ResellerClub's name.

**Who handles support if a client has a hosting issue?**
You do, as the reseller — ResellerClub supports you on infrastructure and platform issues, but you're responsible for your own clients' first-line support.

**Can I migrate existing client accounts into ResellerClub?**
Yes, cPanel-to-cPanel migration tooling is available for Linux plans coming from another WHM-based host; migrations from other platforms may need more manual work.

**Is ResellerClub related to BigRock?**
Yes — ResellerClub is part of the same corporate group as BigRock, both focused on domain and hosting services.

Ready to get started? Check the current [ResellerClub coupon page](/coupons/resellerclub) for active offers, or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) to compare options.

title: Tencent Cloud Review 2026: CVM & Lighthouse Hosting Costs
excerpt: An honest look at Tencent Cloud's CVM and Lighthouse VPS for website hosting — real pricing, free trial terms, and who it actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Tencent Cloud good for website hosting?

This review covers only Tencent Cloud's Cloud Virtual Machine (CVM) and Lighthouse products used as website-hosting VPS — not the company's full enterprise catalog (AI, gaming backends, databases, CDN, and dozens of other services). For that narrow use, Lighthouse is a workable, low-cost VPS from around $4/month, best suited to sites serving mainland China or developers already comfortable managing a bare Linux box.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | ~$4/month (Lighthouse, 1 vCPU/1GB/50GB SSD) |
| Free trial | 3 months, new accounts only |
| Uptime guarantee | Not separately published for Lighthouse/CVM |
| Money-back guarantee | Varies by billing mode; prepaid terms largely non-refundable |
| Best for | Sites targeting China-based traffic, developers comfortable with raw Linux VPS management |

## What Tencent Cloud actually is (for hosting purposes)

Tencent Cloud is one of China's largest cloud infrastructure providers, competing with Alibaba Cloud and Huawei Cloud domestically and with AWS, Google Cloud and Azure internationally. Its catalog spans well beyond hosting — AI/ML tooling, game server infrastructure, IoT, and enterprise databases are all bigger parts of its business than shared or VPS-style web hosting.

For someone shopping for a place to host a website, only two products are relevant: **CVM (Cloud Virtual Machine)**, Tencent's general-purpose configurable VPS, and **Lighthouse**, a simplified, pre-bundled VPS aimed at individual developers and small businesses that don't want to hand-configure networking, security groups and billing the way CVM requires. Lighthouse is the more comparable product to a DigitalOcean Droplet or Vultr instance — fixed monthly pricing, bundled bandwidth, and a lighter console. CVM is closer to raw AWS EC2: more configuration knobs, and pricing that can vary by region, instance family and commitment term.

Neither product ships cPanel, a one-click WordPress installer by default, or the kind of beginner dashboard that shared-hosting-style providers offer — you're provisioning a VPS and are expected to install and manage your own web server stack (or use a marketplace image).

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — always confirm the live checkout price before buying.

| Plan | vCPU | RAM | Storage | Transfer | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lighthouse entry | 1 | 1 GB | 50 GB SSD | 1 TB/month | ~$4/month |
| Lighthouse mid-tier | 2 | 2 GB | 80 GB SSD | 1.5 TB/month | ~$7.50/month |
| CVM (trial config) | 2 | 4 GB | — | — | Free for 3 months (trial only) |

Tencent runs frequent promotional pricing for new sign-ups — Lighthouse has been advertised as low as roughly $1.68/month for an initial short term in past promotions — so the number you see at checkout may be lower than the standard rate above. Treat any promo price as a first-term rate, not the ongoing cost.

## Real cost breakdown

Lighthouse is sold as fixed-term prepaid billing (monthly, semi-annual or annual), not hourly, which is a meaningful difference from DigitalOcean or Vultr where you can spin an instance up and tear it down within the hour and pay only for that usage. If you commit to a longer prepaid term to unlock a lower per-month rate, you're locking in that spend upfront rather than paying as you go.

New accounts get a 3-month free trial on both CVM (2 vCPU/4GB configuration) and Lighthouse (2 vCPU/2GB), available once per account and not open to anyone who has previously purchased either product. After the trial period, or once the promotional first term on a paid plan ends, billing reverts to the plan's standard published rate — budget for that renewal rather than assuming the entry price holds indefinitely.

Signing up for an international Tencent Cloud account requires real-name identity verification before some services, including CVM and Lighthouse, will activate. Build that into your setup timeline if you're trying this for the first time — it isn't instant self-serve the way spinning up a Vultr or DigitalOcean droplet is.

## Which plan should you choose

**Choose the Lighthouse entry tier (1 vCPU/1GB)** if you're hosting a single small site, blog, or a lightweight app and want the lowest committed monthly cost.

**Choose the Lighthouse mid-tier (2 vCPU/2GB)** if you're running a small WordPress or CMS site with moderate traffic, or need more headroom than the entry tier's 1GB of RAM comfortably allows.

**Use the CVM free trial** if you want to evaluate Tencent's more configurable general-purpose VPS product before committing spend, or if your workload needs custom networking/security-group configuration that Lighthouse's simplified console doesn't expose.

**Look elsewhere** if your traffic is primarily outside China and you want hourly billing, a large English-language community, or a one-click app marketplace — DigitalOcean and Vultr are more common defaults for that profile.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Low entry price for a functional Linux VPS | Fixed-term prepaid billing only — no hourly pay-as-you-go on Lighthouse |
| Strong latency and CDN reach for China-based traffic | Real-name verification required before some services activate |
| 3-month free trial available for new accounts on both CVM and Lighthouse | Thinner English-language documentation and support compared to AWS/DigitalOcean/Vultr |
| Frequent promotional first-term pricing | No cPanel or one-click WordPress installer bundled by default |

## Support

Tencent Cloud's support for international accounts is ticket-based through the console, with documentation split across English and Chinese-language resources — the Chinese-language docs and community are considerably more extensive. There's no live-chat-first support model comparable to what beginner-oriented hosts like Hostinger offer; expect a more self-managed, developer-oriented support experience.

## Migration

Moving an existing site onto Lighthouse or CVM means manually migrating your web server stack, database and files onto the new VPS yourself (or using a snapshot/image if migrating from another Tencent Cloud instance) — there's no automated one-click site-migration tool comparable to what some managed shared hosts provide. Budget time for a manual migration, or hire out the setup, if you're not comfortable administering a Linux server.

## Where it's a strong fit

Tencent Cloud's Lighthouse and CVM make sense if your site's audience is concentrated in mainland China and you want infrastructure physically close to that traffic, or if you're a developer who's comfortable managing a bare VPS and wants a low entry price to experiment with.

## Where to think twice

This is not a beginner-friendly, install-and-forget hosting product. If you want a control panel, one-click WordPress, live chat support, or hourly billing flexibility, Tencent Cloud's hosting-relevant products aren't built around that experience — mainstream VPS providers like DigitalOcean or Vultr, or beginner shared hosts, are a better starting point.

## Verdict

Scoped strictly to website hosting, Tencent Cloud's Lighthouse is a legitimate, inexpensive VPS option — particularly for China-facing sites — but it asks more technical comfort from the buyer than shared-hosting-style competitors, ties you into prepaid terms rather than hourly billing, and requires identity verification most international VPS providers skip. It's worth a look for developers already inside the Tencent ecosystem or targeting Chinese audiences; it's not the first stop for someone who wants a simple, beginner-friendly website host.

## FAQs

**Does Tencent Cloud offer shared hosting with cPanel?**
No — CVM and Lighthouse are both VPS products. You manage your own server stack (or use a pre-built marketplace image); there's no bundled cPanel or beginner control panel.

**Is there a free trial?**
Yes — new accounts get a 3-month free trial on both CVM (2 vCPU/4GB) and Lighthouse (2 vCPU/2GB), limited to one trial per account and unavailable to anyone who has previously purchased either product.

**How much does Tencent Cloud Lighthouse cost?**
The entry Lighthouse tier runs around $4/month for 1 vCPU, 1GB RAM, 50GB SSD and 1TB of monthly transfer at standard pricing; promotional first-term pricing has been advertised lower. Confirm the live checkout rate, since promos and renewal pricing differ.

**Is billing hourly or prepaid?**
Lighthouse is billed on fixed prepaid terms (monthly, semi-annual, annual) rather than hourly. CVM's general pricing can vary by billing mode and region — check the live pricing calculator for your specific configuration.

**Do I need ID verification to sign up?**
Yes — Tencent Cloud requires real-name identity verification before some services, including CVM and Lighthouse, will activate on an account.

**Is Tencent Cloud good for hosting a site outside China?**
It can work, but its infrastructure and support are optimized for the Chinese market. If your traffic is mostly outside China, providers with a larger international footprint and hourly billing, like DigitalOcean or Vultr, are usually a simpler fit.

**Does Tencent Cloud help migrate my existing site?**
Not with an automated one-click tool for hosting-style migrations. You'll manually move your files, database and server configuration onto the new VPS, or use a snapshot/image if migrating between Tencent Cloud instances.

**Is Tencent Cloud beginner-friendly?**
Not particularly. Both CVM and Lighthouse assume basic comfort managing a Linux VPS — there's no simplified beginner dashboard, and support leans self-service compared to consumer-focused hosts.

Compare current pricing and check for active promotions on the [Tencent Cloud coupon page](/coupons/tencentcloud), or browse more options on our [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) page.

title: TMDHosting Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: TMDHosting review covering WordPress plan pricing, renewal rates, LiteSpeed performance, support quality, and whether managed cPanel hosting is worth it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is TMDHosting worth it in 2026?

TMDHosting is a solid pick if you want managed cPanel hosting with LiteSpeed-driven speed and support you can reach by phone or chat at any hour. It's not the cheapest host at renewal, and independent reviewers flag inconsistent performance and support outside its core WordPress product, so it fits best for site owners who'll actually use its managed features rather than bargain-hunters chasing the lowest possible bill.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $9.99/mo (Starter, 3-year term) |
| Renewal price | $12.49/mo (Starter) |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days |
| Control panel | cPanel |
| Best for | WordPress sites wanting managed features + real support |

## What TMDHosting actually is

TMDHosting is a managed hosting provider built around cPanel for Linux and Plesk for Windows, running out of nine data centers spread across five continents. Its lineup covers shared/WordPress hosting, managed VPS, and managed dedicated servers, all layered with LiteSpeed Web Server instead of stock Apache — LiteSpeed is the main reason TMDHosting can plausibly claim faster page loads than budget hosts running unoptimized stacks. The company positions itself specifically around WordPress: staging environments, automatic core/plugin handling, and daily backups come baked into every WordPress tier rather than sold as upsells.

## Pricing by plan

TMDHosting's WordPress hosting line has three tiers, all billed on a 3-year term to unlock the lowest advertised rate:

| Plan | Intro price | Renewal price | Storage | Sites |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | $9.99/mo | $12.49/mo | 50GB SSD | 1 |
| Business | $13.03/mo | $16.29/mo | 100GB SSD | Unlimited |
| Enterprise | $19.99/mo | $24.99/mo | Unlimited SSD | Unlimited |

All three include free SSL, a free domain for the first term, unlimited MariaDB databases, 1-click staging, and 30 rolling backup copies. Business steps up to double the CPU/RAM allocation over Starter, and Enterprise quadruples it. Managed VPS hosting sits in a separate line starting from roughly $49.99/month for customers who outgrow shared resources entirely.

Pricing above was accurate as of September 2026 and is subject to change — always confirm current rates at checkout.

## The real cost: intro vs. renewal

The advertised price only applies to your first term, and only if you prepay three years upfront. Starter's $9.99/month intro rate renews at $12.49/month — about a 25% increase. Business goes from $13.03 to $16.29/month, and Enterprise from $19.99 to $24.99/month. Those are the same roughly-25% jumps across every tier, so the discount structure is consistent even if the sticker shock at renewal isn't.

If you don't want to commit three years upfront, shorter terms (monthly, annual, biennial) are available but at meaningfully higher effective rates than the triennial price shown above — the headline price you see on TMDHosting's homepage assumes the longest commitment.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **Starter** if you're launching a single WordPress site and don't need more than 50GB of storage — it covers a typical blog, portfolio, or small business site comfortably.

Choose **Business** if you're running more than one WordPress site, or if daily backup depth and double the performance headroom matter to you — it's TMDHosting's own recommended default, and the unlimited-sites allowance means you can host client work or side projects on the same plan.

Choose **Enterprise** if you're running a higher-traffic site, an online store, or several resource-hungry WordPress installs and want the largest CPU/RAM allocation TMDHosting offers on shared infrastructure before stepping up to VPS.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| LiteSpeed on every plan for faster page loads | Lowest price requires a 3-year prepay |
| 24/7 support with live chat and phone | Renewal prices run about 25% above intro |
| Unlimited MariaDB databases, 30 backup copies | Third-party reviews cite inconsistent performance outside core plans |
| 1-click staging included at every tier | Database size limits despite "unlimited" storage claims on paper |
| Nine global data centers | Support quality reported as uneven by some independent reviewers |

## Support

TMDHosting advertises 24/7/365 support staffed by what it calls "real human support" rather than a bot-first queue, reachable via live chat, ticket, and phone. Independent reviews are mixed here — several report fast first-response times, while others note follow-through on complex tickets can be inconsistent. For a straightforward WordPress setup or routine troubleshooting, the support experience is generally solid; for a harder infrastructure problem, expect variability.

## Migration

Every managed plan includes free site migration assistance from your current host, handled by TMDHosting's team rather than left to a self-service plugin. This matters most for WordPress sites with custom configurations, multiple databases, or non-standard file structures that automated migration tools tend to mishandle.

## Where it's a strong fit

TMDHosting works well for WordPress-focused site owners who want managed backups, staging, and LiteSpeed performance without configuring any of it themselves, and who'll actually call or chat support when something breaks rather than never using it. Agencies managing a handful of client sites on the Business tier get real value from the unlimited-sites allowance.

## Where to think twice

If you're price-sensitive and unwilling to prepay three years, the effective monthly cost climbs fast on shorter terms. And if independent, consistent performance under heavy traffic is your top priority, cross-check current benchmarks before committing — third-party reviewers have flagged variability that a promotional page won't mention.

## Verdict

title: UpCloud Review 2026: Pricing, MaxIOPS Speed and Verdict
excerpt: UpCloud review covering MaxIOPS storage performance, $5/month pricing, hourly billing, data centers and who this developer-focused cloud VPS actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is UpCloud a good choice for hosting?

UpCloud is a solid pick if you're comfortable managing your own server — it's a Finnish cloud VPS provider with genuinely fast MaxIOPS all-flash storage and data centers across Europe, the Americas and Asia-Pacific, but there's no bundled control panel, so it suits developers more than beginners wanting one-click WordPress.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $5/month (Developer, 1 vCPU / 1GB RAM / 25GB MaxIOPS) |
| Billing model | Hourly, capped at the monthly rate |
| Control panel | None bundled — web console, API, CLI, Terraform |
| Trial | Free trial period on signup (check current terms) |
| Best for | Developers, self-managed apps, agencies needing fast disk I/O |

## What UpCloud actually is

UpCloud is a cloud infrastructure company based in Helsinki, Finland. It sells cloud servers (VPS instances), managed databases, object storage and Kubernetes — the kind of building blocks a developer assembles into a stack, not a pre-packaged "website hosting" product. There's no cPanel, no hPanel, no one-click app installer bolted on by default. You spin up a server, then configure it yourself through UpCloud's web console, its CLI, the official API, or a Terraform provider if you're managing infrastructure as code.

That positioning matters for anyone comparing it to a typical shared-hosting company. If you want to upload a WordPress theme and be done in ten minutes, UpCloud is the wrong tool. If you're deploying a Node app, running a database cluster, or self-hosting something that needs predictable, fast disk performance, it's built for exactly that.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — always confirm current rates on UpCloud's own pricing page before buying.

| Plan | vCPU | RAM | Storage | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Developer | 1 | 1GB | 25GB MaxIOPS | $5/month |
| Starter (budget line) | 1-4 | 1-16GB | Standard SSD | from ~€3/month |
| Higher cloud server tiers | scales up | scales up | MaxIOPS | scales with resources |

The $5/month Developer plan is UpCloud's entry point into its flagship MaxIOPS storage tier — the all-flash, clustered storage architecture the company markets around ~100,000 read IOPS, several times what a typical budget-VPS SSD delivers. A separate, cheaper Starter line exists at around €3/month, but it runs on standard SSD storage and older-generation CPUs rather than MaxIOPS, so the storage-speed pitch UpCloud is known for specifically applies to the MaxIOPS tier, not the absolute lowest price on the site.

## Real cost breakdown

UpCloud doesn't use the "cheap intro price that jumps at renewal" model common among shared hosts. Instead, billing is hourly and usage-based, capped at the advertised monthly rate — so a server you spin up for a few days of testing costs a fraction of the monthly price, and a server left running all month costs no more than the number on the pricing page. There's no long prepaid term required to unlock the listed price, and no separate renewal-rate shock to budget around. That said, extras like additional storage, backups, extra IP addresses, managed databases and higher bandwidth tiers are billed separately on top of the base server price, so a real production setup usually costs more than the bare $5/month headline figure.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose the Developer plan ($5/month, 1 vCPU/1GB RAM) if you're testing UpCloud, running a small personal project, or hosting a lightweight app or API that doesn't need much memory.

Choose a mid-tier cloud server (2-4 vCPU, 4-8GB RAM) if you're running a production app, a database-backed site, or anything where MaxIOPS's disk-throughput advantage actually shows up under real traffic.

Choose the Starter line only if MaxIOPS performance isn't a priority and you just want the lowest possible entry price on standard SSD storage — otherwise the Developer plan is the more representative "real UpCloud" starting point.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| MaxIOPS all-flash storage with strong measured read performance | No bundled control panel — self-managed only |
| Hourly billing capped at the monthly rate, no long prepaid lock-in | Not beginner-friendly for simple website hosting |
| Wide data center footprint across Europe, Americas and APAC | Trustpilot reviews are polarized — some report support friction |
| Modern API, CLI and Terraform support for infrastructure-as-code workflows | Add-ons (backups, extra storage, bandwidth) priced separately |

## Support

UpCloud offers support through a ticketing system and documentation/knowledge base covering server setup, networking and the API. Response depth tends to favor technical, infrastructure-level questions rather than beginner "how do I install WordPress" hand-holding — consistent with its developer-first positioning. Community reviews are mixed: UpCloud's own averages show a fairly polarized split between very satisfied and very dissatisfied customers, so it's worth reading recent reviews for your specific use case (e.g. billing disputes vs. technical support quality) before committing a production workload.

## Migration

Moving an existing site or app to UpCloud is a manual process — there's no automated one-click migration tool bundled in for shared-hosting-style sites. In practice this means provisioning a new cloud server, installing your stack (web server, database, runtime) yourself or via a template/Terraform script, then migrating data and DNS over once it's verified working. UpCloud does support standard tooling — SSH access, snapshots, and API-driven provisioning — that make scripted migrations straightforward for anyone comfortable with server administration, but it's not a drag-and-drop transfer for non-technical users.

## Where it's a strong fit

UpCloud makes sense for developers and small teams who want raw cloud server performance without paying enterprise cloud pricing, for workloads that are genuinely disk-I/O sensitive (databases, search indexes, high-write applications), and for anyone who wants hourly billing instead of committing to a long prepaid hosting term.

## Where to think twice

If you want a beginner-friendly experience with a graphical control panel, one-click app installs, or bundled email hosting, UpCloud isn't built for that — you'll be doing the server administration yourself. The mixed Trustpilot record is also worth weighing if you're risk-averse about support responsiveness.

## Verdict

UpCloud earns its reputation as a fast, developer-oriented cloud VPS provider — MaxIOPS storage is a real, verifiable performance advantage at the $5/month entry tier, and hourly billing removes the renewal-shock problem that plagues budget shared hosting. It's not for everyone: skip it if you want a managed, beginner-friendly hosting panel, but if you're comfortable configuring your own stack and want fast storage without a long-term commitment, it's a reasonable pick worth comparing against other developer-focused VPS providers.

## FAQs

### Does UpCloud include a control panel?

No. UpCloud doesn't bundle cPanel, hPanel or any similar dashboard by default — server management happens through UpCloud's own web console, CLI, API or Terraform provider. You install and manage your own software stack.

### How much does UpCloud cost to start?

The entry-level Developer cloud server starts at $5/month for 1 vCPU, 1GB RAM and 25GB of MaxIOPS storage. A cheaper Starter line exists from around €3/month but runs on standard SSD rather than MaxIOPS.

### Is UpCloud billed monthly or hourly?

Both — pricing is calculated hourly and capped at the monthly rate, so you only pay for the time a server actually runs, up to the listed monthly maximum.

### What is MaxIOPS?

MaxIOPS is UpCloud's proprietary all-flash, clustered storage technology, marketed around roughly 100,000 read IOPS — meaningfully faster than standard cloud SSD storage on many competing budget VPS platforms.

### Does UpCloud offer a free trial?

Yes, new accounts can typically try UpCloud through a free trial period before paying — check the current trial length and any credit amount on UpCloud's signup page, since trial terms are adjusted from time to time.

### Where are UpCloud's data centers located?

UpCloud operates data centers across Europe (including Helsinki, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, London, Stockholm, Copenhagen, Madrid, Warsaw and Stavanger), the Americas (Chicago, New York, San Jose) and Asia-Pacific (Singapore, Sydney).

### Is UpCloud good for beginners?

Not particularly. UpCloud is aimed at developers and technical users who are comfortable configuring a server themselves. Beginners wanting a simple, panel-driven website host will likely find a shared-hosting provider with a bundled control panel easier to start with.

### How is UpCloud rated on Trustpilot?

UpCloud holds a 3.0-out-of-5 average on Trustpilot from around 169 reviews, with a notably polarized split between very positive and very negative reviews rather than a broad middle ground.

Check current pricing and any active offers on the [UpCloud coupon page](/coupons/upcloud), or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting).

title: Veeble Hosting Review 2026: Pricing, Plans and Verdict

author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Veeble a good web host?

Veeble is a small cPanel hosting provider with LiteSpeed-powered shared, reseller and VPS plans, notable for owning data center capacity in the US, UK, Germany, the Netherlands and India. It's a reasonable pick if you specifically need an India-region data center or want a renewal-price-lock promise, but it lacks the track record and third-party benchmark coverage of bigger-name hosts — verify current terms directly before committing.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | ~₹95/mo (LaunchPad, 1-year term) / ~$1.90–$4.95/mo on global listings |
| **Renewal price** | Veeble advertises a price-lock — renewal rate matches signup rate |
| **Uptime guarantee** | 99.9% SLA with financial compensation |
| **Money-back guarantee** | 14-day window (per third-party reviews; confirm on Veeble's terms page) |
| **Control panel** | cPanel with LiteSpeed |
| **Best for** | Budget cPanel hosting, India-region sites, reseller/VPS needs |

## What Veeble actually is

Veeble Hosting is a smaller, independently run hosting company rather than one of the handful of brands that dominate hosting-comparison articles. It runs cPanel-based shared and reseller hosting, managed and unmanaged VPS, Windows hosting, and dedicated servers, and markets itself around owning or co-locating in Tier IV data center facilities across the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands and India.

That India data center is the detail that sets Veeble apart from most budget hosts covered on comparison sites — most of the well-known low-cost providers concentrate data centers in North America and Europe, so a site owner specifically targeting Indian visitors may see a real latency benefit here that a US-only host can't match.

Because Veeble is a smaller brand, independent long-term uptime tracking, security-incident history and support-response benchmarking are thinner than for hosts with millions of customers. That's not necessarily disqualifying, but it does mean more of the decision rests on the provider's own claims and a smaller pool of user reviews than usual.

## Pricing

Veeble's India-facing cPanel shared hosting runs three tiers — LaunchPad, ScaleUP and ProMaster — priced in INR and billed monthly, yearly or on a 3-year promotional term. Global listings elsewhere have cited USD pricing in roughly the $1.90–$4.95/month range for entry shared plans, so check the pricing page for your billing region before comparing.

| Plan | Monthly | 1-Year | 3-Year (promo) | Websites | Storage | Email | Databases |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LaunchPad | ₹145/mo | ₹95/mo | ₹65/mo | 1 | 20GB NVMe | 5 | 2 |
| ScaleUP | ₹295/mo | ₹195/mo | ₹125/mo | 10 | 50GB NVMe | 20 | 20 |
| ProMaster | ₹595/mo | ₹395/mo | ₹195/mo | 100 | 150GB NVMe | Unlimited | Unlimited |

All three tiers include unlimited bandwidth, a free Let's Encrypt SSL certificate, LiteSpeed + CDN, free site migration, a drag-and-drop builder, free malware scanning, and the Softaculous one-click installer (400+ apps, including WordPress). Only ProMaster includes SSH/terminal access.

Pricing was accurate as of this article's publish date and is subject to change — always confirm current rates and currency on Veeble's own pricing page before buying.

## The real cost breakdown

The lowest advertised rates require the longest prepaid term — the ₹65/mo LaunchPad figure is explicitly a 3-year promotional rate, not what you'd pay month to month. Sign up monthly instead and LaunchPad costs more than double that per month.

Where Veeble differs from many budget hosts is its stated renewal-price-lock: the company claims the price you sign up at is the price you renew at, rather than the common industry pattern of a steep jump after year one. If accurate, that changes the math significantly in Veeble's favor for long-term cost compared with hosts that discount hard up front and raise prices sharply on renewal — but confirm this in writing at checkout, since promotional claims and actual renewal invoices don't always match everywhere.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **LaunchPad** if you're launching a single small site — a blog, portfolio or brochure site — and don't need more than 5 email accounts or 2 databases.

Choose **ScaleUP** if you're running multiple sites (up to 10) or need more headroom on storage, email and databases without paying for the unlimited tier.

Choose **ProMaster** if you manage many sites (agencies, freelancers hosting client work) or specifically need SSH/terminal access, which is withheld on the two lower tiers.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| India data center — useful for India-targeted sites | Small brand — thinner independent track record than major hosts |
| LiteSpeed + NVMe storage on all tiers | SSH only available on the top plan |
| Renewal price-lock claim (verify at checkout) | Lowest headline prices require long prepaid terms |
| Free SSL, CDN, migration and malware scanning included | Money-back guarantee window (14 days) is shorter than the 30-day standard some competitors offer |

## Support

Veeble advertises 24/7 support with WhatsApp access to what it calls Level 3 certified technicians, alongside the standard ticket system. As with any smaller host, actual response-time consistency is harder to verify independently than with hosts that have thousands of public support reviews — Trustpilot feedback (rated "Great," 4.2/5 from 137 reviews as of this writing) is a reasonable secondary signal, but read recent reviews directly for the latest sentiment.

## Migration

Veeble includes free website migration on its shared hosting plans, per its own marketing. As with most hosts offering "free migration," expect this to cover a standard cPanel-to-cPanel move (files, databases, email) with more complex setups — custom server configurations, non-cPanel sources — potentially needing extra coordination. Confirm scope and turnaround with support before initiating a migration on a live production site.

## Where Veeble is a strong fit

- You specifically want a hosting data center located in India for latency reasons.
- You want cPanel with LiteSpeed and NVMe storage at a lower price point than the biggest-name hosts.
- The renewal price-lock model appeals to you over hosts that hike prices sharply after an intro term.
- You need reseller or VPS options from the same provider as you scale.

## Where to think twice

- You want a host with an extensive independent review and benchmark history — Veeble's public track record is comparatively thin.
- You need SSH access on an entry-level plan — it's restricted to ProMaster here.
- You want a longer money-back guarantee window than the reported 14 days.
- You're not targeting an India-region audience and the data center advantage doesn't apply to you.

## The bottom line

Veeble is a workable budget cPanel host with a genuinely differentiated feature — an India data center most comparably priced Western hosts don't offer — plus a renewal price-lock claim worth verifying at checkout. It's a sensible shortlist candidate for India-targeted or budget-conscious cPanel hosting, but its smaller footprint means doing a bit more of your own due diligence (reading recent reviews, confirming guarantee terms directly) than you would with a larger, more heavily reviewed host.

## FAQs

**Does Veeble use cPanel?**
Yes — Veeble's shared and reseller hosting plans run on cPanel with LiteSpeed web servers, plus Softaculous for one-click app installs.

**Where are Veeble's data centers located?**
Veeble states it owns or co-locates in data centers in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands and India.

**Does Veeble offer a money-back guarantee?**
Third-party reviews report a 14-day money-back guarantee on hosting plans. Confirm the exact terms and any exclusions on Veeble's own policy page before purchasing.

**Is Veeble's advertised price the price I'll always pay?**
Veeble states its renewal price matches the signup price, unlike hosts that raise rates sharply after an intro term — but the lowest headline rates require the longest prepaid commitment (e.g. 3 years), so confirm the exact monthly-term price if you don't want to prepay that far out.

**Does Veeble include a free domain?**
This wasn't confirmed as a standard inclusion across plans in the sources checked for this review — verify current plan inclusions on Veeble's pricing page.

**Does Veeble offer SSH access?**
Only on the ProMaster shared hosting tier; LaunchPad and ScaleUP don't include it.

**How does Veeble compare to bigger hosting brands?**
Veeble is considerably smaller than brands like Hostinger, with a thinner public track record of reviews and independent benchmarks, but it offers a differentiated India data center and NVMe/LiteSpeed performance at a competitive price point.

**Is Veeble good for a WordPress site?**
Yes, via the Softaculous one-click installer on any shared hosting tier — though dedicated managed WordPress hosting elsewhere may offer more WordPress-specific tooling if that's a priority.

Compare current offers on the [Veeble coupon page](/coupons/veeble), or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) to see how Veeble stacks up against other providers.

title: WebHostingPad Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict

body:
## Is WebHostingPad a good choice for hosting?

WebHostingPad is a budget US shared host with unlimited storage, a free domain and SSL, and a 30-day money-back guarantee. It's a reasonable pick for a small personal or brochure site on a tight budget, but its default control panel isn't cPanel, and cPanel costs an extra $1/month if you specifically need it.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $3.99/mo (1-year term, Power Plan) |
| Renewal price | $6.49/mo (1-year term) |
| Storage | Unlimited hosting space |
| Control panel | Custom/DirectAdmin-based by default; cPanel +$1/mo |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days (new accounts, excludes renewals/add-ons) |
| Best for | Small budget sites, beginners not tied to cPanel |

## What WebHostingPad actually is

WebHostingPad is a US-based shared hosting company that's been selling budget cPanel-era hosting for years, built around low entry-level pricing and unlimited hosting space on its core plans. It targets small businesses, bloggers and beginners who want a cheap way to get a WordPress or basic site online without committing to a bigger managed-hosting bill.

The lineup is straightforward: the entry Power Plan, Power Plan Plus (adds WordPress optimization and priority support), a set of Power Plan Plus + WordPress bundles (Basic, Pro, Premium) with progressively more managed WordPress tooling, and a separate low-cost Power Plan Mini that locks in a flat rate instead of escalating at renewal. All the main plans bundle unlimited bandwidth, email accounts and databases along with a free domain for the first year and a free SSL certificate.

## Pricing (1-year term)

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — always confirm current rates on WebHostingPad's own pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Intro price | Renewal price | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Power Plan | $3.99/mo | $6.49/mo | Unlimited storage, free domain + SSL |
| Power Plan Plus + WordPress Basic | $4.99/mo | $7.99/mo | Adds WordPress optimization |
| Power Plan Plus + WordPress Pro | $5.99/mo | $8.99/mo | More WordPress tooling |
| Power Plan Plus + WordPress Premium | $7.99/mo | $9.99/mo | Top managed-WordPress tier |
| Power Plan Mini | $3.50/mo | $3.50/mo | Flat rate, doesn't increase at renewal |

Longer prepaid terms (3-5 years) push the effective monthly rate lower still — WebHostingPad's site has quoted the Power Plan Plus around $2.99/mo on a 3-year term and the base Power Plan near $1.99/mo on a 5-year term — but that requires paying for the whole term upfront.

## The real cost breakdown

The headline numbers only tell part of the story. On the standard 1-year term, the Power Plan is billed at $3.99/month up front, then renews at $6.49/month once that first year ends — a meaningful jump, though smaller in dollar terms than some competitors' renewal cliffs since the base plan is already cheap. The Power Plan Mini avoids this entirely by fixing the rate for the life of the account, which is worth considering if a predictable bill matters more than the lowest possible entry price.

One cost that's easy to miss: WebHostingPad's default control panel isn't cPanel. Accessing cPanel specifically costs an additional $1/month on top of whatever plan you choose. If you're migrating a site built around cPanel-specific tools or a developer workflow that expects it, budget for that add-on or confirm the default panel covers what you need.

The 30-day money-back guarantee also has real exclusions worth reading before you buy: refunds don't cover renewal payments, add-on services (including that cPanel upgrade), or domain registration fees, and the guarantee is limited to new accounts that haven't broken WebHostingPad's Terms of Service.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose the **Power Plan** if you're launching one small site and want the lowest entry price with unlimited storage.

Choose **Power Plan Plus + WordPress Basic** if you're running a WordPress site and want the optimization and priority support bundled in without paying for the higher WordPress tiers.

Choose **Power Plan Plus + WordPress Pro or Premium** if you need more headroom for a busier WordPress install and don't mind the higher monthly cost.

Choose the **Power Plan Mini** if a flat, non-increasing rate matters more to you than the lowest possible starting price.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Unlimited storage on main plans | cPanel isn't the default panel — costs $1/mo extra |
| Free domain (year one) and free SSL | Renewal prices are noticeably higher than intro pricing |
| Flat-rate Mini plan avoids renewal shock | Refund guarantee excludes renewals, add-ons and domains |
| Low headline entry price | Longer prepaid terms needed for the cheapest rates |

## Support

WebHostingPad's Power Plan Plus and WordPress-bundle tiers include priority support on top of standard channels. As with most budget hosts, expect ticket- and chat-based support rather than phone-first service on the entry-level plan — check WebHostingPad's own site for current support hours and channels before signing up if that's a deciding factor.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to WebHostingPad follows the usual shared-hosting pattern: export your current site's files and database, then import them through whichever control panel your plan uses. Because the default panel isn't cPanel, confirm ahead of time whether your current host's export tools and your migration plugins (many WordPress migration plugins assume cPanel-style hosting) will work smoothly, or budget for the cPanel add-on to simplify the move.

## Where it's a strong fit

WebHostingPad works well for a single small site, a personal blog, or a brochure-style business site where the owner mainly wants a cheap way to get online and isn't attached to a specific control panel. The unlimited storage and free domain/SSL bundle cover the basics without extra shopping.

## Where to think twice

If cPanel specifically is a requirement — because of existing scripts, a developer's workflow, or migration tooling built around it — the $1/month add-on and the fact that it isn't the default panel are worth weighing against hosts that include cPanel standard. Sites expecting to scale past a single small install may also outgrow shared hosting's shared-resource limits regardless of host.

## Verdict

WebHostingPad is a reasonable budget option for a small site: unlimited storage, a free domain and SSL, and a fixed-rate Mini plan for anyone who wants to dodge renewal-price jumps. The catch is that its control panel setup isn't cPanel by default, which matters if you have workflows or migration tools built around it — check that detail before signing up, and read the money-back guarantee's exclusions so there are no surprises if you need a refund.

## FAQs

**Does WebHostingPad use cPanel?**
Not by default. WebHostingPad's standard control panel isn't cPanel — cPanel access is available as an add-on for an extra $1/month. Confirm which panel a plan ships with before you buy if this matters to your workflow.

**What does WebHostingPad's hosting actually cost after the first term?**
On a 1-year term, the Power Plan starts at $3.99/month and renews at $6.49/month. The Power Plan Mini is the exception — its rate is fixed and doesn't increase at renewal.

**Does WebHostingPad offer a free domain?**
Yes, WebHostingPad's main plans include a free domain for the first year, plus a free SSL certificate.

**Is there a money-back guarantee?**
Yes — a 30-day money-back guarantee on new accounts. It excludes renewal payments, add-on services like the cPanel upgrade, and domain registration fees.

**Is WebHostingPad good for WordPress?**
WebHostingPad sells several Power Plan Plus + WordPress bundles (Basic, Pro, Premium) with progressively more WordPress-specific optimization, which cover basic to moderately busy WordPress sites.

**How much storage do WebHostingPad plans include?**
The main Power Plan tiers advertise unlimited hosting space, along with unlimited bandwidth, email accounts and databases.

**Can I migrate an existing site to WebHostingPad?**
Yes, through the standard control panel import/export process. Since the default panel isn't cPanel, check that your current export tools or migration plugins are compatible, or add the cPanel upgrade to simplify the move.

**Is WebHostingPad better than the cheapest long-term plans from bigger hosts?**
It depends on what you value — WebHostingPad's Mini plan trades a slightly higher starting price for a flat rate with no renewal jump, while providers with long promotional terms often have lower intro prices but steeper renewals. Compare the full first-term cost and renewal rate, not just the advertised monthly figure, against the [WebHostingPad coupon page](/coupons/webhostingpad) and other [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) before deciding.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **Starter** if you're launching a single small site on a tight budget and don't need much storage headroom.

Choose **Standard** if you're running one active site — a blog, a small business page — and want more storage or bandwidth room to grow into without a hard cap.

Choose **Professional** if you're managing multiple sites (ZNetLive advertises up to 15 on this tier) and want to consolidate hosting for several projects under one account rather than paying for separate plans.
